BBC Radio 2 presenter Jo Whiley has received an outpouring of support following the death of her "lovely" father, whom she described as "the kindest man".

The 61-year-old broadcaster had previously revealed on her Dig It podcast that her father, Martin, had been diagnosed with Parkinson’s disease, a condition she found "heartbreaking".

According to the NHS, Parkinson's is a progressive neurological condition where parts of the brain become damaged over many years, affecting movement, as well as bodily and mental functions.

Whiley announced her father’s passing on Instagram on Tuesday night, sharing a series of photos and videos of them together throughout the years.

open image in gallery Jo Whiley and her dad Martin ( Instagram )

She wrote: “My lovely Dad died today. He was the kindest man, who lived solely to make others happy.

“He was supremely selfless and loved nothing more than caring for others and making people laugh.”

The broadcaster said she has received “so many messages today” praising her father and describing him as “a character” – which she said “sums him up completely”.

Whiley added: “I have Dad to thank for my love of music – he used to walk around the building site where he worked as an electrician with a huge ghetto blaster – the OG DJ and his passion for music never went away.

“His love for Elbow, Coldplay and Dido was unrivalled.”

open image in gallery Jo Whiley gave a 'heartbreaking' update on her father's Parkinson's disease recently. ( Dig It )

The TV and radio star, who was born in Northampton, recounted how her father’s childhood was “as sad as it gets”, saying he was “sent alone to a sanatorium in London for two years” after being diagnosed with tuberculosis.

Whiley added: “(This) is why we’re all Spurs fans!”

The broadcaster also explained that her father had “no parents” from a young age, and was raised by a family friend, adding: “Meeting my mum meant that dad got a family of his own and finally got to experience love.

“Knowing how it felt not to be cared for, he devoted his life to caring for others.”

Whiley, whose younger sister Frances has cri du chat syndrome, a genetic disorder that can cause significant learning disabilities, wrote: “Being the father of someone with learning disabilities (LD) in the 70s meant that life has had its challenges.

open image in gallery Jo Whiley said her father ‘devoted his life to caring for others.’ ( Instagram )

“But Dad has been such a force for good in the LD world simply by embracing and loving everyone with a difference.

“He may have had the saddest childhood but he triumphed by giving me, Frances, and his grandchildren the happiest childhoods anyone could have dreamt of.”

“He was the greatest Dad and he was everybody’s favourite Grandad, but especially to India, Jude, Cass and Coco who adored him,” she added, referring to her four children.

The DJ also wrote a message from her sister at the end of the post, in which she described their father as a “legend” who the family will “miss so very much”.

open image in gallery The broadcaster also explained that her father had “no parents” from a young age, and was raised by a family friend. ( Getty )

Friends fans and fellow stars expressed their condolences, with award-winning screenwriter and TV producer Russell T Davies, best known for reviving Doctor Who, writing: “The OG DJ. So sorry, love to you and the family. Take care.”

“Oh Jo – so so sorry for your loss – sending love,” broadcaster Kate Garraway wrote.

Celebrity chef Jamie Oliver said: “Bless you Jo I’m so sorry for the loss of your father, sending loads of love,” while image consultant and DJ Gok Wan, singer-songwriter KT Tunstall, actor Richard E Grant, TV hosts Gaby Roslin and Vanessa Feltz, and retired radio presenter Bob Harris also sent messages of support.

BBC Radio 2, where Whiley has worked for 15 years after leaving Radio 1, said: “Sending you and your family lots of love Jo.”

Three people have died in Venezuela from hantavirus infections, authorities confirmed on Tuesday, stressing there was no evidence of human-to-human transmission in the country.

Hantavirus was also suspected in the deaths of two health workers in the southwestern state of Barinas, the Health Ministry said, however these cases remain under investigation and were not linked to the three fatalities in the eastern state of Anzoátegui, some 655 kilometres away.

The deaths in Anzoátegui and Barinas were described by the ministry as isolated incidents that "do not represent a risk to the general community."

Nevertheless, it said health workers will be sent to the affected states to "guarantee the health security of all Venezuelans," without elaborating.

A national professional group, The Venezuelan Medical Federation, said the deaths in Anzoátegui were from the same family in the rural municipality of Miranda in the south of the state.

open image in gallery Three people died after being exposed to a rare hantavirus strain while on the MV Hondius cruise ( Getty )

It comes after three people died and 13 were infected after being exposed to a rare hantavirus strain, the Andes virus, while on the MV Hondius cruise.

What is hantavirus?

Hantavirus is mainly spread by contact with rodents or their urine, saliva or droppings, particularly when the material is disturbed and becomes airborne, posing a risk of inhalation.

People are typically exposed to hantavirus around their homes, cabins or sheds, especially when cleaning out enclosed spaces with little ventilation or going into areas where there are mouse droppings.

Hantavirus is “such a severe disease” there are global efforts to try and develop vaccines against it, according to Professor Robin May, chief scientific officer at the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA). The virus is widespread around the world.

“The Andean strain, is the only one for which there is some evidence in the past of human-to-human transmission,” he told BBC Breakfast.

The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention began tracking the virus after a 1993 outbreak in the Four Corners region – the area where Arizona, Colorado, New Mexico and Utah meet.

It was a doctor with the Indian Health Service who first noticed a pattern of deaths among young patients, said Michelle Harkins, a pulmonologist with the University of New Mexico Health Sciences Center who for years has been studying the disease and helping patients.

open image in gallery The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention began tracking the virus after a 1993 outbreak ( Reuters )

Most US cases are in Western states. New Mexico and Arizona are hotspots, Dr Harkins said, likely because the odds are greater for mouse-human encounters in rural areas.

Symptoms of hantavirus

An infection can rapidly progress and become life-threatening. Experts say it can start with symptoms that can include:

Fever

Chills

Muscle aches

Headache

“Early in the illness, you really may not be able to tell the difference between hantavirus and having the flu,” said Dr Sonja Bartolome of UT Southwestern Medical Center in Dallas.

Symptoms of hantavirus pulmonary syndrome usually show between one and eight weeks after contact with an infected rodent. As the infection progresses, patients might experience tightness in the chest as the lungs fill with fluid.

open image in gallery Hantavirus is mainly spread by contact with rodents or their urine, saliva or droppings ( AFP/Getty )

The other syndrome caused by hantavirus — haemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome — usually develops within a week or two after exposure.

Death rates vary depending on which hantavirus causes the illness. Hantavirus pulmonary syndrome is fatal in nearly 40 per cent of people infected, while the death rate for haemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome varies from 1 per cent to 15 per cent of patients, according to the CDC.

How to prevent hantavirus

There is no specific treatment or cure, but early medical attention can increase the chance of survival.

Despite years of research, Dr Harkins said many questions have yet to be answered, including why the illness can cause mild symptoms for some people and very severe symptoms for others. She and other researchers have been following patients over long periods of time in hopes of finding a treatment.

“A lot of mysteries,” she said, noting that what researchers do know is that rodent exposure is a key.

open image in gallery Health officials previously assured the public that there was no risk of a global outbreak following the MV Hondius cruise passengers’ disembarkation ( AFP/Getty )

The best way to avoid infection is to minimise contact with rodents and their droppings, and use protective gloves and a bleach solution for cleaning up rodent droppings.

Public health experts caution against sweeping or vacuuming, which can cause the virus to get into the air.

How is hantavirus different from Covid?

Unlike Covid, most hantaviruses do not spread between humans, although person-to-person transmission is possible.

Health officials previously assured the public that there was no risk of a global outbreak following the MV Hondius cruise passengers’ disembarkation.

The chief of the WHO, Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, said: “This is not another Covid. The current public health risk from hantavirus remains low. My colleagues and I have said this unequivocally, and I will say it again to you now.”

Rep. Andy Biggs, one of Donald Trump's closest allies in Congress and a leading figure in efforts to overturn the 2020 election, won Arizona's Republican gubernatorial primary Tuesday, setting up a high-stakes showdown with Democratic Gov. Katie Hobbs.

Biggs easily defeated fellow Rep. David Schweikert, who had warned that Biggs' hard-line conservatism could drive away the independent voters Republicans need to win in battleground Arizona. Democrats now hold both U.S. Senate seats and the state's top three elected offices.

Backed by Trump's endorsement and Turning Point Action, Biggs celebrated his victory by urging Republicans to "turn Arizona red again." He rejected claims he is too extreme.

open image in gallery Arizona Republican gubernatorial candidate U.S. Rep. Andy Biggs, left, shakes hands with a supporter at after being declared the winner in the primary ( AP )

"I am a conservative — and a principled conservative — but I work with people that don't necessarily agree with me on every issue," Biggs said.

Democrats are expected to make Biggs' role in Trump's failed effort to block certification of the 2020 election a central issue in the general election.

Hobbs, who narrowly defeated Republican Kari Lake in 2022, quickly went on the attack.

open image in gallery Arizona Governor Katie Hobbs speaks to volunteers participating in a phone bank during Arizona’s primary election in Phoenix ( Reuters )

"The more Arizonans learn about Biggs, the more they'll realize he's one big problem they can't afford," she said.

Elsewhere, former Arizona Cardinals kicker Jay Feely, another Trump-backed candidate, won the Republican nomination in the battleground 1st Congressional District.

On the Democratic side, emergency physician Amish Shah held a narrow lead over party-backed Marlene Galán-Woods, a result that could deal another blow to the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee after several establishment-backed candidates have lost primaries this year.

open image in gallery Former Arizona Cardinals kicker Jay Feely, another Trump-backed candidate, won the Republican nomination in the battleground 1st Congressional District ( Reuters )

"I wasn't exactly my party's pick," Shah said. "I was willing to stand up to that establishment."

In another closely watched race, state Rep. Alexander Kolodin won the Republican nomination for secretary of state despite being sanctioned by the Arizona State Bar over his role in baseless lawsuits challenging the 2020 election. He will face Democratic Secretary of State Adrian Fontes in November.

State Senate President Warren Petersen won the Republican nomination for attorney general and will challenge Democratic incumbent Kris Mayes, who won her last race by just 280 votes.

open image in gallery Charlie Kirk shaking hands with President Donald Trump as he speaks on stage at America Fest 2024 in Phoenix, Arizona ( AFP/Getty )

Trump-backed Pinal County Sheriff Mark Lamb also won the Republican nomination for the congressional seat Biggs is vacating. Lamb has denied allegations of sexual misconduct and abuse of power, calling them "slander and lies," and was not charged with a crime.

The results set up another fiercely contested election in one of the nation's most closely watched swing states, where control of key statewide offices and Congress will again be on the line.

News.title: Why Systems Thinking Is Becoming More Relevant in Construction
News.content:
The Independent was not involved in the creation of this sponsored content.

For an industry that delivers some of the most complex physical assets in the economy, construction still tends to make decisions in isolation.

Cost is assessed separately from the programme. Safety is treated as a compliance exercise rather than a design outcome. Environmental impact is often addressed after key decisions have already been made. And disruption to communities is accepted as an inevitable by-product of getting the job done.

Each of these considerations matters. But treated individually, they rarely lead to the best overall result. A more useful question may be how these factors interact, because in practice, project outcomes are often shaped not by a single optimised metric but by how cost, time, safety, embodied carbon, buildability and whole-life value are considered together, from the outset, as part of a joined-up system.

That idea is not new. The UK’s Construction 2025 strategy set out ambitions for 33 per cent lower construction and whole-life costs, 50 per cent faster delivery, and 50 per cent lower greenhouse gas emissions. Yet on the ground, many decisions are still made in ways that fragment the process rather than simplify it.

The consequences are familiar: programmes extend because trades cannot start when planned; costs increase as site conditions force redesign or rework; safety risks multiply as teams carry out repetitive, high-risk tasks; and communities experience prolonged disruption from noise, dust and traffic.

None of this is fixed. Much of it is the result of how construction is organised.

A productivity problem disguised as a delivery model

The industry is under growing pressure. Demand for new infrastructure, housing and energy projects continues to rise, while the available workforce is increasingly constrained.

The Construction Industry Training Board estimates that the UK will need more than 206,000 additional construction workers by 2030 to meet demand. At the same time, projects are being asked to do more with less: tighter programmes, greater cost certainty and higher expectations for safety and sustainability.

In this context, methods that rely on multiple trades, sequential working and heavy on-site processing are increasingly difficult to sustain. Every additional step in a construction process creates another interface to manage. Another opportunity for delay. Another source of risk. While each step may appear justified in isolation, the cumulative effect can be a system that is slower, more complex and more expensive than it might otherwise be.

This is where systems thinking becomes more relevant. Instead of asking how to optimise individual elements of a build, it asks a different question: how can the number of steps, interfaces and uncertainties be reduced altogether?

The case for off-site and system-led delivery

One answer that has been gaining traction is off-site manufacturing and system-led construction, often grouped within the wider category of Modern Methods of Construction (MMC).

By moving more of the work into controlled factory environments, these approaches aim to reduce the amount of activity required on site. Fewer processes, fewer trades and fewer unknowns. The benefits are not limited to speed.

The NHBC Foundation has highlighted that off-site construction can lead to faster on-site operations, improved safety, reduced waste and significantly lower levels of noise and disruption for surrounding communities.

When tasks such as drilling, cutting, or repeated assembly are reduced or removed, there can be an impact on workforce health. The Health and Safety Executive (HSE) identifies silica dust as one of the biggest long-term risks in construction, with hundreds of deaths each year linked to exposure. Common site activities such as drilling concrete can exceed 85 dB(A) noise thresholds and contribute to harmful vibration exposure. Designing out those activities altogether is fundamentally different from trying to manage them more safely.

Environmental performance can also improve. Industry research has shown that Modern Methods of Construction can reduce on-site waste by up to 70–90 per cent and significantly cut delivery movements, while more efficient precast solutions have demonstrated material reductions and embodied carbon savings in controlled conditions.

Perhaps most importantly, outcomes may become more predictable. Quality is less dependent on site conditions, and programme risk is reduced because fewer variables are left to chance.

None of this suggests that traditional construction methods are obsolete. There will always be projects where in situ solutions are the right answer. But it does highlight a broader point: when construction is approached as a system rather than a series of separate tasks, different options may become more viable.

Where systems thinking becomes tangible

This shift is easiest to see in construction elements that have historically relied on multiple stages and interfaces. Take something as straightforward as a retaining wall. The underlying engineering principles are well understood and have been for decades. But how those principles are delivered on site can vary significantly.

Traditional approaches often involve separate foundations, fixings, alignment processes and follow-on trades before the structure becomes fully stable. Each stage adds time, cost and risk.

System-led approaches aim to integrate those elements into a single solution where there are fewer components, fewer site operations and a structure that is stable as soon as it is installed.

One example of this approach can be seen in the work of CBS Retaining Walls. Its integrated precast retaining wall system treats design, manufacture and installation as a single, co-ordinated process rather than separate stages, reducing the number of interfaces and activities required on site.

Comparative modelling undertaken by CBS Retaining Walls suggests that reducing construction sequences can have a meaningful impact. In one example, according to the company, a 100-metre retaining wall installation was completed in seven days using its integrated precast system, compared with 15 days for a bolt-down approach and 20 days for an in situ solution, while also reducing overall construction costs.

At the same time, reducing activities such as drilling and on-site fixing may help limit associated noise, dust and vibration, which can improve conditions for site teams and nearby communities.

More importantly, the benefits compound. Shorter programmes may help reduce site overheads, while simpler installation can ease labour demands. Fewer processes may also reduce the likelihood of errors, and less time on site can help limit disruption to the surrounding environment.

This is what systems thinking looks like in practice. It is not a new form of engineering, but a different way of designing, manufacturing and delivering it.

From individual decisions to better outcomes

The challenge for the industry is not a lack of innovation. It also involves procurement, design and delivery models that are able to account for the value innovation may create.

Procurement models often prioritise upfront cost over whole-life value. Design and construction are still frequently treated as separate stages rather than parts of a continuous process. And responsibility for outcomes is fragmented across multiple parties.

In that environment, it is easier to optimise individual components than it is to rethink the system as a whole. Yet the direction of travel is clear. As pressure mounts to deliver projects faster, more safely and with lower environmental impact, the case for integrated, system-led approaches becomes harder to ignore.

A different way of thinking about value

At its core, systems thinking challenges one of the industry’s most persistent assumptions: that the lowest unit cost delivers the best value. In reality, the cheapest component can often lead to the most expensive outcome once programme delays, additional labour, risk and disruption are taken into account. The projects that succeed are rarely the ones that cost the least at the outset. They are often the ones that function most effectively as a whole.

That requires a shift in mindset. From focusing on individual elements to understanding how they interact. From managing risk to removing it. And from reacting to problems on site to designing them out before construction begins.

For an industry facing growing demands and tighter constraints, that shift is not just desirable. It is increasingly necessary. As the UK seeks to deliver more infrastructure, housing and low-carbon projects, the ability to think beyond individual components and towards integrated systems may become increasingly important as the sector evolves. In that context, success may depend less on optimising individual parts in isolation and more on how effectively the wider system is designed.

News.title: Mamdani rows back on arresting Netanyahu, says NYC doesn’t have ‘legal authority’
News.content:
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani says the city doesn’t have the “legal authority” to arrest Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu, on Tuesday (21 July).

“My administration reviewed every avenue to determine whether New York City could execute the ICC’s arrest warrant if Benjamin Netanyahu came here. It is clear we do not have the independent legal authority,” Mamdani said.

The statement follows earlier comments to The Telegraph, where Mamdani suggested NYC was exploring ways to execute the International Criminal Court warrant ahead of Netanyahu’s visit to the UN General Assembly in September.

Mamdani added that enforcing ICC warrants rests solely with the federal government, declaring: “Benjamin Netanyahu is not welcome in New York City.”

Lebanon's prime minister Wednesday visited a battered southern village as a Lebanese-Israeli agreement brokered by Washington appears to have started following a monthslong war.

Nawaf Salam's appearance in Zawtar Al Gharbieh comes a day after President Joseph Aoun's landmark White House meeting with U.S. President Donald Trump, who promised to back the Lebanese government in its bid to claim state control across the country.

Lebanon and Israel in late June signed the agreement, which calls for the Lebanese military to deploy in areas in southern Lebanon where Hezbollah had a military presence and influence, and from where Israeli troops that have occupied dozens of villages would withdraw.

Both sides later agreed on a pilot zone made up of a series of villages to test the implementation of the agreement. While Israeli troops have struck and conducted ground operations in those towns and villages, none of them are under their occupation, but the Lebanese army has also not been there in large numbers.

The latest war between Israel and the Hezbollah militant group started March 2, after the group fired rockets towards Israel in solidarity with war-torn Iran, its main backer. In response, Israel launched an aerial campaign and ground invasion in Lebanon, killing more than 4,000 people and displacing 1.2 million others.

Lebanon's top political leadership criticized Hezbollah for dragging the country into another war, but also condemned Israel for its widespread bombing and ground invasion.

Salam, alongside Lebanon’s defense minister and senior military officials, pitched a Lebanese flag near a destroyed building in the town, vowing the government will start rebuilding destroyed homes and infrastructure.

“We have insisted since the beginning that our goal is the complete Israeli withdrawal from all our territory,” Salam said. “What we are seeing today is just the beginning, but we remain determined and steadfast, and will continue to mobilize all political and diplomatic efforts to secure a full withdrawal from all of Lebanese territory.”

Hezbollah has condemned the government for holding direct talks with Israel and rejected the agreement, but the militant group has not tried to sabotage it through military means. Its leadership believes Israel cannot be pressured to withdraw its troops by diplomatic means only, and that Lebanon lacks the leverage of its key ally Iran in negotiations.

Trump, in his meeting with Aoun, did not speak much about the pilot zone going into its implementation phase, but pledged to support Lebanon without going into details.

Aoun and the Lebanese government have urged the international community to invest in the tiny country and its army to help rebuild its infrastructure and military capacity.

The death toll from a methane explosion inside a hydropower tunnel in the Indian Himalayas jumped to 20 even as five workers remained trapped two days after the collapse.

The toll was updated after rescue crews recovered more bodies from the under-construction tunnel at Samardung-Jholungey, in Namchi district of Sikkim state, where 27 men were working when the blast struck on Monday afternoon.

Since two workers had escaped in the moments after the explosion, the state's chief minister Prem Singh Tamang said, five remained unaccounted for.

Sikkim is a small, mountainous state in India's northeast bordering Nepal, Bhutan and China.

The collapsed tunnel forms part of the Teesta Stage VI hydroelectric project run by the state-owned National Hydroelectric Power Corporation.

The company said a suspected burst of methane trapped within the rock strata caused the explosion, releasing fumes and toxic gases, and that emergency protocols were immediately activated.

Gas building up naturally in the rock is a principal hazard of tunnelling since methane is odourless, displaces oxygen and ignites readily.

Authorities said high methane concentration inside the tunnel continued to obstruct the search and rescue teams had been using breathing apparatus after detecting toxic levels of the gas.

National Disaster Response Force personnel prepare for a rescue operation at the site of a collapsed tunnel at Samardung village of Sikkim, India ( AP )

Most of the dead were migrant labourers from outside Sikkim. It’s common for large infrastructure projects to hire workers from poorer states in northern and eastern India.

Of the 13 victims identified so far, nine came from Jalpaiguri and two from Alipurduar, both in West Bengal, and one each from Punjab and Sikkim.

Mr Tamang said a special investigation team would be set up to establish what caused the explosion. He described it as India’s worst incident of its kind since a road tunnel collapsed at Silkyara in the northern state of Uttarakhand in November 2023, trapping 41 men for 17 days before all were pulled out alive.

The state government announced a compensation of Rs 400,000 (£3,460) for each victim’s kin while prime minister Narendra Modi announced a further Rs 200,000 (£1,730) for each bereaved family as well as Rs 50,000 (£430) for each of the injured.

Mr Modi said in a post on X that he was pained by the deaths and wished the injured a quick recovery.

"I extend my deepest condolences to the bereaved families,” he said. “I pray that those injured recover at the earliest.”

Police in Jalpaiguri said they were arranging transport for relatives of the dead workers to reach the site.

The Teesta project is one of a chain of hydropower installations along the river of the same name, which runs from the high Himalayas through Sikkim and into West Bengal. Such projects are central to India's drive to expand renewable electricity, but the geology of the region is unstable and prone to landslides and earthquakes, making construction dangerous.

In October 2023, a glacial lake burst high in the mountains and sent a torrent of water down the Teesta, destroying a dam at Chungthang and killing at least 40 people.

Scientists warn that as the climate warms and the Himalayan glaciers retreat, the risks of building at scale on these slopes are increasing.

The wreckage of a Pan American Airways flight that crashed off the coast of Puerto Rico has been found sitting on the ocean floor, 74 years on.

The remains of the Pan Am “Clipper Endeavor” were found in June at the bottom of the Atlantic Ocean, the Discovery Channel said on Tuesday.

It was located by the channel’s series Expedition Unknown, along with the Air/Sea Heritage Foundation and other groups.

The Douglas DC-4 plane took off from Puerto Rico on 11 April 1952, as Pan Am Flight 526A to Idlewild Airport (now known as JFK) in New York City.

Sixty-four passengers and five crew members were on board.

open image in gallery The Pan American World Airways logo on the nose section of the Clipper Endeavor wreck ( Air/Sea Heritage Foundation and Deep Sea Vision via AP )

It crashed into the sea shortly afterwards, breaking into two sections and coming to rest on the ocean floor.

Everyone on board survived the initial impact, but 52 passengers subsequently drowned. Twelve passengers and all five crew members were rescued.

The disaster led to sweeping reforms in the aviation industry, and pre-flight safety briefings and demonstrations of emergency procedures were instituted shortly afterwards.

“We are all stunned and elated by this discovery yet also humbled to remember what happened in that place so long ago,” Russ Matthews, the president of the Air/Sea Heritage Foundation, said.

The search, which involved the Deep Sea Vision company, used high-resolution sonar and autonomous underwater drones.

The wreckage was found almost 2,000 feet under the Atlantic Ocean.

open image in gallery From left, Air/Sea Heritage Foundation (ASHF) president Russ Matthews, ASHF director Idee Matthews-Montijo, Expedition Unknown's Josh Gates and Deep Sea Vision president of operations Craig Wallace inside a hangar

Why did Pan Am Flight 526A crash?

One of the engines on the plane’s right wing failed just after takeoff, and the pilots decided to return to San Juan Airport.

As they climbed to 550 feet, the other right-wing engine failed.

The flight’s captain, experienced pilot John C. Burns, declared an in-flight emergency and told the control tower that he planned to attempt a water landing.

Clipper Endeavor ditched in the Atlantic Ocean nine minutes after take-off.

The plane broke in two and the wreckage sank less than three minutes later.

Survivors later reported that many passsengers had panicked, fearing the rough seas and sharks, and had refused to leave the sinking aircraft to board life rafts.

An investigation and subsequent legal proceedings found that the crash was caused by inadequate maintenance and faulty plane parts.

News.title: Private sector pay suffers worst growth since Covid
News.content:
Private sector wages are growing at their slowest pace since the pandemic, piling pressure on Andy Burnham as he enters Downing Street facing a fragile economy and strained public finances.

Salaries rose by 2.9pc in the three months to May, the first time growth has dipped below 3pc since October 2020 and only narrowly ahead of inflation at 2.8pc.

The slowdown was most acute in key industries, with wages in finance and business services up just 2.3pc, manufacturing at 2.5pc and construction earnings falling by 0.2pc over the year.

In contrast, public sector pay accelerated to 5.5pc after striking workers secured higher settlements, widening the gap between state and private sectors.

The cooling labour market came as borrowing overshot official forecasts, leaving John Healey, the new Chancellor, with a £2.7bn gap against expectations.

The Government borrowed £57.6bn between April and June – less than a year earlier but still ahead of projections – pushing public debt to nearly £3tn, or 94.9pc of GDP.

Mr Healey said: “The Prime Minister and I have talked about how we will work in lockstep to meet the fiscal rules with a buffer against uncertainty and how we’ll make life more affordable for working people right across the UK.”

However, Sir Mel Stride, the shadow business secretary, said: “If Andy Burnham and John Healey are really serious about the future of our economy then they must get borrowing under control.”

News.title: Scammers stole $114 billion as Southeast Asia’s crime gangs go corporate
News.content:
Scam gangs stole up to $114 billion from people in Asia-Pacific alone in 2025, the UN has warned, as crime syndicates rapidly professionalise their tactics to evade law enforcement in Southeast Asia.

By way of comparison, the sum dwarfs the $85 billion the UK spends each year on defence.

The Asia-Pacific region has emerged as an epicentre for massive cyber fraud operations since the Covid pandemic. Scammers – some willingly, others under duress – are now stealing billions from internet users across the world via fake romance and cryptocurrency investment schemes.

In 2025, these fraud operations stole between $88.3 and $114.1bn from just people across East Asia, Southeast Asia, Australia and New Zealand, according to a report on Tuesday from the UN Office on Drugs and Crime (UNODC).

Those figures are triple the estimated losses in 2023, between $18 and $37bn, and don’t account for victims in Europe or the US.

The scam centres – which began in fortified compounds but are now increasingly housed in innocuous office blocks and villas – are found across the region, but have especially exploited power vacuums caused by war, corruption and weak governance in Cambodia, Myanmar and Laos.

Although the scammers initially targeted people in China, they have dramatically expanded their ambitions. The UNODC said people from at least 80 countries and territories had been identified in compounds, with recruiters seeking people from outside Asia as they look to expand new markets.

News.title: UK borrowing costs rise at fastest pace in G7
News.content:
Britain’s borrowing costs rose at the fastest pace in the G7 after Andy Burnham said he would take a “flexible” approach to the UK’s fiscal rules.

In his maiden speech as prime minister, Mr Burnham on Monday signalled he could bend the rules underpinning Britain’s finances, spooking financial markets fearful of higher government spending.

UK gilts – a benchmark for how much the Government pays on its debt – saw yields rise 0.08 percentage points to an eight-week high of 5.03pc for the 10-year bond. Thirty-year gilts also pushed higher.

The rise was the fastest in the G7, excluding Japan, whose markets are closed for a national holiday.

After markets closed on Monday, Mr Burnham surprised the City by picking John Healey as his next Chancellor.

Mr Healey, who quit over defence funding rising too slowly, will now be tasked with finding billions of pounds in Britain’s stretched public finances.

Shabana Mahmood, the Home Secretary, had widely been expected for the role. Ed Miliband, the former Energy Secretary, was also in contention.

Mr Healey will replace Rachel Reeves, who resigned on Monday.

The appointment of Mr Healey, a veteran of the Blair-Brown government, may calm fears in the City after Mr Burnham pledged to stretch the fiscal rules by using “flexibility” within them.

Speaking in Downing Street, Mr Burnham said: “I’ve said we’ll stick to the fiscal rules, and by that I mean the existing fiscal rules, and use obviously any flexibility within them.”

James Athey, a fund manager at Marlborough, said: “It’s not a good start because bandying around the words fiscal rules seems to be believed within government circles to be a sufficient condition to get financial markets on side, and that just misunderstands an element of the problem.”

He added that investors were watching closely for any signs that the Government will increase borrowing.

Matt Amis, investment director at Aberdeen, said Mr Burnham’s comments had “got the markets’ attention.”

He said “It just shows this week in particular the language from the Burnham administration, the new chancellor, is going to be key here. The gilt market is on edge.”

Mr Burnham, who has become the UK’s seventh prime minister in just a decade, has inherited a troubled economy as businesses grapple with low confidence and strained public finances.

Monday’s comment suggests the new prime minister will use measures to raise borrowing while keeping the additional sums off the Government’s book.

The Resolution Foundation, a think tank, said he could do this by expanding the remit of institutions like the National Wealth Fund, an arms-length government investment vehicle.

His plan to use “flexibility” in the fiscal rules comes after Ms Reeves altered the main indicator of government debt in 2024.

She tweaked the primary measure of the UK’s debt to Public Sector Net Financial Liabilities, meaning that when public financial institutions borrow to invest in a private business it does not count towards the government’s fiscal rules.

However, the think tank warned that boosting the financial capacity of public financial institutions like the National Wealth Fund by £16bn would cost around £400 million a year in debt interest.

Helen Miller, director at the Institute for Fiscal Studies, warned that challenging public finances will mean Mr Burnham will be forced to make tough choices on spending.

She said: “While chancellors come and go, the underlying fiscal constraints remain the same. Public debt, borrowing and debt-interest costs are all high. One in every £12 the government spends currently goes on debt interest.”

Higher borrowing costs threaten to increase the Government’s debt interest bill, which is already forecast to hit £111.2bn for the financial year - equivalent to 8.3pc of public spending.

Mr Burnham said he would announce a set of measures on Tuesday to give households “breathing space” to help with the cost of living.

“I will set out some of those measures starting tomorrow, including how we pay for them,” he said.

“We will help more young people into education... and we will build more council homes. That is the fair and sustainable way to bring the welfare bill down, to meet our fiscal rules and to honour our commitments on defence to our international partners.”

Mr Amis said: “Tomorrow we’re getting some cost of living news. [Burnham] said he was going to state where that funding’s come from. I think that’s key, any unfunded spending from here would get the market’s attention.”

News.title: India approves first dengue vaccine as cases surge in South Asia
News.content:
India has approved its first dengue vaccine as cases of the mosquito-borne disease surge in South Asia.

Japan’s Takeda Pharmaceutical’s dengue vaccine QDENGA has been approved by India’s drug regulator, the Centre Drugs Standard Control Organisation (CDSCO).

The global threat posed by dengue has been rising for years, as climate change, urbanisation and international travel aid the spread of the mosquitoes that transmit it.

The approval comes as hospitals across South Asia grapple with a surge in dengue infections.

In Sri Lanka, health authorities reported 2,652 new cases on Sunday alone, taking the total to 76,044 dengue cases so far this year. At least 53 people have died.

Bangladesh is also suffering a major outbreak with over 9,000 cases and 30 deaths that has piled pressure on its health system even as it battles a measles epidemic.

Dengue is transmitted to humans through the bites of infected Aedes mosquitoes.

Its symptoms include fever, severe muscle pain, and in severe cases, shock and internal bleeding that can be fatal.

Although mortality is relatively low, outbreaks place a substantial burden on health systems.

Takeda’s QDENGA jab is a live-attenuated tetravalent vaccine designed to protect against all four dengue virus serotypes. It can be given regardless of previous dengue infections.

“The approval comes at a critical time for public health, as reported dengue cases in India have increased 11-fold in the past two decades,” the company said in a statement.

News.title: Burnham’s plan to restore UK aid spending
News.content:
Andy Burnham is planning to reverse the cuts to Britain’s aid budget made by his predecessors Sir Keir Starmer and Rishi Sunak, according to reports.

A roadmap for returning the UK to spending 0.7 per cent of Gross National Income (GNI) on international aid will be drawn up as part of a major shake-up of the Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office (FCDO), The Independent reported.

Ed Miliband is set to be named Foreign Secretary and put in charge of overhauling Britain’s international development aims, as well as prioritising climate goals, senior Labour sources said.

The aid spending plan was absent from Mr Burnham’s brief first speech as Prime Minister, in which he pledged to end rough sleeping and bring down the welfare bill in order to fund defence and council housing.

But it follows anger within the Labour Party over what was seen as a broken manifesto promise, when Sir Keir and Rachel Reeves, the Chancellor, slashed aid spending to 0.3 per cent of GNI.

Senior Labour MPs have been lobbying for a return to the 0.7 per cent commitment, a target first established by the United Nations in the 1970s.

It has since become a key yardstick for international efforts to reduce poverty and tackle major health issues like the HIV/AIDS epidemic, vaccine access, and maternal mortality in poor countries.

News.title: The best bars and nightlife in Lyon
News.content:
While drinking in this gourmet city remains firmly rooted in the surrounding Rhône Valley’s ancient wine-growing heritage, new-gen addresses have embraced world cocktail culture in style. They’re using Lyon’s long-envied gastronomic know-how and rich bounty of local seasonal produce to create some sensational new drinks and food pairings as only the French can. Artisanal spirits meanwhile are increasingly fashionable: cornichon gin, Mezcal-fuelled soirées at chef Carla Kirsch’s gourmet tacos joint in Croix-Rousse, and the stunning Christian Drouin gin and pine-needle liqueur cocktail with stick of Comté cheese to stir I recently had at Hôtel Dieu’s Le Dôme bar all spring to mind.

Come the warmer days of spring and summer, the city’s fervent café-life spills onto pretty pavement terraces, while floating bars moored along Les Berges du Rhône (the landscaped river banks of the Rhône’s Rive Gauche or Left Bank) hum with after-dark dance parties and festivities. Clubbing remains fairly mainstream.

Sports.title: Amazon chief Jeff Bezos with £192BILLION fortune ‘holds talks about buying stake in Liverpool’
Sports.content:
LIVERPOOL’S latest consortium is flirting with Amazon tycoon Jeff Bezos in a bid to lure him to Merseyside.

Initial talks with Bezos and a syndicate of investors led by British-Indian millionaire businessman Amit Bhatia have been held, according to Sky Sports.



Reports suggest that Bezos did not immediately jump on the opportunity to add the Premier League club to his £192billion empire.

English football has seen a wave of American investment in recent years so, while unlikely that the world’s fourth-richest man will proceed, it is not impossible.



Around 50 per cent of Prem clubs have predominantly US-based investors.

Crystal Palace, for one, is continuing to explore sale options.



Bezos, 62, has previously held talks with the 2026 Super Bowl winners Seattle Seahawks, as well as the Washington Commanders.

But the Amazon and Blue Origin billionaire did not go ahead with either investment.

The Liverpool consortium is led by former QPR co-owner Bhatia, who is also the son-in-law of billionaire steel tycoon Lakshmi Mittal.

They are currently in talks to purchase a minority stake in Anfield, having hired advisers to put together a deal with current owners Fenway Sports Group (FSG).



BEST FREE BETS AND BETTING SIGN UP OFFERS

A small stake in the club – reportedly four per cent – was sold by FSG to Dynasty Equity, a US private equity firm, for £164million in 2023.

With the money raised, the Reds were reportedly able to pay down their debt and help raise money to finance capital expenditure.

But it was not used for transfers.

According to the Financial Times, a deal with the consortium led by Bhatia would value Liverpool at more than £4.5bn.



A spokesperson for FSG said: “An investment consortium led, managed, and represented by Amit Bhatia has expressed interest in making a strategic minority investment in Liverpool Football Club.”

It is understood the Blues submitted a £64million offer for Scott, but saw it rejected as Bournemouth told the London side in no uncertain terms they wanted to keep their star central midfielder.



Arsenal also saw an approach rebuffed in June.

The Red Devils can offer Champions League football and therefore a host of minutes to the former Bristol City star in their revamped engine room.



However, the ace up their sleeve to convince Scott to head to Old Trafford could be sourced from their women’s team.

The captain of Man Utd Women is Lionesses star Maya Le Tissier, who is Scott’s step-sister.

Le Tissier, 24, and England Under-21 star Scott – who was involved with Thomas Tuchel‘s team during last November’s international camp and the World Cup pre-camp team, but is yet to make his senior debut – both come from the Channel Island of Guernsey.

She has spoken glowingly about her relationship with Scott, whom she has known since they were children and even travelled and trained together, including playing football in their hotel room.

Sports.title: Chelsea have £64m-plus bid for Premier League star REJECTED as transfer race with Man Utd and Arsenal hots up
Sports.content:
CHELSEA have been rebuffed in their pursuit of a Premier League star.

The Blues have enjoyed a busy window so far as they sealed a £117million deal for Morgan Rogers on Tuesday, a record fee for a British footballer.

Sports.title: Two Spain stars have stadiums named after them and given bizarre reward for winning World Cup
Sports.content:
FABIAN RUIZ and Spain team-mate Gavi were spoiled by their hometown as they named TWO stadiums after the World Cup winning pair.

La Roja became world champions on Sunday after Ferran Torres‘ goal in the depths of extra time sealed a 1-0 win and left Argentina in pieces.



Ruiz, 30, and Gavi, 21, both hail from the southern Spanish city Los Palacios y Villafranca, which boasts a population of 35,225.

In their honour, the current Marismas and San Sebastian stadiums have officially be renamed “Fabian Ruiz” and “Pablo Paez Gavira ‘Gavi'”.



Ruiz began playing football at Los Palacios CF, while Gavi was six when he joined the youth teams at La Liara Balompie.

The two amateur teams, who compete in regional leagues in Andalusia, play their home matches at the Marismas and San Sebastian stadiums, respectively.



But they are not the only World Cup winners to see their efforts rewarded in the city just south of Seville.

Former Sevilla star and 2010 World Cup champion Jesus Navas already had the sports complex put in his namesake by the City Council.

In a grand ceremony on Tuesday, Ruiz and Gavi were also given their weight in tomatoes as per the local tradition.

The champs stepped on to scales to make sure they got the exact weight correct for the juicy red prize – reportedly around 140kg.



BEST FREE BETS AND BETTING SIGN UP OFFERS

Sixteen years ago, Navas received the “bombon colorao” tomatoes, the flagship variety of Los Palacios’s vegetable gardens, after his success in South Africa.

Sports.title: Morgan Rogers takes brutal swipe at Arsenal after choosing Chelsea over them as he completes £117m transfer
Sports.content:
MORGAN ROGERS has taken a cheeky dig at Arsenal after signing for Premier League rivals Chelsea.

The Aston Villa attacker completed a monster £117million move on Tuesday which made him the most expensive British transfer ever.



And he wasted no time in ingratiating himself with the Stamford Bridge faithful with a subtle jab at the North London outfit.

In his official Blues announcement, Rogers said: “I’m so excited,



“For me, Chelsea are the biggest club in London and a club I’ve always admired since I was a kid.”

The comment comes after extensive interest in his services from Mikel Arteta and Co.



And they did not go down well with Gunners fans, with Piers Morgan expressing his ire as he wrote on X: “They’re not even the biggest in West London… Brentford finished higher in the League last season.”

Another fuming fan responded: “The flop of this massive ego will be incredibly satisfying to watch. Sold to Burnley in a year.”

And a third added: “Can’t wait to play against Chelsea. They need to be reminded who the best club in London is.”

Rogers, 23, was one of the defending champions’ primary targets, with the club yet to really make any marquee signings in this window.



BEST ONLINE CASINOS – TOP SITES IN THE UK

Illan Meslier arrived from Leeds on a free transfer as a depth option in goal, while Club Brugge winger Christos Tzolis is set for his medical for a potential £35m move.

But their real prize is now set to join up with old friend Cole Palmer under new Blues boss Xabi Alonso.

Rogers added: “I’m really excited about the project with the new manager, the players we’ve got and where the club is heading.

“That’s why I’m here and I can’t wait to get started.”

Sports.title: Trump ‘wants to nominate “respected” Fifa boss Gianni Infantino as next UN Secretary-General’ after World Cup success
Sports.content:
DONALD Trump wants to nominate Gianni Infantino to become the next UN Secretary-General, a report claims.

The US and Fifa presidents are close buddies with Don being awarded the inaugural Peace Prize earlier this year and their bromance spilling across World Cup screens.



Trump thinks Infantino could possibly be the next boss of the global body as the candidates currently in the race are “lame”, a source close to the President told The Post.

Infantino “is respected by everyone around the world, and recognizes he has a special ability to bring people together,” Trump believes, according to the source.



But it is unclear if Infantino wants the job and if Trump has actually told him about the prospect of a nomination.

The current Secretary-General, António Guterres, will complete his second term at the end of 2026.



The most well known candidates campaigning to succeed him includes Michelle Jeria, the former President of Chile, Rafael Grossi, Director General of the IAEA, Rebeca Mayufis, the Secretary-General of the UN Conference on Trade and Development, and Macky Sall, ex-President of Senegal.

Infantino would take a major pay cut if he took the role – slashing his whopping $6m (£4.48m) salary to $418,000 (£312,000).

One other issue that could complicate what Trump reportedly wants is Infantino has declared his candidacy already for re-election as Fifa President.

Whoever eventually replaces Guterres will oversee the UN’s tens of thousands of staff members, manage its budget, and use their independent “good offices” to mediate disputes and prevent international conflicts – an important role to say the least.



Paolo Zampolli, the Italian-American businessman and diplomat serving as Trump’s US Special Representative for Global Partnerships, told The Post that “only Trump could have such a genius idea.”

He said Infantino “would do a great job” and is “liked by everybody”.

He added that “there is some similarity” between his current role as Fifa president and UN Secretary-General.



“At the United Nations, you have to deal with 193 member states,” he said.

“In Fifa, there are over 200 members [and] Gianni’s great record shows he knows how to manage.”

Less than 24 hours ago, Trump declared this World Cup as “the most spectacular by far” and praised his pal for elevating the tournament “to a level that nobody thought was possible.”

“The World Cup turned out to be a spectacular success,” he posted on Truth Social.

He added: “Thank you to… the fantastic president of FIFA, Gianni Infantino, on a job well done!



“Few people will ever be able to accomplish what he has done in elevating the World Cup to a level that nobody thought was possible.”

Serious questions have been raised about some particularly controversial decisions made by Infantino during the tournament.

One of them is the overturning of US striker Folarin Balogun’s red card after considerable political pressure.



UEFA blasted the decision to suspend the ban as “unprecedented, incomprehensible and unjustifiable,” saying FIFA had “crossed a red line.”

Additionally, European Parliament lawmakers Barry Andrews, Lara Wolters and Niels Fuglsang said in a joint statement that the decision is a “disgrace and a perversion of justice.”

How is the UN Secretary-General elected? THE UN Secretary-General is elected by the 193-member General Assembly based on the formal recommendation of the 15-member Security Council. In practice, the five permanent members of the Security Council – the US, the UK, China, France and Russia – wield the ultimate decision-making power. The actual selection and appointment is a complicated and lengthy process that starts months in advance. Nomination: Candidates must be formally proposed by one or more member states

Vision statement: Each candidate outlines priorities for the role

Interactive dialogues: Public sessions with member states and civil society

Security Council recommendation: At least nine votes, with no veto from permanent members

General Assembly appointment: Majority support from the 193 member states

“Once again, we’ve seen Infantino and FIFA surrender to the demands of the Trump administration,” the statement said.

It added: “The beauty of sport is that it is based on impartial and transparent rules.

“When Infantino allows political pressure to determine who gets to play, this sense of fairness goes out the window.”



Speculation about a nomination comes months after Trump won the Fifa Peace Prize in a star-studded ceremony in December.

At the time, the president was handed the massive trophy, which is three times bigger than the World Cup’s, by Infantino.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

He said Trump had earned the award for his “unwavering commitment to advancing peace and unity throughout the world,” citing the wars he is said to have ended.

After shaking the sport’s leader’s hand and putting on a medal, the president called the prize “truly one of the great honours of my life.”

Sports.title: What World Cup 2030 could look like with 64 teams as Gianni Infantino told to step down over insulting plans
Sports.content:
PICTURE the scene — it is prime time Saturday and the World Cup is on the box.

San Marino are taking on Angola in a group opener, while the rest of the weekend’s schedule includes Luxembourg v Kazakhstan and Faroe Islands v Libya.



Welcome to Gianni Infantino’s brave new world.

The Fifa president has been accused of systematically destroying football – and his latest brainwave is his most absurd yet.



Not content with watering down this summer’s tournament with 48 teams, Infantino is now plotting to expand the 2030 World Cup to a monstrous SIXTY-FOUR countries.

It is an insult to the beautiful game. This would mean almost one in three Fifa member nations will get a pass to the biggest show on Earth.



We will be forced to watch endless, meaningless group games while Fifa counts its broadcasting billions.

Though I suppose there is one silver lining — at least four-time champions Italy might finally qualify without suffering another humiliating play-off defeat against North Macedonia.

Make no mistake, Infantino does not care about the quality of football.

His endless expansion is not about growing the global game — it is a shameless vote-buying machine designed to keep him sitting on his Fifa throne until the end of time.



BEST ONLINE CASINOS – TOP SITES IN THE UK

As LaLiga chief Javier Tebas warned, Fifa is destroying the entire football ecosystem for a 40-day circus.

A 64-team World Cup means an absurd 128 MATCHES dragged out over six gruelling weeks. Player welfare? Don’t make me laugh.

Elite stars will be expected to run themselves into the ground playing up to 60 games for their clubs before flying across continents for a slog of group fixtures.

We already saw the warning signs this summer when Haiti, Tunisia, Iraq, Jordan, Uzbekistan and Panama all finished without a single point.

Curacao and Qatar barely fared better.



If a country wants to play on the grandest stage, there is already a perfectly fair mechanism to get here — it’s called qualifying.

Earn it on the pitch, lads.

But with 64 nations, can you imagine how many more meaningless qualifiers will be created, too?

And do not rule out the possibility of introducing fifth and seventh-place play-offs.

It sounds crazy but the way Infantino is going, anything considered ridiculous cannot be ruled out.



The leadership at the top is rotten. Infantino’s ten-year reign has become a masterclass in shameless bootlicking and corporate pandering.

Look at the utter joke of the 2030 scheduling already. Three opening matches are being staged in South America: Uruguay, Paraguay and Argentina.

It will mark 100 years since they participated in the first competition held in Uruguay. This is before dragging teams across the Atlantic to Portugal, Spain and Morocco. All SIX automatically qualify as co-hosts, too.

Meanwhile, England — the actual home of football — have not hosted the tournament since winning it 1966.

At this rate, we will be waiting until 2066 for a measly ‘celebration game’.



And who could forget Infantino’s cringe-inducing brown-nosing?

Denied a Nobel Prize, Donald Trump was magically handed a newly manufactured ‘Fifa World Peace Prize’ by Infantino.

It was an embarrassing stunt to ingratiate himself with USA’s President.

Add to that the grotesque Americanisation of the matches.

Hydration breaks in air-conditioned stadiums as a shameless excuse for TV ad breaks and a ridiculous 27-minute half-time interval in the final to have Super Bowl-style entertainment with Madonna, Shakira and Ted Lasso.



Football became the biggest sport on Earth because it is fast, furious and continuous.

The Americans have always wanted to chop it into quarters and clog it up with commercials, but the World Cup final has always been bigger than the Super Bowl.

I’d love a return to 16 teams with guaranteed groups of death where every single game matters.

However, I accept 32 teams as a compromise between quality and being more inclusive. But Infantino has to go.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

And if Fifa won’t stop him, European heavyweights like England, France, Spain, Germany and, yes, even Italy must step up and BOYCOTT the tournament.

Without the elite nations from Europe, Infantino’s bloated 64- team circus is meaningless.

Sports.title: Vinicius Jr makes first public appearance after CHIN surgery as he packs on PDA with girlfriend after reigniting romance
Sports.content:
VINICIUS JR showed off the results of his chin surgery as he snogged his on-off influencer girlfriend.

The Real Madrid star, 26, is reported to have gone under the knife for the cosmetic procedure after Brazil’s World Cup exit.



And he showed off the results in his first public appearance since at the opening of Virginia Fonseca’s gym in Goiania.

The pair shared a smooch as Virginia posted: “Another dream come true!! Our @wegym_br 💜 thank you to everyone who came to support us on this special day and I hope you all from Goiania will train with us.”



Brazilian outlet TMC reported Vini Jr underwent a chin harmonisation procedure in Goiania after the tournament, which saw Brazil lose 2-1 to Norway in the last 16.

In a photo with dermatologist Dr Alessandro Alarcao, Vinicius’ chin was visibly different and more defined compared to before.

While there is no set cost for the cost of such a procedure, in the UK it can range anywhere from £3,000 to more than £14,000 depending on the treatment.

His new look comes as he confirmed his relationship with Virginia was back on.

She announced their split before the World Cup, after dating on and off since first being linked in 2025.

But they appeared to be very much back on when they were pictured on a superyacht together this month.



BEST ONLINE CASINOS – TOP SITES IN THE UK

Vini Jr sparked outrage back home after snaps of the bikini-clad influencer sitting on his lap came out days after Brazil’s exit.

The Los Blancos star scored four times in the USA but did not net in the knockouts as Brazil were humbled by Erling Haaland.

He also copped flak for not stepping up to take the penalty against Norway, which Newcastle’s Bruno Guimaraes missed while the game was still 0-0.

And there was more fury when just ONE of Carlo Ancelotti’s squad flew home to Brazil to face the music.

Sports.title: Wolves forced to CANCEL training as banned star refuses to leave pitch
Sports.content:
Wolves forced to CANCEL training as banned star refuses to leave pitch

New Wolves manager Cesar Peixoto has laid down the law during the club's pre-season campaign, with striker Tolu Arokodare being asked not to train with the first-team squad

View 2 Images Tolu Arokodare has been frozen out by Wolves (Image: Brett Patzke - WWFC/Wolves via Getty Images)

Championship side Wolves CANCELLED their training session on Monday after striker Tolu Arokodare refused to leave the pitch. Extra security was also deployed the following day to ensure that the 25-year-old didn't return to the club's training ground.

The extraordinary development comes just weeks into Cesar Peixoto's reign as manager. The Portuguese was brought in to replace Rob Edwards, who was sacked after Wolves were relegated from the Premier League by finishing rock bottom of the table.

Arokodare, who scored just six goals in 38 games, was part of the squad responsible for Wolves' dismal season and had been linked with a move away. And his future at Molineux has been plunged into further uncertainty following Monday's debacle.

‌



The Wolves Poddy report that training was cancelled because of Arokodare's refusal to leave the pitch when asked not to train with the rest of the squad. On Tuesday, Wolves increased security at Compton Park in order to stop the ex-Genk star from entering.

JOIN US ON FACEBOOK! Latest news, analysis and much more on Mirror Football's Facebook page

Arokodare won't be involved when Wolves face non-league outfit Maidenhead United in a pre-season friendly on Wednesday night. Clubs from Serie A including Genoa and Fiorentina are interested in signing Arokodare, with the latter having seen a bid rejected earlier this month.

The decision to block Arokodare from training is viewed as a show of power by Peixoto, who's tasked with bringing Wolves back to the Premier League - and he made it clear in his first interview exactly what type of manager he'll be. "Firstly, I'm a very demanding coach," the former Gil Vicente boss said.

"But, I believe in giving others maximum freedom and maximum responsibility. I want us to work as a team and as a unit and build a good environment. This is important to me, but I know very well what I want from the team. I want my team to be organised with and without the ball.

Will Wolves come straight back up? Give us your prediction in the comments section.

‌



View 2 Images Cesar Peixoto was appointed in June (Image: Brett Patzke - WWFC/Wolves via Getty Images)

"Secondly, I want a team with intensity and to be aggressive and win duels. "The third one is I want to show the quality of the players. To play an offensive game and to try and press high. To try and be the main character of the games. I want to win games, but I want to win while playing good football. With passion and energy.

"[The supporters can expect] a team with ambition. A strong character and identity and a strong idea of the game. A team that never gives up to win three points and to try and make the fans proud."

Wolves have made three new signings alongside making defender Ladislav Krejci's loan move permanent for a total fee of £26million. Right-back Kieran Trippier and striker Raul Jimenez arrived on free transfers under Edwards before the club paid a reported £7.7m for left winger Rafiki Said.

Sports.title: David Beckham's huge payment for World Cup appearance blows away Shakira and Justin Bieber
Sports.content:
David Beckham's huge payment for World Cup appearance blows away Shakira and Justin Bieber

It was hard to miss David Beckham during the World Cup

View 3 Images David Beckham topped up his huge wealth at the World Cup (Image: Andy Stenning/Daily Mirror)

David Beckham has left Shakira and Justin Bieber trailing in his wake after his mammoth World Cup earnings were revealed. The England and Manchester United icon was one of the most visible celebrities at the tournament, attending numerous games and appearing in a succession of adverts for brands like McDonald's, Walkers and Stella Artois.

‌



Beckham, who boasts a combined net worth of £1.85billion with wife Victoria, made an estimated £19m from the tournament, according to market analysts. That tops World Cup regular Shakira (£15m), who performed at the opening ceremony and the final's half-time show and Bieber (£12m), who performed a solo at the latter.

‌



'Brand Beckham' carries huge clout in the United States, where David is a part-owner of Inter Miami, having spent five years with LA Galaxy as a player. One of his sons, Brooklyn, who has had a public falling out with his family, has even coined it in, making an estimated £1m, mostly from a lucrative commercial with DoorDash.

‌



Brand and culture expert Nick Ede said via The Sun: "While he's [Brooklyn] often criticised, global brands clearly believe his surname, social media reach and international recognition still have significant marketing value during events watched by billions. The advert, along with increased eyes on him, will have elevated his brand and value even more."

JOIN US ON FACEBOOK! Latest news, analysis and much more on Mirror Football's Facebook page

On actors and pop stars' eagerness to be associated with the World Cup, Ede said: "Brands are willing to spend tens of millions securing celebrities who can instantly grab attention during the commercial breaks because they know they're reaching an audience of billions.

‌

England World Cup player ratings: Bellingham shines but Arsenal duo suffer after gruelling season READ MORE :

"For many stars, appearing in this year's World Cup campaigns can be just as valuable as starring in a blockbuster film or releasing a hit album because the exposure is truly global."

But Beckham, 51, has become the celeb to beat when it comes to World Cup earnings. His £19m was £8m more than the England squad combined received for finishing third.

View 3 Images Shakira continued her long-running relationship with the World Cup (Image: FIFA via Getty Images)

‌



The FA received a £22m share from the tournament's huge prize fund, of which about half went to the squad and coaching staff. The players will earn between £350,000 and £420,000 each.

The FA sets aside a specific backroom bonus pool, with head coach Thomas Tuchel - under fire for his tactics in the semi-final defeat to Argentina - receiving a handsome standalone payment.

View 3 Images Justin Bieber performed at the half-time show during the final (Image: Getty Images)

Article continues below

The players' money does not include their £2,000 match fees, which, thanks to a deal established by the England Footballers Foundation in 2007, are donated in full to charity. Still, no England player or staff member can get close to Beckham, who will walk away from the tournament even richer.

Sports.title: Amazon founder Jeff Bezos 'approached' as FSG enter talks over Liverpool investment
Sports.content:
Amazon founder Jeff Bezos 'approached' as FSG enter talks over Liverpool investment

Liverpool's owners Fenway Sports Group have confirmed that a consortium, which is led by the businessman Amit Bhatia, have expressed interest in making a strategic minority investment

View Image Jeff Bezos

A consortium in talks to buy a stake in Liverpool have reportedly approached Jeff Bezos. Amazon's founder and executive chairman is the fourth-richest man in the world, with a net worth of over £190billion.

‌



Liverpool's owners, Fenway Sports Group, confirmed on Tuesday that a consortium led by Amit Bhatia expressed interest in investing in the Premier League club. Bhatia was previously a co-owner and director of Queens Park Rangers.

‌



FSG said in a statement to our sister title the Liverpool ECHO: "An investment consortium led, managed and represented by Amit Bhatia has expressed interest in making a strategic minority investment in Liverpool Football Club."

‌



Sky News reports that Bezos has spoken about joining Bhatia's syndicate. However, they cite a source when claiming the billionaire is not certain to invest.

The consortium is understood to have already the backing of Lakshmi Mittal, Bhatia's father-in-law. He is worth over £20billion and led a £1billion-plus takeover of the Indian Premier League's Rajasthan Royals in May.

‌



However, according to sources with knowledge of the situation, no investment deal is in place with Liverpool yet, with discussions over a "significant minority stake" only at a preliminary stage. FSG struck a £82m - £164m deal with Dynasty Equity in 2023.

Sports.title: Italy chief confirms Pep Guardiola talks despite major hurdle holding up return
Sports.content:
Italy chief confirms Pep Guardiola talks despite major hurdle holding up return

The Italian Football Federation (FIGC) are in talks to appoint Pep Guardiola as their national team's new manager, just two months after he waved goodbye to Manchester City

View 2 Images Pep Guardiola's salary would force Italy to make an 'exception' (Image: Robbie Jay Barratt - AMA/Getty Images)

The president of the FIGC has confirmed that they've held talks with Pep Guardiola over becoming Italy's new manager - even though they'd need to make 'exceptions' for his wages. Guardiola, 55, is currently out of work for the first time in 10 years after stepping down as Manchester City boss in May.

‌



Despite never having worked in international management, the Catalan has often spoken about his desire to coach at a World Cup, European Championship or Copa America. After failing to qualify for a third successive World Cup this summer, the Italian Football Federation (FIGC) are searching for a new manager who can transform their national team.

‌



Guardiola is among their top targets, with it being reported over the weekend that new Italy technical director Paolo Maldini and his special advisor, Leonardo, flew to Barcelona for talks with the former Bayern Munich and Barcelona boss. FIGC president Giovanni Malago confirmed this in an interview with Cronache di Spogliatoio and Gazzetta dello Sport.

‌



"There are certain financial aspects to be considered, and it's an understatement to say we'd have to grit our teeth for this," Malago explained. "Some exceptions have been made, for example exceptions that regard the name making such waves at the moment: Pep Guardiola.

"I don't need to sit here and explain the obvious reasons why he'd be an exception, but that is also no guarantee that this will go through." Malago added: "I think it was right and important to open a dialogue and keep it alive."

‌



Guardiola reportedly earned an eye-watering £20million per year at City. That's a far cry from the modest £680,000 salary which Gennaro Gattuso signed up to before his departure in May following Italy's World Cup play-off failure.

Malago was also quizzed on ex-Azzurri boss Antonio Conte, who recently said that hadn't been contacted regarding the vacancy. The chief replied: "It is certainly not a lack of respect towards other people, because there has already been a discussion with others, and one can opt for someone who is perhaps of a more recent school of thought, so it’s a very subjective matter."

Should Pep Guardiola take the Italy job? Have your say in the comments section.

Malago was then asked if Guardiola, Andrea Pirlo and another former Italy manager in Roberto Mancini were the remaining candidates. "Absolutely not," he affirmed. "We are thinking about a certain profile, and these names are definitely within that category."

Sports.content:
New Man Utd signing gets green light from Harry Maguire as exciting comment made

Manchester United fans have a lot to be excited for ahead of the new season

View 2 Images Andrey Santos has been impressing many at Manchester United (Image: Ash Donelon/Manchester United via Getty Images)

Andrey Santos has received glowing praise from Harry Maguire after signing for Manchester United. The midfielder has settled in well under Michael Carrick, who was full of praise for the midfielder.

Maguire appeared on the Sky Sports Golf channel during The Open and made his thoughts clear on Santos. He said: "Andrey played yesterday. He really impressed us in the first week and I think we've signed two great players there," as he mentioned fellow newcomer Youri Tielemans.

The centre-half played with Santos during the first half against Wrexham and enjoyed the 22-year-old's first 45 minutes as a Red Devil. Santos signed a five-year deal worth an initial £48million after joining from Chelsea.

The midfielder had already impressed Carrick before he made his debut. Carrick said: "He's settled in really well, he's a fantastic character. He's settled in so quickly and he's buzzing to be here, you can see that."

Sports.title: Six standout World Cup stars who Man Utd could sign next for Michael Carrick rebuild
Sports.content:
Six standout World Cup stars who Man Utd could sign next for Michael Carrick rebuild

Manchester United could turn to some of the World Cup 2026's standout performers this summer as they continue adding to their ranks

View 2 Images Antonio Nusa is among the World Cup stars who Manchester United might look to pursue (Image: NurPhoto via Getty Images)

Manchester United have already been busy this summer, making multiple new signings as they look to give Michael Carrick plenty to work with ahead of a return to the Champions League. More are set to follow, with the World Cup putting plenty of stars in the shop window.

‌



Youri Tielemans was well known to United long before he took a prominent role for Belgium in North America. He isn't the only new face to arrive, with Andrey Santos, Karl Darlow and youngster Tynan Thompson all brought in.

‌



More players could be offloaded in order to free up space in Carrick's squad, with European football meaning more bodies are likely to be needed. We've taken a look at some of the World Cup standouts who could fit the bill.

‌

Ayyoub Bouaddi

One of the most sought-after youngsters in global football at present, Bouaddi penned a fresh Lille contract last season - evidence that there was attention to fight off long before the World Cup. Judging by his standout display against Brazil, however, that new deal is unlikely to deter potential suitors.

United have prioritised younger targets in recent years and the 18-year-old midfielder certainly matches that profile. They also conducted recent business with Lille when they signed Leny Yoro in 2024.

‌



There will be hurdles, naturally. Bouaddi's performances have attracted interest from the likes of Manchester City and Paris Saint-Germain, both of whom boast substantial financial muscle and may bid more than United can spare right now.

Maxi Araujo

View 2 Images Maxi Araujo impressed at the World Cup despite Uruguay's struggles (Image: Michael Regan - FIFA, FIFA via Getty Images)

Araujo is familiar to former United manager Ruben Amorim, having featured under him at Sporting CP. Premier League supporters may recall the Uruguayan as the other goalscorer when a Viktor Gyokeres hat-trick propelled Sporting to a memorable Champions League triumph over Manchester City in 2024.

‌



The 26-year-old impressed despite his national team crashing out at the group stage. He contributed to all three goals from Marcelo Bielsa's side, netting twice and laying on a goal for Agustin Canobbio

Capable of playing at left-back or on the left wing, Araujo's adaptability could appeal to United. However, they may be wary of spending too much on a Sporting star with Gyokeres blowing hot and cold for Arsenal and Manuel Ugarte - also once of the Portuguese side - struggling in United red.

Antonio Nusa

Staying with wide options, Nusa has been linked with a Premier League switch for a number of years. At his first World Cup, the Norway winger demonstrated precisely why that's been the case.

‌



The 21-year-old was chiefly deployed on the left by Stale Solbakken, finding the net in the round of 32 triumph over Côte d'Ivoire. His ability to dovetail with Erling Haaland won't have gone unnoticed and it could be time to give him a chance in English football.

Nusa's youth means there's considerable room for growth. That said, current club RB Leipzig are unlikely to let him go on the cheap.

Manu Kone

United are already believed to be among the contenders for Kone as they aim to add one more central midfielder. The Roma man is anticipated to be available for just over £40m, enabling the Giallorossi to more than double their investment.

‌



Kone caught the eye during his outings for France and some believed he was underutilised by Didier Deschamps. The 25-year-old was left out of the starting XI for the semi-final against Spain and was unable to make up for lost time when he entered at the break.

The former Toulouse man previously attracted interest from the Premier League during his time at Borussia Monchengladbach, with United, Liverpool and Chelsea all thought to be admirers. Liverpool could yet emerge as rivals this summer too, should Michael Carrick's side fail to move swiftly.
