Sports.title: Sam Noakes Refuses To Write Off Denys Berinchyk
Sports.content:
“Keyshawn’s an anomaly. He’s different. We have to watch and study the other fights. Not so much that one,” Noakes said to Ring Magazine when asked how much weight he puts on Berinchyk’s loss to Davis. “He’s still a very good fighter. Losing to Keyshawn Davis don’t make him like, ‘Oh, he’s rubbish. It’s an easy fight for me now.’ There’s things to take away from that, but at the end I’m still going in there thinking he’s still a dangerous fight. He’s a live fighter, so I’m focusing on that.”

Noakes meets Berinchyk on the undercard of the Moses Itauma versus Filip Hrgovic heavyweight event. The former WBO lightweight champion remains the biggest name on Noakes’ resume since his unanimous decision loss to Abdullah Mason last November.

Berinchyk built his reputation long before the Davis fight. The Ukrainian captured the WBO lightweight title with an upset victory over Emanuel Navarrete after an accomplished amateur career. Noakes believes Berinchyk should be judged by his body of work rather than one disappointing performance.

The English contender admitted Berinchyk presents a difficult assignment despite the recent criticism directed at the former champion.

A victory would move Noakes closer to another world title opportunity. He expects a demanding fight rather than the one-sided contest many people anticipate after Berinchyk’s defeat to Davis.

Sports.title: Andy Ruiz Jr. Reveals Anthony Joshua’s Key to Beating Tyson Fury
Sports.content:
“It’s going to be a good fight. I’m going to tell you the truth. If Tyson Fury gets in Joshua’s head, he boxes around, moves around, throw his combinations, maybe it could affect Anthony Joshua,” said Ruiz to talkSPORT Boxing. “But if Anthony Joshua goes in there and starts banging out with Tyson Fury, he could probably win. It only takes one punch to change the whole fight. That’s going to be an exciting fight.”

Ruiz’s perspective is unique because he forced Joshua into a dramatic change in approach after their first meeting at Madison Square Garden. Joshua boxed cautiously during their rematch six months later to regain his heavyweight titles. Since then, he has relied more on discipline than sustained aggression.

Ruiz believes that style gives Fury an advantage. In his view, Joshua improves his chances only by forcing the action from the opening bell. That approach leaves Fury reacting instead of controlling the pace.

Ruiz will first try to restart his own title pursuit against Knyba after nearly two years away from competition. A victory would keep the former unified champion in the heavyweight picture following Oleksandr Usyk’s decision to vacate his heavyweight titles.

Sports.title: Andy Cruz Targets Raymond Muratalla While Eyeing 130 Pounds
Sports.content:
If he’s serious about dropping to 130, he’ll need to begin climbing the rankings in a new division. If the priority remains a rematch with Muratalla, staying at lightweight makes more sense. Trying to keep both options open may leave him waiting for opportunities that never arrive.

After his victory over Montoya, Cruz said he’s prepared for a new challenge.

“I like challenges, and tonight was just that. My last fight didn’t go my way, but I was able to demonstrate what I have this time,” said Cruz,

Cruz made it clear that Muratalla remains the opponent he wants most.

“Truthfully, the No. 1 thing on my list is to get the rematch against Muratalla,” said Cruz to The Ring.

“I can beat [WBO lightweight champion Abdullah] Mason. I can beat whoever isn’t Mason. I think Mason is a great fighter with a bright future. The only question is when the fight will happen. “I think the fights on August 1 are going to be great as well. I see Muratalla coming out victorious. Zepeda and Roach will be an even more interesting fight, but I have to give Roach more of the edge.”

Cruz also discussed Lomachenko, saying the former three-division champion has long been someone he admired because of their accomplished amateur careers.

The challenge for Cruz isn’t identifying opponents. It’s creating a realistic path to those fights.

Champions at 130 and 135 have little incentive to volunteer for a technically gifted opponent who isn’t yet a major commercial draw. Unless Cruz earns another mandatory position through the rankings or a titleholder has no better alternatives, he may find himself waiting longer than expected despite possessing the talent to compete with anyone in either division.

Sports.title: Sugar Ray Robinson Rallies Past Rocky Castellani After Knockdown
Sports.content:
Robinson came into the Cow Palace carrying more questions than answers. The former welterweight champion and two-time middleweight king had retired in late 1952 to pursue an entertainment career before returning to boxing. His comeback had already suffered a setback in a decision loss to Ralph “Tiger” Jones, leaving many to wonder if the brilliant fighter from the previous decade still had enough left to compete with the best middleweights in the world.

His opponent provided the perfect measuring stick. Castellani was the No. 1 ranked middleweight contender after falling short in a title challenge against Bobo Olson the previous year. Oddsmakers installed him as roughly a two-to-one favorite, believing the younger contender’s pressure and strength would be too much for the 34-year-old Robinson.

Neither man had a championship on the line, but the fight carried enormous significance. Robinson needed a victory to earn another opportunity at Olson and the middleweight title. Castellani knew a win over boxing’s biggest star would almost certainly lead him back into championship contention.

Both fighters weighed 160 pounds for the scheduled 10-round bout. The nationally televised contest drew 8,230 fans. The live gate totaled $39,819. Referee Jack Downey officiated the fight, with Jack Silver and Frankie Carter serving as judges.

The action lived up to expectations from the opening bell. Castellani pressed the fight immediately, forcing Robinson to give ground while looking for room to box. Early in the contest, he landed several heavy punches, including one that visibly shook Robinson. His legs briefly buckled. Robinson answered with crisp combinations, a sharp jab, and steady body punching whenever Castellani crowded inside.

The dramatic moment arrived in the sixth round. Castellani connected with a powerful left hook before following with a right hand that sent Robinson to his knees. Robinson took a nine-count before climbing to his feet. He survived the remainder of the round. It was the only knockdown of the fight and one of the few times Robinson appeared seriously hurt during his comeback.

Instead of fading, Robinson produced his best boxing over the final four rounds. He invested heavily downstairs, slowing Castellani’s attack with repeated body shots before opening space for clean punches to the head. His footwork also became more effective as the fight wore on. That approach allowed him to dictate the range. Accurate combinations steadily increased his lead on the scorecards.

When the final bell sounded, the scoring reflected how competitive the contest had been. Referee Jack Downey scored it 56 to 54 for Robinson. Judge Frankie Carter also favored Robinson by a 56 to 54 margin, while Judge Jack Silver saw Castellani ahead 56 to 54. The split decision awarded Robinson the victory, although some observers believed Castellani had done enough after scoring the bout’s only knockdown. The Associated Press scored the fight 57 to 53 for Robinson, noting that he controlled nearly every round except the sixth.

The victory earned Robinson the opportunity he had been chasing. Five months later, he challenged Bobo Olson for the world middleweight championship and stopped him in two rounds to begin his third reign as champion. Castellani remained one of the division’s toughest contenders, but he never captured a world title despite giving Robinson one of the sternest tests of his celebrated comeback.

Sports.title: Ryan Garcia Accuses Devin Haney of Hookah Habit
Sports.content:
The exchange started after Ariel Helwani shared a clip of Garcia discussing Zuffa Boxing. Ryan praised Dana White’s early work with the promotion. He also said he would keep his own identity instead of dressing like a company spokesman if he ever signed with Zuffa. Haney posted, “Ryan back doing that twitch with his face again.”

Garcia answered with a series of posts on X, insisting Haney has no room to question his professionalism while hiding what Garcia described as his own vice.

“Devin just claimed I’m on some type of bender 😂😂 My dude you smoke hookah you are destroying your lungs you about to get ran over my Keyshawn for all the smoking in those lungs.”

Ryan rejected one fan’s suggestion that he delete the post.

“I got solid proof he smokes hookah as well. So he can’t deny this claim,” said Ryan on X about Haney. “Nah, he wants to pish the narrative like I’m not some professional while hiding behind his hand, knowing he has vices he’s hiding nah sorry I’m not his friend or his buddy f*** him.”

Ryan also predicted Haney’s hookah use will hurt him when he eventually defends his WBO title against Keyshawn Davis, who became the mandatory challenger after moving up to welterweight.

The latest exchange is another sign the rivalry between the former opponents remains bitter. Their April 2024 bout was later changed to a no contest after Garcia tested positive for Ostarine. Both fighters have continued trading insults as the possibility of a rematch has taken a back seat to other fights.

Sports.title: Yoenli Hernandez Named WBO Mandatory for Denzel Bentley
Sports.content:
The designation came in the same WBO resolution that accepted Janibek Alimkhanuly’s decision to relinquish the title and elevated Bentley from interim champion to full WBO titleholder.

The committee, however, stopped short of ordering the fight immediately.

Instead, the WBO reserved the right to determine later whether Bentley’s first title defense must come against Hernandez or if the new champion will be permitted to make a voluntary defense first. No timetable for that decision was included in the resolution.

If the WBO orders the mandatory defense, Bentley would begin his championship reign against one of the division’s most dangerous contenders.

Hernandez (10-0, 9 KOs) has built a reputation as one of boxing’s top middleweight prospects after a decorated amateur career that included multiple Cuban national titles plus international success. Since turning professional, the southpaw has continued to climb the rankings while establishing himself as one of the division’s most avoided contenders.

The committee’s ruling leaves Bentley’s immediate future uncertain. A voluntary defense would give him an opportunity to make his first title defense against another opponent before eventually satisfying the mandatory obligation.

Hernandez, 29, now occupies the front of the line for the WBO championship.

The next move belongs to the WBO, which must determine whether Bentley opens his reign with a mandatory defense against Hernandez or receives approval for a voluntary bout before the title shot is enforced.

Sports.title: Alan Chaves Defends WBO Latino Title Against Eridson Garcia September 4
Sports.content:
The 25-year-old Chaves is one of Matchroom’s rising prospects at 135 pounds. He remains several steps away from landing fights against the division’s established contenders, but each outing gives him another opportunity to strengthen his position in the rankings.

Chaves (22-0, 19 KOs) comes into the fight after stopping Miguel Madueno in April with a crushing left hook in the third round that became one of the year’s most discussed knockouts. He has stopped his last five opponents. Chaves enters the bout ranked No. 2 by the WBO, No. 4 by the IBF and No. 7 by the WBC.

“I appreciate Eridson accepting the fight when others didn’t,” said Chaves. “He earned the opportunity. Now he has to earn the victory. That’s a much harder task.” “Alan Chaves is undefeated, dangerous and coming off a knockout everyone is talking about,” Garcia said. “Good, that means there will be no excuses when I beat him. He has never faced anyone with my experience or the ability to take away his weapons. “They call him ‘Veneno,’ but I’m bringing the antidote, and I’m coming to hand him the first loss of his career.”

Garcia hopes to rebound after a ten-round defeat in April snapped his six-fight winning streak. He can score the biggest victory of his career by upsetting Chaves. That result would strengthen his standing in the lightweight rankings.

The fight joins a September 4 card headlined by Ruiz’s comeback against Knyba. Vito Mielnicki Jr. meets Austin Williams in the co-feature. Zaquin Moses, Dennis Thompson and Brooke Mullen are also scheduled to appear. The event will air on TNT, truTV and DAZN in the United States. DAZN will also carry the broadcast internationally.

Sports.title: Ryan Garcia Predicts Conor Benn Knockout After Bold Las Vegas Warning
Sports.content:
“You’re going to get hit, and you’re like, ‘What the hell just hit me?’ And it’s going to happen over and over and over,” Ryan said on the Mr. Verzace podcast. “Then before you know it, you’re going to get so angry, and you’re going to run into something bad. Then you’re going to be on the floor like, ‘What happened?’ Then I’m going to finish you off. That’s all that’s going to happen.”

Benn quickly rejected that forecast, remaining convinced Ryan will not survive past the middle rounds. The British challenger questioned Ryan’s toughness, pointing to previous fights where Garcia took a knee after getting hurt.

“Five rounds or less,” Benn stated. “I mean it, and I stand on that. You would not make it past five. I just don’t respect people who have no heart who want to look for the easy way out. He has talent, athleticism, and youth. Yeah, I give him that. But I’m a fighter. So when I put it on him in there, we’ll see how he handles that. Come meet me in the middle of the ring first round. Let’s have a shootout.”

Ryan said his experience is the edge. He believes Benn will realize there are answers for everything he brings once the rounds begin.

Ghana News.title: Police arrest two at Asawase Market over suspected narcotic drugs concealed in fertiliser sacks
Ghana News.content:
The Manhyia District Police Command has arrested two men in connection with the unlawful possession and transportation of substances suspected to be narcotic drugs following an intelligence-led operation at the Asawase Market in Kumasi.

The operation, conducted on July 21, 2026, resulted in the seizure of 100 compressed parcels of dried leaves suspected to be narcotic drugs concealed in fertiliser sacks hidden among second-hand clothing.

The suspects have been identified as Osman Bassein, 37, and Mohammed Abdul-Razak, 38.

In a statement signed by the Head of the Public Affairs Unit of the Ashanti Regional Police Command, Superintendent Godwin Ahianyo, the Police said the operation was launched after receiving credible intelligence that suspected narcotic drugs were being transported in fertiliser sacks.

Acting on the information, a team led by the Manhyia District Commander, supported by personnel from the Manhyia Divisional Criminal Investigations Department (CID) and the Zongo Police Station, proceeded to the location and arrested the two suspects.

During a search conducted in the presence of independent witnesses, officers recovered 13 fertiliser sacks.

Police said further inspection revealed that the sacks contained second-hand clothing concealing 100 compressed parcels of dried leaves suspected to be narcotic drugs.

The exhibits were photographed at the scene in accordance with evidential procedures and have since been secured for forensic examination.

The suspects are currently in police custody assisting with investigations and will be processed in accordance with the law, subject to the outcome of the investigations.

The Ashanti Regional Police Command commended members of the public for providing timely and credible information that contributed to the operation.

It also encouraged the public to continue supporting law enforcement efforts by reporting suspicious activities through the Police emergency numbers 18555 (MTN toll-free), 191 or 112.

Police noted that investigations are ongoing and further updates will be provided as the case progresses.

Ghana News.title: Accra to host Pan-African conference on economic restructuring, political reforms
Ghana News.content:
Kwame Danquah, President of Harakati Za Muungano

Accra is set to host more than 200 delegates from across Africa for an international conference on economic restructuring, political reforms and regional integration.

The conference, scheduled for June 24, 2026, at the GNAT Hall, will bring together policymakers, academics, business leaders, traditional authorities, civil society organisations, youth leaders and development partners.

Organised by Harakati Za Muungano, a pan-African movement whose name means “Union Movement” in Swahili, the conference will focus on practical strategies to accelerate Africa’s development through deeper regional integration.

Key issues expected to be discussed include constitutional reforms, economic restructuring, regional market integration, industrialisation, governance continuity and sustainable financing models for development.

The organisers say the discussions are expected to produce practical recommendations to inform policy decisions at both national and regional levels.

Harakati Za Muungano, established in November 2023, has expanded its operations to 17 African countries, where it engages governments, regional institutions, traditional leaders, professionals, youth groups and community organisations.

Its work focuses on policy advocacy, research, civic engagement and humanitarian initiatives aimed at promoting inclusive development, strengthening regional cooperation and supporting reforms to improve the quality of life of Africans.

The movement advocates a more integrated Sub-Saharan Africa, where barriers to trade and movement are reduced, economic cooperation is strengthened and governments adopt policies that promote long-term planning, investment and shared prosperity.

According to the organisers, greater integration could create new opportunities for businesses, boost job creation, promote industrial growth and enhance Africa’s competitiveness in the global economy.

They say the conference will provide an opportunity for African leaders and stakeholders to examine bold and innovative approaches to the continent’s future while strengthening partnerships and advancing a shared vision of an economically resilient, politically stable and fully integrated Africa.

Ghana News.title: When Chairman Wontumi’s 20-year sentence marks a turning point in the fight against political impunity
Ghana News.content:
Bernard Antwi Boasiako, aka Wontumi

There is an old legal truth that deserves renewed attention: “Justice delayed is not justice denied where the law permits prosecution, but justice obstructed by power is a betrayal of the Republic.”

Chairman Wontumi's conviction is therefore not merely about one individual. It is an indictment of a culture that believed political influence could permanently silence the law.

For years, Ghana watched forests disappear, rivers turn brown, communities flood, and livelihoods vanish beneath the greed of illegal mining. Petitions after petitions were reportedly submitted. Warnings were allegedly issued. Yet decisive enforcement appeared conspicuously absent. The question is not whether government officials knew illegal mining existed. The more uncomfortable question is what they did with that knowledge.

If petitions concerning Akonta Mining reached the highest levels of the previous administration, then history will judge not only those accused of illegal mining but also those who chose hesitation over constitutional duty. A government that preaches the rule of law while allowing influential allies to enjoy what many perceived as political immunity weakens public confidence in justice itself.

Former President Nana Akufo-Addo and former Vice President Dr. Mahamudu Bawumia cannot simply escape legitimate public scrutiny over allegations that repeated concerns about illegal mining involving politically exposed persons failed to receive timely and decisive action. Hence the nickname “Mr clearing agent”. Leadership carries responsibility not only for acts committed but also for opportunities ignored.

The High Court has now demonstrated something profoundly important: no political office, party title or financial influence should place anyone above the law. As for the critics of the decision, their arguments speak for themselves, and the less said about them, the better.

It is obvious the court's ruling is based on the evidence and the law, not politics. After reading the judgment several times, I am convinced by the judge's reasoning, especially the circumstantial evidence and the cross-examination of the defence witness. In my view, attempts to politicise the case and the opposition's press conference fail to address the legal issues in the judgment.

Justice Audrey Kocuvie-Tay deserves commendation for discharging her constitutional mandate without apparent regard for the political stature of the accused. Delivering judgment against an ordinary citizen requires legal competence. Delivering judgment against a politically influential figure demands something more than judicial courage. Courts exist precisely for moments when power expects exemption.

Predictably, the conviction has generated accusations of selective justice. Equality before the law does not require every suspect to be prosecuted simultaneously. Criminal investigations mature at different times, evidence is gathered at different speeds, and prosecutions proceed according to available proof. The constitutional guarantee is equal application of the law, not synchronised arrests.

However, those defending the judgment must also embrace the same principle consistently. If investigations reportedly exist concerning persons associated with the current administration or any other political party, they must proceed with equal determination. Justice cannot become a revolving door that prosecutes yesterday's favourites while protecting today's allies. The law must remain gloriously indifferent to party colours.

Illegal mining is not an NPP crime or an NDC crime. It is a crime against Ghana.

Every poisoned river denies children safe drinking water. Every destroyed forest mortgages the country's environmental future. Samreboi community pays the price for someone's unlawful profit. Nature conducts no political registration before delivering disaster. Floodwaters do not ask whether victims voted NPP, NDC or any other party. Environmental destruction is ruthlessly non-partisan.

Some people in the NPP seem determined to create more disaffection for their own party than their political opponents ever could.

How on earth do you tell Ghanaians that if you return to power, Chairman Wontumi will simply be set free? Then others chime in with the familiar "the tables will turn" refrain, as though justice is a football match with home and away fixtures. Such utterances are not only childish but very damaging to their party.

If you genuinely believe there are legal grounds, then support an appeal and seek a reduction of the sentence through the courts. That is how the rule of law works.

How do you expect the average Ghanaian to willingly vote for a message that appears to put political power above due process? In the end, the electorate will decide. We wish you all the best.

But the hard truth is whatever the outcome on appeal, one lesson should already be unmistakably clear: political influence has an expiry date; accountability does not.

The true measure of this moment will not be whether one prominent individual was convicted. It will be whether Ghana finally develops the institutional courage to pursue every alleged illegal mining kingpin, regardless of wealth, office, surname or political affiliation. Until then, prosecutions risk appearing episodic rather than transformative.

The Republic cannot afford selective outrage or selective justice. It needs selective fear by every public official, financier and politically connected individual contemplating environmental crime. Fear that one day the Constitution, the courts and the evidence will meet.

At the very least, it is a matter of public record that President Mahama's first administration prosecuted some of its own officials. There was even a deputy minister who expressed a personal wish and was subsequently dismissed from office.

For too long, Ghana's forests have carried the scars of human greed while politics supplied convenient insurance policies. If this judgment marks the cancellation of those policies, then history may remember it not simply as the conviction of one man, but as the day the law finally found its voice and reminded the powerful that the Republic belongs not to politicians, but to justice.

Ghana News.title: ADRA Ghana donates relief items, calls for sustainable recovery support for June 29 flood victims
Ghana News.content:
The Adventist Development and Relief Agency (ADRA) Ghana has called for a shift from emergency relief to long-term recovery support for families affected by the June 29 floods, saying many victims now face the challenge of rebuilding their homes and livelihoods.

The organisation appealed while presenting relief items to the National Disaster Management Organisation (NADMO) in Accra to support ongoing assistance for flood victims.

Citing NADMO data, ADRA Ghana said nearly 90,000 households were affected by the floods, leaving many families displaced after losing homes, personal belongings and sources of income.

Speaking at the presentation, ADRA Ghana Country Director, Dr Isaac Kankam-Boadu, said although emergency relief remains critical, sustainable recovery should focus on helping affected families regain their livelihoods.

"Our mandate calls us to action, and that is why we have mobilised resources from our international office, our regional office and within the Seventh-day Adventist Church in Ghana to support victims of the floods," he said.

Dr Kankam-Boadu disclosed that ADRA Ghana had mobilised about US$20,000, equivalent to approximately GH¢224,000, to procure relief items, including toiletries, student mattresses, detergents, washing powder and other household essentials identified by NADMO as urgent needs.

He said the organisation intends to work beyond relief distribution by partnering with NADMO and development partners to help affected families rebuild their livelihoods.

"After this presentation, we will engage our donor partners and, once NADMO identifies the beneficiaries, work collaboratively to provide skills training and livelihood support so affected victims can generate income and bounce back to their former state," he said.

He added that ADRA Ghana is also prepared to deploy volunteers to provide psychosocial support and health education during community-level relief distribution.

Dr Kankam-Boadu attributed the growing severity of flooding in Ghana to the combined effects of climate change and human activities.

"Climate change is leading to higher rainfall, while the rapid concretisation of our urban areas reduces the ability of the soil to absorb excess water. At the same time, citizens must be educated on how to manage the environment to reduce flood risks," he stated.

Receiving the items on behalf of the government, NADMO Deputy Director-General in charge of Technical, Alhaji Ahmed-Rufai Afarahim, expressed appreciation to ADRA Ghana and assured that the relief items would reach the affected communities.

"We promise these items will get to the victims of the June 29 flood disaster," he said.

He described the donation as a demonstration of national solidarity, noting that disasters affect people regardless of their religion or background.

"The disaster doesn't know who is a Christian and who is a Muslim. We thank ADRA for what they have done," he added.

The June 29 floods affected several communities across Ghana, causing widespread destruction and displacing thousands of households. As recovery efforts continue, ADRA Ghana says sustained partnerships and livelihood support will be critical to helping affected families rebuild their lives.

Ghana News.title: GRA Customs explains how imported vehicles are classified and valued for duty assessment
Ghana News.content:
Officials of the Ghana Revenue Authority (GRA) Customs Division have explained the process used to classify and value imported vehicles, stating that duty assessments are based on internationally accepted customs procedures designed to ensure fairness and consistency.

Speaking on Joy FM's Super Morning Show, Principal Revenue Officer at the Safe Bond Car Terminal in Tema, Emelia Ewenam Ankrah, and Senior Revenue Officer at the Technical Services Bureau, Daniel Kwame Ntem, said vehicle duty assessment follows two key stages — classification and valuation.

According to the officials, Customs first classifies a vehicle to determine the applicable tax rate before establishing its customs value for the calculation of duties and taxes.

Ms Ankrah explained that once an importer or declarant submits an application for duty assessment, Customs officers identify the vehicle using its unique Vehicle Identification Number (VIN), commonly referred to as the chassis number.

She said the VIN is decoded to retrieve key technical information, including the vehicle's fuel type, whether petrol, diesel, electric or hybrid, the year of manufacture, seating capacity and other specifications.

These details, she noted, enable Customs to assign the appropriate Harmonized System (HS) Code, which determines the tariff classification and corresponding import duty.

The officials explained that certain vehicle characteristics can significantly affect classification. For instance, buses are classified differently from passenger vehicles because of their seating capacity and intended purpose.

They stressed that accurate VIN decoding is critical to ensuring every imported vehicle is placed under the correct tariff heading.

Once the classification process is completed, Customs proceeds to the valuation stage, where the customs value of the vehicle is determined before the applicable duties and taxes are calculated.

The officials said classification and valuation are separate but complementary processes that help ensure transparency, consistency and compliance with international customs standards.

Their explanation comes amid heightened public interest in Ghana's vehicle import duty regime, particularly following discussions on customs valuation methods and the application of the Home Delivery Value (HDV) system.

The GRA Customs Division maintained that the established procedures are intended to ensure that all imported vehicles are assessed fairly and in accordance with the law.

Ghana News.title: MP Elikplim Akurugu commissions renovated KG block at Taifa Community School
Ghana News.content:
The Member of Parliament for Dome-Kwabenya, Faustina Elikplim Akurugu, has commissioned a renovated kindergarten block at the Taifa Community School, describing education as the foundation for the constituency's development.

The renovation of the kindergarten block was sponsored by Imperial Homes through its Imperial Charity Foundation as part of efforts to provide pupils with a safe and conducive environment for teaching and learning.

The commissioning ceremony was attended by the Ga East Municipal Chief Executive, Edmund Agboh; the Assembly Member for Taifa; the Queenmother of Taifa; members of the Council of Elders; Unit Committee Members; the Municipal Director of Education; the Chairman of the Conference of Heads of Schools; the School Management Committee (SMC); the PTA Chairman and executives; headteachers, teachers, pupils and residents.

Speaking at the event, Madam Akurugu thanked Imperial Homes and the Imperial Charity Foundation for partnering with her office to improve educational infrastructure in the constituency.

"I want to express my sincere appreciation to Imperial Homes and the Imperial Charity Foundation for supporting this important project.

“By investing in this kindergarten block, you are investing in the future of our children and the future of Dome-Kwabenya," she said.

The MP said education remains one of the key priorities of her tenure and highlighted several interventions she has undertaken to improve access to quality education in the constituency.

According to her, these include the distribution of desks to schools, exercise books to pupils, mathematical sets to BECE candidates, renovation of the Kwabenya Senior High School library, distribution of school uniforms, financial assistance to needy students and the introduction of the Elikplim Scholarship Scheme.

She noted that creating a conducive learning environment would help improve academic performance and inspire children to reach their full potential.

The Ga East Municipal Chief Executive, Edmund Agboh, urged teachers, pupils and the community to ensure the facility is properly maintained.

"This facility is for the benefit of our children. Let us all take responsibility for protecting it and ensuring that it serves generations of pupils," he said.

The Municipal Director of Education, Eric Sey, commended the MP for prioritising education and assured that the renovated facility would be put to good use.

"We are grateful to the Member of Parliament for this intervention. The Education Directorate will ensure that this facility is well maintained and used to support effective teaching and learning," he stated.

Ghana News.title: What Is Wrong With Us: We cannot always choose our circumstances. We can always choose our response
Ghana News.content:
Ing. Professor Douglas Boateng Chartered Director (UK) • Chartered Engineer (UK) • Fellow Institute of Directors (UK) • Fellow Ghana Institution of Engineering

Africa has endured colonialism, conflict and extraction. It possesses minerals, land and the world's youngest population. And still the question persists, quietly and without mercy: what are we choosing to do with what we have?

At Some Point, The Explanation Becomes The Prison

Perhaps no continent has endured more genuine historical adversity than Africa. Colonialism disrupted societies, arbitrarily drawn borders fragmented communities, slavery robbed millions of their dignity and global inequalities continue to distort trade and development. These facts must never be minimised or forgotten.

And yet. There is another truth, far less comfortable to acknowledge, that sits beside those facts and refuses to leave. History may explain where we started. It cannot permanently excuse where we choose to remain.

Across Africa, it has become common to attribute almost every contemporary challenge to circumstances beyond our control. When institutions fail, we blame history. When infrastructure deteriorates, we blame previous governments. When corruption flourishes, we blame politics. When cities flood, we blame climate change. Many of these explanations contain truth. But explanations are not solutions. And at some point, which few of us are brave enough to name precisely, explanations become excuses. Circumstances become hiding places for choices we simply refuse to make.

That is the question this article will not look away from. What is wrong with us?

“Circumstances introduce us to life. Choices introduce us to history.”

NyansaKasa — Words of Wisdom

Sit with that for a moment. We rarely control how the story begins. But we are never without agency in how it continues. Every society that has ever transformed itself understood, at some point, that waiting for circumstances to improve was itself a choice, and one of the most expensive a nation can make. The question is not what happened to us. It is what we are doing, right now, with what remains.

When Circumstances Become Convenient Excuses

No nation chooses whether rain falls. But every nation chooses whether drains are maintained. No country chooses global commodity prices. But every country chooses whether to diversify its economy. No government chooses where minerals are located. But every government chooses how transparently those resources are managed. No community chooses every disease outbreak. But every community chooses whether refuse is dumped into gutters or whether sanitation becomes a daily non-negotiable.

The distinction matters because too often Africa confuses unavoidable circumstances with entirely avoidable decisions. When plastic waste blocks drainage systems, rainfall is not the primary problem. When roads deteriorate because overloaded vehicles repeatedly destroy them, weather is not the principal issue. When schools fall into disrepair despite substantial investments in their construction, time is not the enemy. Neglect is. Choice is. Circumstances present challenges. Choices determine outcomes. That sentence deserves to be read again slowly, and then applied to every institution, every community and every individual on this continent.

“History rarely rewards those who waited for perfect circumstances. It remembers those who created better ones.”

NyansaKasa — Words of Wisdom

Japan rose from the ruins of a world war. Singapore built a global economy from a city with almost nothing beneath its soil. South Korea was once poorer than many African nations and chose, in the space of two generations, to become a technological powerhouse. Rwanda emerged from the darkest hour a people can endure and chose, deliberately and consistently, to rebuild. None of them had perfect circumstances. They had something rarer and more powerful: the collective decision to stop waiting for permission from history to move forward.

Africa's Greatest Resource Is Not Beneath the Ground

Africa holds approximately 30% of the world's known mineral reserves. It has vast arable land, immense renewable energy potential and the youngest population of any continent on earth. By 2050, Africa's population will approach 2.5 billion people, one of the greatest concentrations of human potential anywhere in human history. And yet natural wealth has never, in the whole of recorded history, guaranteed national prosperity.

Because resources are circumstances. Institutions are choices. Minerals do not govern themselves. Rivers do not educate children. Sunlight does not eliminate corruption. Population growth alone creates not prosperity but pressure, unless it is met by the deliberate choices of governance, education, investment and accountability that convert human potential into lasting human progress.

‘Resources are circumstances. Institutions are choices.’

“Natural resources may enrich a nation temporarily. Wise choices enrich generations.”

NyansaKasa — Words of Wisdom

Botswana has no ocean. It has no strategic port. It sits landlocked in southern Africa, blessed with diamonds and governed, crucially, with a seriousness of purpose that most resource-rich nations have failed to sustain. Mauritius has even fewer natural endowments and has nonetheless built one of Africa's strongest and most diversified economies through precisely that quality: the consistent, unglamorous, deeply disciplined choice to govern well when it would have been so much easier not to.

The Cost of Choosing Convenience Over Responsibility

Many of Africa's greatest challenges are not the product of insufficient knowledge. They are the product of insufficient discipline. We know that dumping refuse into gutters contributes to flooding, yet many continue. We know that routine maintenance costs far less than replacing destroyed infrastructure, yet maintenance budgets are routinely sacrificed. We know that corruption diverts scarce public resources from schools, hospitals and roads, yet many continue to participate in it whenever it appears personally convenient. None of these outcomes result primarily from ignorance. They result from choices. And that is the most uncomfortable truth of all, because it means the solution does not lie elsewhere. It lies with us.

Africa's children are watching. They are learning not only from speeches but from behaviour. They observe how we respond to adversity, how we treat public property, how seriously we take our responsibilities as citizens. One day they will inherit our institutions. More importantly, they will inherit our habits. And habits, unlike policies, do not change because an election was held.

“Wisdom is not measured by what we know. It is measured by what we consistently choose to do.”

NyansaKasa — Words of Wisdom

That distinction should stop every one of us cold. We have attended the conferences. We have written the reports. We have delivered eloquent speeches about transformation and the Africa we want. And then, in the car on the way home, some of us have thrown plastic out of the window. Knowledge tells us what is right. Wisdom is what happens when we choose it anyway, even when no one is watching, even when it costs something.

The Choice That Still Belongs To Us

Africa's story is not finished. It is not predetermined. It is not imprisoned by colonial history, economic inequality or global competition, however real and however painful those realities remain. The next chapter will be determined not by what was done to Africa but by what Africa chooses to do next. Every road properly maintained instead of neglected. Every river protected instead of poisoned. Every young person inspired instead of abandoned. Every act of honesty chosen over corruption. Every citizen who decides that integrity matters even when no one is watching. These choices may appear small in isolation. Together, they are the only force in human history that has ever genuinely changed a nation.

History will record that Africa possessed minerals, land, brilliant young people, extraordinary resilience and immense potential. But history will ask one question that no continent can escape: what choices did we make with the gifts we were given? Circumstances may explain where we are today. They do not determine where we must be tomorrow. That decision, still, belongs to us.

“Your circumstances may influence your journey, but your choices determine your destination.”

NyansaKasa — Words of Wisdom

Before we blame history, geography, politics or fate, perhaps we owe ourselves one moment of genuine reflection. Not the comfortable kind, performed in public, in eloquent language, to an admiring audience. The uncomfortable kind. The private kind. The kind that asks, without flinching, what we have personally chosen today that made this continent even slightly better than it was yesterday. And if the answer is nothing, then perhaps that is precisely what is wrong with us. And perhaps, more importantly, it is exactly where the healing begins.

ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Ing. Professor Douglas Boateng is a pioneering international industrial engineer, governance strategist and Pan-African thought leader whose work continues to shape boardroom thinking, supply chain transformation and industrialisation across the continent and globally. Africa's first Professor Extraordinaire in Supply Chain Management, he is an International Chartered Director and Chartered Engineer, a recipient of numerous lifetime achievement awards, and the author of several authoritative books. He is also the founder and scriber of NyansaKasa (Words of Wisdom), whose daily reflections on leadership, accountability and purposeful living have reached one million readers worldwide. His driving conviction: Africa's transformation is not waiting for better rhetoric. It is waiting for better choices, made by leaders willing to serve something larger than themselves.

Ghana News.title: THE LAW 101: The Akonta Mining Judgment
Ghana News.content:
Bernard Antwi Boasiako, popularly known as Chairman Wontumi

Introduction

This is a bit of hard law. After an early morning court session Monday, I entered this courtroom and spent about 45 minutes listening to the delivery of this judgment before heading to a case in the Commercial Court two floors up in the complex. A judgment of this magnitude, touching on environmental degradation and the exploitation of public resources, carries legal significance that resonates far beyond the courtroom.

By the time I left, the judge was concluding her detailed analysis of the facts and evidence on Counts 4 and 6. Her meticulous approach was striking. Initially, I was under the impression that Chairman Wontumi had still not filed his address. What emerges is a judgment with profound implications for corporate governance, statutory compliance, and the national fight against galamsey.

This brief unpacks the judgment - from the preliminary constitutional challenges and the piercing of the corporate veil to the evidentiary standards, statutory prison remission calculations, and financial penalties imposed by the court.

Case Overview and the Legal Framework

In The Republic v. Bernard Antwi Boasiako @ Chairman Wontumi, Kwame Antwi (at large), and Akonta Mining Company Limited, the High Court of Justice (Criminal Court 4), Accra, presided over by Her Ladyship Justice Audrey Kocuvie-Tay, delivered the judgment addressing the regulatory and criminal frameworks governing national mineral exploitation. That is what this case was essentially about - allowing third parties onto an exclusive concession without the required prior ministerial approval.

The State mounted six charges against the 1st Accused, Bernard Antwi Boasiako (A1). The 3rd Accused is Akonta Mining Company Limited (A3), which he co-owns with the 2nd Accused, Kwame Antwi (A2), who remained at large throughout the trial.

All charges were grounded in the Minerals and Mining Act, 2006 (Act 703), as amended by the Minerals and Mining (Amendment) Act, 2019 (Act 995). The charges centered on two primary offences:

Assignment of mineral rights without approval, contrary to Section 14(1) (which prohibits transferring, assigning, mortgaging, or encumbering a mineral right without written ministerial approval) and Section 99(2)(b) of Act 703 (Counts 1, 2, and 3).

Purposely facilitating an unlicensed mining operation, contrary to Section 99(2)(b) of Act 703 (which creates penal liability for aiding, facilitating, or promoting any breach of the Act where no specific penalty is listed) (Counts 4, 5, and 6).

Factual Background: The Samreboi Operation and Seized Evidence

The narrative established by the Prosecution revealed that on April 16, 2025, police officers embarked on an "anti-galamsey" operation in the Samreboi Forest within the Western Region. The next day, the team arrested Michael Gyadu Ayisi (PW1) alongside 28 workers occupying a physical structure bearing the bold corporate name of Akonta Mining Company Limited (A3).

At the site, law enforcement seized an array of equipment and contraband, including:

25 serviceable excavators and 4 non-serviceable excavators.

8 pump-action guns, 1 single-barrelled gun, and 310 AAA/BB cartridges.

5 pieces of metal suspected to be gold contained in a sachet.

4 motorcycles, 2 vehicles, water-pumping machines, a grease gun, 4 machetes, and GH¢ 157,000.00 in cash.

During police interrogation, Michael Gyadu Ayisi (PW1) named Henry Okum (PW2) as his employer who directed operations on the concession. Following his arrest, Henry Okum (PW2) disclosed that in September 2024, he struck an oral arrangement with Bernard Antwi Boasiako (A1) to enter Akonta Mining’s concession to extract gold from unmined portions while using part of the gold proceeds to fund land reclamation (specifically planting coconut seedlings) on degraded, mined-out areas.

In his caution statement (Exhibit C) and witness statement, Bernard Antwi Boasiako (A1) admitted to granting verbal permission to Henry Okum (PW2), but asserted that his authorization was strictly restricted to land reclamation. A1 maintained that PW2's gold mining activities were unauthorized and conducted without his knowledge.

Key Evidence and How the Court Resolved the Issues

To resolve the case, the court isolated the essential legal requirements for each charge and evaluated the evidence to determine whether those legal tests were met beyond a reasonable doubt.

1. Resolution of Preliminary Constitutional Challenge

Before examining the facts, the court addressed a submission by new Defence Counsel Samuel Atta Akyea requesting a stay of judgment to refer Section 14(1) and Section 99(2)(b) of Act 703 to the Supreme Court under Article 130(2) of the 1992 Constitution - the provision vesting the Supreme Court with exclusive original jurisdiction over genuine questions of constitutional interpretation and requiring lower courts to refer such issues. The Defence argued these statutory provisions were unconstitutionally vague under Article 19(11) of the Constitution, which establishes the fundamental constitutional principle that every criminal offence and its penalty must be clearly defined and prescribed in a written law.

Justice Kocuvie-Tay refused to refer the matter, holding that lower courts should not delay trials unless a genuine ambiguity exists. Quoting settled constitutional law:

"A trial court is not obliged, upon the mere say-so of a party that a question of constitutional interpretation arises, to down its tools and refer the matter upstairs."

Citing The Republic v. Maikankan, Aduamoa II v. Twum II, Ex Parte James Gyakye Quayson, and The Republic v. Special Tribunal; Ex Parte Akosah, the court resolved that the written statutes clearly defined both the forbidden conduct and the penalties, making a Supreme Court referral unnecessary. Procedurally, Section 236 of the Criminal and Other Offences (Procedure) Act, 1960 (Act 30) operates as a similar, lawful statutory mechanism for criminal procedure generally, ensuring offences function by referencing substantive prohibitions without violating constitutional clarity.

This statutory framework gives effect to the Article 257 constitutional provision governing national resources, whereby all minerals in their natural state in Ghana are vested in the President on behalf of, and in trust for, the people of Ghana - thereby requiring strict statutory authorization and ministerial oversight before any third party can exploit or deal in mineral rights.

2. Applying Burdens of Proof and Standards of Evidence

The court anchored its evaluation on Section 15(1) of the Evidence Act, 1975 (NRCD 323), the codified rule establishing that the party alleging a crime (the Prosecution) bears the burden of persuasion throughout, and the general evidentiary rules under Part II of NRCD 323 regarding presumptions and proof.

Relying on landmark authorities:

Woolmington v. DPP & COP v. Antwi: The Prosecution carries the duty to prove every element of guilt, and the Defence only needs to raise a reasonable doubt to be acquitted.

Miller v. Minister of Pensions (per Lord Denning): Proof beyond reasonable doubt requires a high degree of probability, excluding purely "fanciful possibilities."

Trial of William Palmer: A court cannot convict an accused person based on mere suspicion, no matter how strong.

3. Resolving the "Land Reclamation" Defence via Circumstantial Evidence

Because there was no written agreement between A1 and PW2, the court applied the legal rules governing circumstantial evidence set out in Duah v. The Republic, The State v. Anani Fiadzo, and Logan & Laverick v. The Republic. Under these cases, circumstantial evidence can ground a conviction only if it leads to an irresistible conclusion that points solely to guilt.

The court resolved the conflict between A1’s claim (that he only allowed coconut planting) and PW2’s claim (that he was allowed to mine gold to pay for the coconut planting) by examining the common-sense facts:

Professional Background: Henry Okum (PW2) was a licensed small-scale miner, not a land reclamation specialist.

Reclamation Costs: Defence expert Wisdom Edem Gomashie (DW1) admitted under cross-examination that reclaiming mined land is very expensive.

Lack of Funding: A1 admitted he gave no money to PW2 to perform the reclamation.

The court concluded that it defied human reason for a small-scale miner to fund expensive land reclamation deep in a forest out of his own pocket for free. The only logical, irresistible conclusion was that A1 expected PW2 to finance the reclamation using gold mined from the concession.

4. Resolving the Absence of Statutory Approvals

Through Josef Iroko (PW4), an expert witness from the Minerals Commission, the Prosecution proved that Akonta Mining (A3) never submitted an application to assign or transfer its mineral rights. Under Clause 1(d) of Exhibit G (Mining Lease), the concession belonged exclusively to A3. Allowing a third party onto the land without written approval created an illegal encumbrance under Section 14(1) of Act 703.

In addition, land reclamation is legally classified as a "Mine Support Service" under Section 59 of Act 703, the regulatory provision requiring service providers to register with the Minerals Commission and obtain a license, and Regulation 2 of the Minerals and Mining (Support Services) Regulations, 2012 (L.I. 2174), which explicitly categorizes contract mining and reclamation under Categories A to C. Because PW2 was not registered or licensed as a support service provider, allowing him onto the land breached Section 59. Because Act 703 lists no specific penalty for breaching Section 59, it triggered the penal sanctions under Section 99(2)(b).

5. Lifting the Corporate Veil and Rejecting Technical Defences

Defence Counsel argued under the legal principle of ejusdem generis (that general words must be interpreted narrowly) that "otherwise dealt in" under Section 14(1) required a formal written document. He also cited Section 147(1) of the Companies Act, 2019 (Act 992), which provides that acts done by a managing director in the ordinary course of business are acts of the company as principal, and Dalex Finance v. Ebenezer Denzel Amanor to argue that corporate liabilities belong strictly to the company, not individual directors.

The court rejected both technicalities:

Statutory Purpose: A narrow reading of Section 14(1) would allow illegal miners to bypass the law simply by making informal, oral agreements.

Piercing the Corporate Veil: Applying Salomon v. Salomon & Co., Morkor v. Kuma (No. 1), and Kwabena Duffour & Others v. The Republic, the court held that separate corporate identity is not absolute. While Section 107(1)(a) of Act 703 automatically extends derivative criminal responsibility to directors and officers when an offence is established against a corporate body, the court directly pierced the veil based on the facts: A1 admitted that co-director Kwame Antwi (A2) had been missing since 2021/2022, no annual returns were filed, and PW2 testified that "Chairman Wontumi owns Akonta Mining, and Akonta Mining is Chairman Wontumi." Finding no functioning board or corporate structure, the court held A1 to be the true, de facto mineral rights holder.

6. Resolving Purposeful Facilitation

The court resolved that A1 actively and purposefully facilitated the illegal operation under Section 99(2)(b) based on three facts:

A1 admitted introducing PW2 to an equipment vendor to acquire heavy machinery.

PW2 testified that A1 wrote a letter on Akonta Mining letterhead to the Western Regional Security Council (REGSEC) to provide operational security.

Despite knowing the security threats surrounding illegal mining, as confirmed by defence witness Kwabena Okyere Darko-Mensah (DW3), A1 never once visited the site to inspect or ensure PW2 was only planting trees.

Statutory Provisions for Sentence Imposition

In passing sentence, the court applied the statutory penalty rules enacted under Section 3 of the Minerals and Mining (Amendment) Act, 2019 (Act 995), which amended Section 99(2)(b) of Act 703.

This statute establishes mandatory sentencing limits for any person who facilitates or abets an unlicensed mining operation or breaches provisions of the Act lacking a specific penalty. The law prescribes:

A mandatory fine ranging between 10,000 penalty units and 15,000 penalty units .

. A mandatory prison term ranging between 15 years and 25 years.

Taking into account that A1 and A3 were first-time offenders and considering their plea in mitigation, the court selected sentences within these statutory boundaries.

Failures of A1, A3, and Their Counsel

Throughout the judgment, the court underscored a series of critical failures by A1 and A3, which were compounded by lack of cross-examination by their lawyer, Andy Appiah-Kubi in respect of a “critical piece of evidence”.

A1 neglected to establish basic corporate governance structures, failing to maintain a functioning Board of Directors, convene meetings, or file annual returns for A3, while co-director Kwame Antwi (A2) had been absent since 2021/2022. This lapse enabled the court to pierce the corporate veil and hold A1 personally liable. He further admitted that his arrangement with PW2 was entirely verbal, attempting to argue that the absence of a written contract did not transform a reclamation arrangement into mining. The court, however, interpreted this informality as a deliberate attempt to evade regulatory oversight. A1 also failed to provide funds for the supposed reclamation work or verify PW2’s credentials, background, or licensing, demonstrating a reckless disregard for due diligence. Moreover, despite the strict legal duty of mineral rights holders to reclaim mined land, A1 conceded that he never visited or supervised the site to ensure reclamation was actually being carried out rather than gold mining.

The Defence strategy itself was marred by serious omissions attributable to Counsel. The observed that he failed to cross-examine PW2 on crucial testimony, particularly when PW2 stated in court that he extracted gold and used the proceeds for reclamation with A1’s full knowledge. Once PW2 refuted A1’s claim that the arrangement was solely for coconut planting, the evidentiary burden shifted to A1 to substantiate his version of events. Yet no witnesses, receipts, or financial records were produced to support the defence, leaving the court with unchallenged testimony and uncorroborated assertions. These combined failures, both by the accused and their lawyer, fatally weakened their case and solidified the court’s finding of liability - (see pages 28 and 29 for instance).

Judicial Findings, Conviction, and Sentence

Summary of Guilt and Sentences Imposed

The court found Bernard Antwi Boasiako (A1) guilty on Count 1 (Assignment of mineral rights without approval) and Count 4 (Purposely facilitating an unlicensed mining operation).

Count 1: 20 years imprisonment in hard labour, plus a fine of 10,000 penalty units (or 3 additional years in hard labour in default).

Count 4: 20 years imprisonment in hard labour, plus a fine of 10,000 penalty units (or 3 additional years in hard labour in default).

Custodial Term Execution: The court ordered both prison terms to run concurrently, meaning A1 faces a single head sentence of 20 years imprisonment.

The court found Akonta Mining Company Limited (A3) guilty on Count 3 and Count 6.

Count 3: A fine of 15,000 penalty units.

Count 6: A fine of 15,000 penalty units.

Prison Sentence Calculation and Statutory Remission

In the prison calendar, 20 years is not exactly 20 calendar years. Let’s attempt some calculations in the event he is unsuccessful with his promised appeal. Under Section 34(1) of the Prisons Service Act, 1972 (NRCD 46), the statutory execution rule allowing prisoners serving sentences of six weeks or more to earn time off for good conduct, a convict may earn a remission of up to one-third (1/3) of their sentence through steady industry.

Applying this statutory rule to A1's 20-year sentence:

Full Judicial Sentence: 20 calendar years.

Maximum Statutory Remission (1/3 Reduction): 6 years and 8 months.

Actual Time in Custody: If A1 earns full remission through good conduct, his actual execution time in prison will be 13 years and 4 months.

Monetary Fine Conversions

Under our laws, fines expressed in penalty units convert to Ghana Cedis at a fixed statutory rate where 1 penalty unit = GH¢ 12.00.

Bernard Antwi Boasiako (A1): 20,000 penalty units (10,000 + 10,000) = GH¢ 240,000.00 .

20,000 penalty units (10,000 + 10,000) = . Akonta Mining Company Limited (A3): 30,000 penalty units (15,000 + 15,000) = GH¢ 360,000.00 .

30,000 penalty units (15,000 + 15,000) = . Combined Fine Payment: GH¢ 600,000.00 total.

Ancillary Orders of Forfeiture

Pursuant to Section 9 of Act 703 (as amended by Act 995), which mandates the forfeiture of illegal mining equipment to the State, Her Ladyship Justice Audrey Kocuvie-Tay ordered that all 25 serviceable excavators, firearms, ammunition, gold samples, vehicles, machinery, and the GH¢ 157,000.00 in cash seized during the raid be forfeited to the State. The Minister is required to handle and dispose of these forfeited items in strict compliance with the administrative procedures set out under Section 10 of Act 703.

World.title: Trump pleads not guilty to 34 felony counts
World.content:
News outlets will not be allowed to broadcast former President Donald Trump’s arraignment on Tuesday in a New York state court, a judge said Monday night, but he will allow some photographers to take pictures in the courtroom before the proceedings formally begin.

Acting New York Supreme Court Judge Juan Merchan rejected the request by several media organizations, including CNN, for permission to broadcast the historic proceedings. Trump’s arraignment — like most arraignments in the Manhattan courthouse — is a public proceeding, but news cameras are not usually allowed to broadcast from inside the courtroom.

However, the judge is allowing five pool photographers to take still photos at the beginning of the proceedings “until such time as they are directed to vacate the jury box by court personnel.”

Earlier on Monday, Trump’s lawyers urged the judge to reject the media’s request for live cameras in the courtroom. The Manhattan District Attorney’s office told the judge they didn’t have a position.

The media outlets that tried to get cameras into the courtroom argued that “the gravity of this proceeding … and, consequently, the need for the broadest possible public access, cannot be overstated.”

Trump is now in Manhattan ahead of the arraignment. A grand jury indicted the former president last week.

The arraignment is also expected to bring the unsealing of the criminal charges against Trump, which have not yet been seen by his lawyers or the public.

The indictment stems from Manhattan District Attorney Alvin Bragg’s investigation into hush-money payments, made during the 2016 presidential campaign, to women who claimed they had extramarital affairs with Trump, which he denies.

Trump denies all wrongdoing and his lawyers said last week that they’ll fight to get the charges dropped.

World.title: Russian authorities detain suspect over St. Petersburg cafe blast
World.content:
A Ukrainian tank is seen near the frontline area amid the Russia-Ukraine war, in Bakhmut, Ukraine, on April 02. (Muhammed Enes Yildirim/Anadolu Agency/Getty Images)

The Ukrainian military has reported little change to the front lines but heavy fire from Russian forces at various parts of the front line in the Donetsk region.

The General Staff said that more than 45 enemy attacks had been repelled over the past day, with the focus on Lyman, Bakhmut, Avdiivka and Mariinka.

It said there were 17 air strikes and more than 20 strikes by multiple launch rocket systems.

“In the Bakhmut direction, the enemy is trying to take full control over the city of Bakhmut and continues to storm it,” the General Staff said.

West of the city, Ukrainian defense forces repelled about 20 enemy attacks, according to the General Staff.

Oleksandr Syrskyi, commander of Ukrainian Land Forces, posted on Telegram that in Bakhmut he had met with “soldiers and commanders who destroyed the myth of invincibility of the Wagner fighters and Russian paratroopers.”

“The enemy is weakening and trying to cover up its failures with new fakes about the capture of Bakhmut,” Syrskyi said.

Syrskyi referenced the possibility of a future counter-offensive, saying that “the forward movement of our entire army depends on what every soldier is doing right now on their section of the front.”

Some of the most intense fighting is to the northwest and west of the city of Donetsk – as the Russians continue months-long efforts to dislodge Ukrainian defenses in Avdiivka and Mariinka. The General Staff said that some 20 assaults had been repelled.

“There are also some operational successes of our military in the Donetsk area. Our military have taken some positions. They have taken a more strategic and favourable position,” said Oleksii Dmytrashkivskyi, spokesperson for the military in that zone.

He also noted that Russian special forces had been introduced in the area.

“The enemy is trying to attack our positions between Avdiivka and Marinka. These attempts do not stop. It should be noted that the enemy has suffered quite significant losses,” Dmytrashkivskyi said.

He also claimed that the Russians “don’t have the same amount of equipment and, as they themselves say, they are on a ‘diet’ of ammunition for assaults.”

Social media video showed both sides engaged in heavy fire in the Avdiivka area, which the Russians have surrounded on three sides.

Denis Pushilin, the leader of the self-declared Donetsk People’s Republic, claimed that Russian forces were still advancing in the Avdiivka direction.

“It is still premature to speak of encirclement, but the situation is being created, if not critical, then extremely difficult for the enemy… After clearing Kamianka, our units are moving further. There are difficulties both with the terrain, which must also be overcome, and there are also similarities with weather conditions. But these difficulties are mutual — both for the enemy and for us,” Pushilin said.
