Why David Vélez Joined OpenAI’s Boards

OpenAI announced the appointment on July 21, 2026, adding Vélez alongside Robin Vince to bring what the company called “complementary perspectives” as it serves more businesses and people globally.

Bret Taylor, OpenAI’s board chair, said the new members will help ensure artificial intelligence benefits everyone as the company scales.

For foreign readers unfamiliar with OpenAI’s structure, the company operates through a hybrid model: a nonprofit foundation oversees a for-profit entity called OpenAI Group PBC, a public-benefit corporation designed to balance profit with social good.

Bringing in a Latin American fintech leader signals that OpenAI wants governance voices beyond Silicon Valley as its tools reach emerging markets where Nubank already dominates.

From Colombian Engineer to Global Fintech Builder

OpenAI describes Vélez as a Colombian entrepreneur, engineer, and banker who founded Nubank in 2013 after experiencing firsthand the high cost and complexity of banking in Brazil.

Before Nubank, he held roles at Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley, and was a partner at General Atlantic focused on Latin America.

Under his leadership, Nubank grew into the world’s largest digital bank by customer count, surpassing 135 million users with a digital-first, customer-focused model.

For expats and investors watching Latin America, Nubank’s rise from a São Paulo startup to a publicly traded giant on the New York Stock Exchange remains the region’s most visible fintech success story, though our reporting has shown Vélez’s resumed direct control in 2025 sharpened its global operational focus.

What the David Velez OpenAI Appointment Signals for Governance

The Wall Street Journal and Bloomberg framed the board expansion as part of OpenAI’s effort to bolster governance with public-market and financial-services expertise ahead of a possible initial public offering.

The WSJ reported that Robin Vince will chair the audit committee, though no specific committee assignment was disclosed for Vélez.

His appointment to both the nonprofit foundation and for-profit PBC boards reflects OpenAI’s hybrid structure as it balances mission and commercial growth.

For investors tracking the artificial intelligence sector, adding a seasoned operator who scaled a regulated financial institution across multiple countries suggests OpenAI is serious about the compliance and oversight demands of life as a public company.

Nubank’s Quiet AI Ambitions

Nubank has not issued a formal statement about a new companywide AI strategy tied to Vélez’s OpenAI board role.

However, the Brazilian digital bank already maintains a partnership with OpenAI, including a promotional offer of ChatGPT subscriptions for its customers.

Vélez’s proximity to frontier-AI governance may signal deeper AI integration ahead for Nubank’s product roadmap, though no concrete plans have been confirmed.

Industry analysts have long expected Latin America’s largest digital bank to embed generative AI into customer service, credit underwriting, and fraud detection, areas where Nubank’s massive user base provides a rich testing ground.

What This Means for Expats and Investors in Latin America

For the foreign community living and investing in Brazil, Mexico, and Colombia, Vélez’s elevated global profile reinforces Nubank’s position as the region’s most internationally connected financial institution.

A tighter relationship with OpenAI could accelerate the rollout of AI-powered features inside the Nubank app, potentially improving everything from instant customer support in Portuguese and Spanish to personalized financial insights.

Investors holding Nubank shares listed on the NYSE may view the board appointment as a long-term strategic asset, giving the bank an inside view of where commercial AI is heading before competitors do.

While no immediate product changes have been announced, the move places a key Latin American voice inside the world’s most influential AI company at a moment when emerging markets are often an afterthought in technology governance debates.

What Happens Next

OpenAI has not set a date for a potential IPO, but the board expansion is widely read as a preparatory step toward public markets.

Vélez’s dual role on both boards means he will have a say in the nonprofit’s mission-guarding function as well as the commercial strategy of the for-profit arm.

For Nubank customers, the most visible near-term signal will be whether the existing ChatGPT partnership expands into deeper product integrations inside the banking app.

Foreign observers should watch for any announcements from Nubank’s investor relations team or OpenAI’s governance pages that clarify committee assignments or strategic priorities linked to Vélez’s appointment.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who is David Vélez?

David Vélez is a Colombian-born entrepreneur, engineer, and former General Atlantic partner who founded Nubank in 2013. He serves as its Chairman and Global CEO, having built the company from a single credit-card product in Brazil into the world’s largest digital bank by customer count, with more than 135 million users across Latin America.

What boards did David Vélez join at OpenAI?

He joined both the OpenAI Foundation board, which oversees the nonprofit entity, and the OpenAI Group PBC board, which governs the for-profit public-benefit corporation. This dual appointment reflects OpenAI’s hybrid governance structure and gives Vélez influence over both mission and commercial decisions.

Does Nubank have an AI strategy?

Nubank has an existing partnership with OpenAI and offers ChatGPT subscriptions to customers, but the company has not announced a formal, expanded AI strategy tied to Vélez’s board appointment. His new role, however, places him at the center of frontier-AI development and may shape Nubank’s future product direction.

World.title: Brazil Holds Fire as US Tariff Takes Effect
World.content:
Brazil · Trade

Key Facts —Tariff rate. A 25% US tariff on Brazilian goods took effect on July 22, 2026. —Exports affected. The Brazilian government estimates the tariff hits about 18% of its exports to the US, worth roughly US$7.4 billion. —Immediate response. Brazil invoked its Reciprocity Law process and is preparing a WTO dispute, but is not applying counter-tariffs yet. —Key pressure. Vice President Geraldo Alckmin and industry groups urged Lula to avoid immediate retaliation to protect exporters and jobs. —Exposed sectors. Steel, pig iron, ethanol, machinery, apparel, sugar, and agricultural goods are among the products facing the new levy.

A sweeping US tariff on Brazilian goods took effect today, July 22, but President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva is holding off on immediate retaliation, choosing instead to pursue negotiations and a World Trade Organization dispute while buying time with domestic aid for affected firms.

Brazil’s Port of Santos; Brasilia holds off on retaliation as a US tariff takes effect.

Why Brazil Is Not Hitting Back Yet

The decision to show restraint comes after intense pressure from Vice President and Industry Minister Geraldo Alckmin, along with powerful industry lobbies. They warned that a rapid tit-for-tat escalation could deepen the damage to Brazilian exporters and threaten jobs.

Publicly, the government is prioritizing room for a negotiated settlement with Washington. Officials want to explore potential tariff reductions, suspensions, or sectoral exemptions before launching any direct countermeasures.

Behind the scenes, the political calculus is delicate. Vice President Alckmin, a seasoned politician and former governor of São Paulo, Brazil’s industrial heartland, has been a moderating voice, arguing that a trade war would hurt the very factories and farms that drive employment.

For foreign investors and expats watching from São Paulo or Rio de Janeiro, this caution signals that the Lula administration is trying to avoid the kind of sudden economic shock that could destabilize the Brazilian real and erode purchasing power.

The Scale of the US Tariff Brazil Blow

The Brazilian government calculates the 25% levy affects roughly 18% of the country’s exports to the United States, totaling about US$7.4 billion based on 2024 trade data. The National Confederation of Industry (CNI), a powerful business lobby, puts the share at risk even higher, near 26%.

An estimate from consultancy MB Associados, using 2025 figures, pegged the impact at US$9.51 billion, or 25.2% of exports. The tariff covers thousands of products, though some key goods like coffee and beef were exempted in the US order.

To put this in context, the United States is Brazil’s second-largest trading partner after China, and a vital market for manufactured and semi-finished goods. A sudden 25% cost increase makes Brazilian steel, machinery, and ethanol far less competitive overnight.

For readers unfamiliar with Brazil’s export profile, the country is a global powerhouse in commodities but has spent decades trying to move up the value chain. This tariff hits precisely those higher-value industrial sectors, potentially reversing years of hard-won export diversification.

Lula’s Multi-Pronged Strategy

President Lula said his government would begin procedures under Brazil’s Reciprocity Law immediately, a legal framework that allows for countermeasures. However, the final decision on any retaliation rests solely with him.

In the meantime, Brazilian ministries will present him with a menu of options. The government is also expanding the Brasil Soberano domestic aid program to cushion companies hit by the new trade barrier.

The Reciprocity Law, enacted in 2023, gives the executive branch a flexible toolkit to respond to foreign trade barriers without needing immediate congressional approval. It is a strategic asset, allowing Brazil to threaten counter-tariffs on US goods or suspend intellectual property protections if talks fail.

For expats and tourists, the domestic aid expansion means the government is trying to prevent a sudden spike in unemployment or factory closures that could ripple through local economies. Stability in industrial regions helps keep the broader Brazilian economy, and the currency, on an even keel.

What It Means for Expats, Investors, and Tourists

For foreigners living in or visiting Brazil, the immediate effect is likely to be felt in currency markets. Trade tensions can weaken the Brazilian real against the US dollar, which might make your dollars stretch further on the ground but also signals underlying economic uncertainty.

Investors with exposure to Brazilian equities should watch industrial and steel stocks closely. Companies like Gerdau, a major steel producer, and ethanol exporters could see margin compression if they cannot quickly redirect sales to other markets.

Tourists are unlikely to notice direct price changes in the short term, but a prolonged trade dispute could feed into broader inflation if the government eventually imposes retaliatory tariffs on American goods imported into Brazil. That would raise prices on everything from electronics to processed foods.

What Comes Next

Formal litigation at the WTO is expected to proceed, though that process is notoriously slow. Direct talks with Washington remain the preferred channel for a faster resolution.

While a Reuters report indicated Brazil was preparing a tough retaliation package in the background, the official posture remains one of caution. The government is signaling that any countermeasures will be carefully studied before being applied.

The coming weeks will be critical. Brazilian diplomats are expected to intensify contacts with their US counterparts, while industry groups press for sectoral carve-outs. If negotiations stall, Lula may face mounting domestic pressure to act more forcefully.

For now, the message from Brasília is one of strategic patience. The government is betting that a measured approach preserves leverage, keeps export jobs intact, and avoids a full-blown trade war that neither economy wants.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is Brazil immediately retaliating against the US tariff?

No. Brazil has chosen not to apply immediate counter-tariffs, opting instead to start a WTO dispute and seek negotiations while preparing legal countermeasures under its Reciprocity Law. The final decision on any retaliation rests with President Lula, who is under pressure from his vice president and industry to prioritize talks.

Which Brazilian sectors are most affected by the 25% tariff?

Exposed sectors include steel, pig iron, ethanol, machinery, apparel, sugar, and various agricultural goods. Coffee and beef were notably exempted from the US order. These industries represent a significant share of Brazil’s higher-value exports to the American market.

What is the value of Brazilian exports hit by the tariff?

The Brazilian government estimates the tariff affects about US$7.4 billion in exports, representing roughly 18% of all goods it shipped to the United States in 2024. The National Confederation of Industry puts the figure higher, at about 26% of exports, while consultancy MB Associados estimates the impact at US$9.51 billion using 2025 data.

World.title: Uruguay Peso Bonds See 4x Demand in July Auction
World.content:
Uruguay · Economy

Key Facts —Auction date. July 21, 2026. —Instrument. Series 13 nominal peso Treasury notes due June 29, 2030. —Bids received. UYU 9.67 billion (roughly US$242 million). —Amount accepted. UYU 4.41 billion (about US$110 million). —Yield. 7.039% annual cutoff yield.

Investor demand for Uruguay peso bonds surged this week, pushing the government to double the size of a local-currency debt auction after bids reached nearly UYU 9.7 billion (roughly US$242 million).

Montevideo; Uruguay drew heavy demand for its local-currency bonds.

Strong Demand Drives Upsized Sale

Uruguay’s finance ministry had initially offered UYU 2.25 billion in Series 13 nominal peso Treasury notes due June 29, 2030. Bids flooded in at UYU 9.67 billion, a cover ratio of about 4.3 times the base amount.

The ministry accepted UYU 4.41 billion (about US$110 million), using almost all of the auction’s built-in capacity to issue up to 100% extra. The notes were priced at a 103.67 cutoff with a 7.039% annual yield.

A Strategy to Borrow in Pesos

The strong result fits Uruguay’s broader plan to reduce reliance on US dollar debt. Finance Minister Gabriel Oddone said earlier this year that the country aims to issue about 50% of its debt in pesos.

Borrowing in pesos reduces exposure to currency shocks and better matches the currency the government collects in taxes. A World Bank presentation in April noted that Uruguay’s Debt Management Office has been shifting toward fixed-rate nominal peso securities.

Why Uruguay Peso Bonds Attract Investors

Declining inflation and inflation expectations have made fixed-rate peso notes more appealing. The government has responded by increasing supply at 2-, 5-, and 5-year maturities to lock in attractive rates.

For international investors, the auction signals confidence in Uruguay’s economic management. Local-currency bonds offer a way to gain exposure without taking on direct dollar risk.

What the Auction Tells the Market

A 4.3x oversubscription is a strong demand indicator for a small, open economy. It suggests that both local pension funds and foreign portfolio managers see value in Uruguayan peso paper.

The single-price Dutch auction mechanism allowed the ministry to capture that demand efficiently. The result reinforces the view that Uruguay can deepen its local-currency debt market.

Background: Uruguay’s Steady Economic Course

Uruguay has long stood out in Latin America for its political stability, strong institutions, and investment-grade credit rating. These qualities make its government bonds, whether in pesos or dollars, a relative safe haven in a volatile region.

The country’s central bank has pursued a credible inflation-targeting regime, which has gradually brought price rises under control. That success directly supports demand for fixed-rate peso instruments, as investors worry less about inflation eating away their returns.

What It Means for Expats and Investors

For foreigners living in Uruguay or considering a move, a government that borrows responsibly in its own currency is less likely to face the kind of dollar-debt crises that have hit other emerging markets. That translates into a more stable economic environment for property values and local business.

International investors looking at Uruguayan assets can take the auction as a vote of confidence. The high demand for peso bonds suggests the market believes Uruguay will continue to manage its finances prudently, keeping the currency relatively stable against the dollar over time.

For foreign investors, strong demand for local-currency bonds shows confidence in Uruguay’s stability and its ability to borrow in its own money. That reduces reliance on dollar debt and currency risk.

Uruguay holds investment-grade ratings, rare in the region, which helps it attract conservative funds. Deep demand lets the treasury lengthen maturities and lock in funding.

Issuing in pesos rather than dollars also shields the budget from exchange-rate swings. It is a sign of a maturing local capital market.

Frequently Asked Questions

What are Uruguay peso bonds?

They are government debt securities issued in Uruguayan pesos rather than US dollars, paying a fixed interest rate to investors. By issuing in pesos, Uruguay matches its debt obligations to the currency it collects from taxpayers, reducing the risk of exchange-rate swings.

Why did Uruguay double the auction size?

Bids reached nearly 4.3 times the base amount offered, so the ministry used its built-in option to accept up to 100% extra. This mechanism lets the government capture strong demand without holding a new auction.

What was the yield on the Series 13 notes?

The cutoff yield was 7.039% annually, with a price of 103.67 and accrued interest of 0.52. The yield reflects investor confidence that Uruguay’s inflation will remain under control over the life of the bond.

World.title: Brazil Electoral Court Keeps 2022 Spending Caps for 2026 Vote
World.content:
Brazil · Politics

Key Facts —Rule issued. The TSE published Ordinance No. 449/2026 on July 21, 2026, formalizing the limits. —2022 caps kept. The court decided on July 1, 2026, to maintain the same spending ceilings from the 2022 election. —Penalty for excess. Overspending triggers a fine of 100% of the excess amount, payable within five business days. —What counts. Limits cover direct contracts, cash transfers to parties or candidates, and in-kind donations. —Legal basis. The caps follow Law No. 9,504/1997 and TSE Resolution No. 23,607/2019.

TSE campaign spending limits for Brazil’s 2026 general elections were officially published on July 21, keeping the same ceilings used in the 2022 race and setting clear financial rules for every office from president to state deputy.

Brazil’s electoral court, the TSE, set campaign spending caps for the 2026 vote.

How the TSE campaign spending limits work

The spending cap applies to the total cost of a candidacy, not just directly contracted expenses. It also includes cash transfers to parties or other candidates and the estimated value of donated goods and services.

Any amount spent above the limit results in a fine equal to 100% of the excess. The violation can also be prosecuted as an abuse of economic power, which may lead to further electoral sanctions.

Presidential and congressional race caps

A presidential candidate can spend up to R$88.9 million (US$17.4 million) in the first round. If a runoff is needed, an additional R$44.4 million (US$8.7 million) is allowed.

Candidates for federal deputy face a limit of roughly R$3.1 million (US$608,000). Those running for state or district deputy can spend about R$1.2 million (US$235,000).

State-level races: governors and senators

In São Paulo, Brazil’s richest state, a governor candidate can spend up to R$26.6 million (US$5.2 million) in the first round, with an extra R$13.3 million (US$2.6 million) for a runoff. A Senate seat in the same state is capped at R$7.1 million (US$1.4 million).

In Bahia, Minas Gerais, and Rio de Janeiro, the governor’s race limit is R$17.7 million (US$3.5 million) in the first round, plus R$8.8 million (US$1.7 million) for a second round. Senate candidates in those states can spend up to R$5.3 million (US$1.04 million).

Smaller states have lower caps. A governor’s race in Ceará is capped around R$11.5 million (US$2.25 million), while in Rondônia the limit is roughly R$6.2 million (US$1.2 million) for the first round.

Enforcement and penalties

Brazil’s Superior Electoral Court (TSE) enforces the limits. A candidate, party, or responsible individual who exceeds the cap must pay the fine within five business days after being notified of the judicial decision.

The court calculates limits based on the number of eligible voters and the office being sought. The full table of limits by state and office is available in the TSE ordinance.

Background: why spending limits matter in Brazil

Brazil introduced strict campaign spending caps to curb the influence of big money in politics after a series of high-profile corruption scandals. The rules are designed to level the playing field and reduce the advantage of wealthier candidates backed by large corporate donors.

For foreign investors and expats, these limits signal a maturing regulatory environment. Transparent spending rules help reduce political risk, making Brazil’s economic policy landscape more predictable during election cycles.

What it means for expats, investors, and the 2026 race

The 2026 election will shape Brazil’s fiscal and regulatory direction for years to come. Clear spending caps give observers a framework to gauge campaign scale and potential influence, especially in key states like São Paulo and Rio de Janeiro.

For tourists and short-term visitors, the election period may bring heightened political activity and occasional protests. Understanding the financial rules behind the campaigns offers useful context for anyone following local news during their stay.

Frequently Asked Questions

What happens if a candidate spends more than the TSE campaign spending limits?

The candidate or party is fined 100% of the excess amount and must pay within five business days after being notified of the judicial decision. The violation may also be prosecuted as an abuse of economic power, which can lead to additional electoral sanctions including the potential annulment of the candidacy.

Do the 2026 spending limits apply to both rounds of the election?

Yes. A separate, additional limit is set for the second round for president and governor races if a runoff is necessary. The first-round cap and the runoff cap are distinct amounts, and spending in each round is tracked independently.

Are in-kind donations included in the spending cap?

Yes. The estimated monetary value of donated goods and services counts toward the total spending limit for a candidacy. This includes any item or service with economic value that a candidate receives without direct payment.

World.title: Hattieville man fined $305 for $50 sledgehammer from employer who would not give him payment in advance
World.content:
Hattieville man fined $305 for $50 sledgehammer from employer who would not give him payment in advance

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A Hattieville construction worker has been fined more than six times the value of a sledgehammer he admitted stealing from a man who hired him for a day’s work after he would not give him an advance in payment.

Forty-two-year-old Felix Larance Petillo appeared unrepresented in the Belize City Magistrate’s Court on Tuesday and was charged with stealing a red Truper-brand sledgehammer, valued at $50, from a construction worker who had hired him.

Petillo initially pleaded not guilty and was offered bail of $1,000. However, while waiting to secure bail, he returned to court and changed his plea to guilty.

Senior Magistrate Mannon Dennison fined him $300, along with $5 in court costs. He was given until August 31, 2026, to pay or serve two weeks in prison.

According to the allegations, the construction worker hired Petillo on July 19 to assist with removing cement material from a demolished house on Locario Street in Hattieville.

Later that evening, Petillo reportedly asked for an advance payment for work scheduled for the following day. When the construction worker refused, Petillo allegedly threatened to take some of his tools.

The following morning, the construction worker discovered that his sledgehammer was missing and reported the matter to police.

Police later detained Petillo, who reportedly admitted placing the tool inside a mechanic’s vehicle. The mechanic subsequently handed the sledgehammer over to police and was not charged.

World.title: Businessman Miguel Guerra shot during armed robbery at Hand Money Loans; $80 stolen
World.content:
Businessman Miguel Guerra shot during armed robbery at Hand Money Loans; $80 stolen

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Police are investigating an armed robbery in Belize City that left a 67-year-old businessman injured on Tuesday morning.

The incident occurred at approximately 11:15 a.m. at Handy Money Loans on Handyside Street.

Police said the suspect entered the establishment under the pretense of pawning a cellphone before producing a firearm and demanding money.

The robber reportedly fled with approximately $80 in cash after firing a single shot at the businessman, Miguel Angel Guerra.

Guerra was transported to the Karl Heusner Memorial Hospital, where he is receiving medical treatment.

Police investigations continue.

World.title: Joseph Vaccaro receives disclosure in Gaston Barrow murder case
World.content:
Joseph Vaccaro receives disclosure in Gaston Barrow murder case

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Thirty-year-old taxi operator Joseph Gabourel Vaccaro has received disclosure in the murder case stemming from the September 2025 shooting death of Gaston Barrow at Old Belize.

Vaccaro, a resident of Cumberbatch Street, appeared unrepresented before the Chief Magistrate in the Belize City Magistrate’s Court on Tuesday.

He was provided with 154 pages of disclosure, five compact discs and photographs forming part of the prosecution’s evidence. The matter was adjourned until September 7, 2026, when a preliminary inquiry is scheduled to begin.

Vaccaro was first arraigned for Barrow’s murder on October 6, 2025, and was remanded to the Belize Central Prison.

Police said Barrow and another man, Hank Carr, were shot at the Old Belize compound on the night of September 28, 2025. Barrow was pronounced dead on arrival at the Karl Heusner Memorial Hospital, while Carr was treated and later released.

Investigators allege Carr was driving a vehicle with Barrow in the front passenger seat when a gunman near a taxi opened fire. The shooter reportedly entered the taxi and escaped towards the nearby police checkpoint.

Police later reviewed surveillance footage from the area, which reportedly led to Vaccaro’s detention and subsequent charge.

World.title: Ministry of Sustainable Development and Statistical Institute of Belize sign 4-year MoU to strengthen coordination of National Development Data
World.content:
Ministry of Sustainable Development and Statistical Institute of Belize sign 4-year MoU to strengthen coordination of National Development Data

By Zoila Palma: The Sustainable Development Unit (SDU), under the Ministry of Sustainable Development, Climate Change and Solid Waste Management (MSDCCSWM), and the Statistical Institute of Belize (SIB) signed a four-year Memorandum of Understanding to strengthen the coordination, management, and dissemination of Belize’s national development data.

The agreement was signed during the National SDG and Statistical System Workshop at the Grand Resort Residences on July 16, 2026, by Milagro Matus, Chief Executive Officer of the Ministry of Sustainable Development, Climate Change and Solid Waste Management, and Diana Castillo, Director General of the Statistical Institute of Belize.

“The partnership establishes a collaborative framework for coordinating the collection, validation, reporting, and dissemination of three important sets of development indicators: the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), the Antigua and Barbuda Agenda for Small Island Developing States (ABAS), and the #PlanBelize Medium-Term Development Strategy (MTDS) 2.0. These indicators will be made publicly available through the Belize National Statistical System (BNSS) Portal, providing policymakers, researchers, and the public with improved access to official development statistics,” the Ministry explained.

Through this Agreement, the SIB will collect the data from the respective producing agencies, validate the information, and publish the indicators on the portal. The SDU will lead national coordination for SDG and ABAS reporting, including Belize’s Voluntary National Reviews, while promoting stronger collaboration among ministries, departments, and agencies to improve data sharing, harmonize indicator frameworks, and encourage the use of the BNSS Portal as the country’s primary source of official development statistics.

The signing concluded a workshop during which participants approved the Interim SDG Progress Report 2025, the SDG Data Ecosystem Prioritization and Action Plan 2026-2030, and the Statistical Capacities and Needs Assessment 2026, all of which will guide future work. The workshop was supported by the Protected Areas Conservation Trust (PACT), the Green Climate Fund (GCF), and the Korea International Cooperation Agency (KOICA).

World.title: Government of Belize and UNICEF launch landmark Climate Landscape Analysis for Children and Vulnerable Populations
World.content:
Government of Belize and UNICEF launch landmark Climate Landscape Analysis for Children and Vulnerable Populations

By Zoila Palma: On July 17, 2026, the Ministry of Sustainable Development, Climate Change and Solid Waste Management, through its Sustainable Development Unit (SDU) and Climate Change Department (CCD), in partnership with UNICEF Belize, officially launched the Climate Landscape Analysis for Children Plus (CLAC+) Report.

The CLAC+ Report is the first comprehensive national assessment of how climate change, environmental, energy, and disasters (CEED) affect children and other vulnerable populations in Belize, including persons with disabilities, Indigenous Peoples, and pregnant and lactating women. It provides evidence-based recommendations to strengthen climate resilience and promote more inclusive policies and programmes that better address the needs of those most at risk.

The Ministry explained that the report offers a critical foundation for strengthening national policies, investments, and programmes that protect children and vulnerable communities from the growing impacts of climate change. Its recommendations encourage a whole-of-government and whole-of-society approach to climate action by fostering stronger collaboration across sectors, including health, education, social protection, disaster risk management, environmental management, and sustainable development.

The official launch marks an important milestone in Belize’s efforts to advance evidence-based climate action and resilient development.

It brought together representatives from government, development partners, civil society, academia, youth organizations, and other stakeholders to share the report’s findings, discuss priority actions, and strengthen partnerships for implementation.

World.title: International News: Extreme weather raises concerns over commodity markets
World.content:
International News: Extreme weather raises concerns over commodity markets

By Zoila Palma: Commodity strategists are warning that financial markets may be underestimating the impact of increasingly volatile weather, as Europe experiences intense heat and forecasters raise concerns about a potentially powerful El Niño event later this year.

The World Meteorological Organization expects a strong El Niño to develop in the tropical Pacific between July and September, a climate pattern that can trigger shifts in temperatures and rainfall and contribute to extreme weather worldwide.

Agriculture is expected to be among the sectors most affected, with crops including corn, coffee, cocoa and wheat particularly vulnerable to heat stress, drought and changing rainfall patterns, CNBC reports.

Analysts say prolonged extreme weather could reduce crop yields and drive food prices higher.

The potential impact on commodities is expected to vary widely.

Bank of America analysts have identified corn as particularly vulnerable to weather risks in Europe, Brazil and the United States, while warning that sugar production in Brazil and Thailand could decline sharply due to El Niño-related conditions.

Meanwhile, milder winters could reduce demand for natural gas, potentially putting downward pressure on prices.

Extreme heat is also raising concerns for metals, with drought threatening water-intensive copper production and high temperatures increasing electricity demand for aluminum smelting.

World.title: International News: US urges isolation of Nicaragua after Ortega vows to end elections
World.content:
International News: US urges isolation of Nicaragua after Ortega vows to end elections

By Zoila Palma: The United States is urging countries across the Western Hemisphere to isolate Nicaragua after President Daniel Ortega vowed that his government would no longer hold elections.

U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Ortega’s declaration exposes the “true authoritarian nature” of his government and warned that Nicaragua cannot expect “business as usual” with other nations while rejecting democratic rule.

Rubio said Ortega and his wife, Vice President Rosario Murillo, have “abandoned even the pretense of popular consent.”

In a separate statement, the U.S. Bureau of Western Hemisphere Affairs called on regional partners to work together to ensure that Nicaraguans can eventually choose a future free from what it described as tyranny.

Ortega made the pledge during a speech on Sunday, saying elections would no longer be held because they could allow U.S.-backed movements to take power.

“There won’t be any more elections here for them to try to seize the government and seize power,” Ortega said, as he defended his government’s continued grip on power.

Ortega, 80, has been in power continuously since 2007, while constitutional reforms adopted last year established his wife as co-president and extended the presidential term to six years.

World.title: Schools under scrutiny
World.content:
Ministry of Education, Skills, Youth & Information’s Region One Director Ottis Brown addressing the region’s One Back-to-School Conference held at Grand Palladium Hotel and Spa in Point, Hanover, on Tuesday.Anthony Lewis

POINT, Hanover — The Ministry of Education, Skills, Youth & Information’s Region One Director Ottis Brown has sounded the alarm over what he alleges are numerous accounting breaches in primary schools within Kingston and St Andrew.

“The breaches are too many. Here is what is happening now, colleagues. We are getting documents from the Integrity Commission (IC) for principals to be investigated… Accountability is stepping up,” he said.

Brown made the revelation, Tuesday, during the second of a three-day back-to-school conference for Region One that was held at Grand Palladium Hotel and Spa in Point, Hanover.

“Stakeholders in the communities are writing to the ministry. They talk about what they observe in schools. They go to a school and they get no receipt for the money they pay. They call you and ask if they should get a receipt and what it should look like,” he told an audience of educators.

The regional director said primary schools are the main offenders.

“Do you know where we tend to find the bulk of the breaches now? The primary schools. It’s a serious problem,” said Brown.

While he conceded that there may be administrative issues such as inadequate staff that impact how money is handled, he said there can be no excuse for some of the behaviour seen.

“Some simple things. Why would you keep money in excess of a million dollars locked up in a room for two, three weeks, months, and so forth? The bursar not being there caused that? So what I’m saying: I know you need those people, and we are working on that, but don’t do things to set up yourselves in the process,” added the senior officer.

Brown used the opportunity to explain proper administrative procedures when handling school funds.

“I beg you, lodge the money in a reasonable time frame. Money must be lodged intact. Can somebody please explain what the FAA (Financial Administration and Audit) Act means when it says ‘money must be lodged intact’? ‘[It means as soon] as collected,” he emphasised.

He explained that if five $100-notes are collected, that exact configuration must be deposited into the account.

“Don’t use it to make any change for anybody who wants to pay somebody something. That is what they mean [by] to lodge the money intact. If you are guilty, don’t say anything. Just sit like nothing is wrong but pray a prayer in your heart. I’m giving you 30 seconds to ask God to forgive you,” stated Brown to an outburst of laughter.

“You saved the money, but the law says treat it a particular way,” added the senior officer.

During his address Brown also expressed gratitude to the Ministry of Education for providing the region with additional professionals to conduct audits of schools within the region.

“We want to publicly say thanks to the members of the central ministry team, our CEO, [and] the permanent secretary. We spoke and they have given us a large number of people to build out the finance unit in the region. I have about five or six additional staff members now so we can do more audits. Clap the central team for that,” he said magnanimously.

World.title: Danger in John’s Hall
World.content:
A bedhead and concrete block are among items used to alert commuters to danger on the John’s Hall road in St James..

MONTEGO BAY, St James — An old bedhead and the top of a broken table used to cobble together a crude guard rail serve as warning that there is danger on the road between John’s Hall and Spring Mount in southern St James. One section appears on the verge of collapse, much like a nearby house whose foundation was eroded by Hurricane Melissa, last October, and commuters are worried.

“I’m afraid but mi just have to drive on it, can’t do better,” a shopkeeper who identified herself as Sancia told the

Jamaica Observer Tuesday.

“If little rain fall it gone, because underneath it, it’s deteriorating,” she explained.

The gaping cavern in a section of the Spring Mount Road is just a few kilometres up the hill, impassable as residents eagerly await word from the Government on when it will be repaired. Now, they have added the danger at John’s Hall to their list of urgent issues.

When contacted, community relations officer for the National Works Agency (NWA), Western Region, Janel Ricketts said they are aware of this latest development at John’s Hall. Though none were seen by the Observer, she said signs are in place to help guide motorists.

“This too, like Spring Mount, is on the radar of the NWA but in terms of an update, I don’t have that right now,” she told the Observer.

For shopkeeper Sancia and others who use the road, help cannot come soon enough as the alternative route is longer and more costly. What was once a straight route from John’s Hall to Montego Bay has now become a meandering journey to Sunderland, around Blackshop, and through Patosi.

“And the hottest part is we dropping out right at the square down there and we don’t reach Montego Bay as yet. It’s going to be more money, more gas, more everything,” Sancia lamented.

She also highlighted challenges being faced by students in that area of the community.

“Children that live here now that have to go Maldon are paying double or triple fare because they have to take taxi from here go to Montego Bay and a next taxi go and vice versa,” Sancia explained.

“It bad for everybody: Parents, children, business owners,” she added.

A roadside vendor in John’s Hall who chose not to provide his name spoke of the downturn in business he has seen as commuters from southern St James have had to find new routes.

“It rough because the road block up that side so people can’t come down. They would stop and buy drinks, food stuff, shop stuff; that’s not happening again,” he said.

He also pointed to the impact it has had on other areas of life that used to generate income, such as sporting competitions.

“Football was a thing where the different communities partake in and now them can’t come,” he said.

“Spring Mount people a bawl now because nobody can’t come down. We just want to see the road fix, the two place; because without it we don’t have any real livelihood, nobody can’t come, nobody can’t go,” he said.

A motorist who gave his name as Richard said travelling to the area has been a financial challenge and, like area residents, he is also worried about the increasing deterioration at John’s Hall.

“With this breakaway now, we would have to find a next way to go in town, it’s really pressuring. I hope they do something fast, whether it’s construction to start the new road or they find something better that we can travel on. But do something better,” Richard appealed.

World.title: Stacious savours emotional return to Sumfest
World.content:
Stacious is all the rage on the Sumfest stage last weekend. (Photo: Garfield Robinson)

When Stacious stepped onto the Reggae Sumfest stage on Saturday night as a surprise guest during Mavado’s set it was more than a welcome return for the dancehall artiste; it was an opportunity to be part of a moment that will be remembered as one of the festival’s most significant.

The entertainer joined Mavado during his historic showcase with fellow headliner Vybz Kartel, a performance that celebrated unity over division and marked a new chapter in one of dancehall’s most defining rivalries.

For Stacious, whose catalogue includes one of the most notable collaborations with Mavado in dancehall history, the occasion carried both personal and cultural significance.

“I can’t remember the last time I did Sumfest,” she told the Jamaica Observer following the performance. “I know I’ve done the show three times in the past, but I can’t remember when was the last time. It’s a good feeling being back.”

Her return came after years away from the festival’s stage, making the appearance all the more meaningful.

“I’m here tonight not just as an artiste, but as a fan of dancehall because Gully/Gaza did a run road, and now both deejays will come together in unity on one stage. It’s an honour to be a part of it,” she told the Jamaica Observer.

The sentiment echoed what many fans experienced inside Plantation Cove in St Ann as thousands watched two of dancehall’s biggest icons perform together, putting years of division behind them in favour of celebration.

For Stacious, the night also marked a long-awaited reunion with the man who helped produce, Come Into My Room, one of her most memorable collaborations.

“Mavado also hasn’t performed in Jamaica for a while and I’m here to witness the return of the Gully Gad, so it’s a great night,” she said. “Mavado and I haven’t performed together in maybe over 10 years, so it’s been a long time. The awesome thing is that it’s always good when we connect, and we enjoyed ourselves, which was most important.”

Stacious was among the female voices who helped shape dancehall during the late 2000s and early 2010s. Her surprise appearance on Saturday served as a reminder of that era while signalling that she still has plenty left to offer.

Away from the nostalgia, the deejay says she is focused on new music and reconnecting with supporters. She is currently promoting two singles, Tears and Velvet Sweetheart, the latter of which recently received the visual treatment and is now available for streaming across digital platforms.

Stacious is encouraging fans to subscribe to her YouTube channel and follow her social media pages to stay updated on upcoming releases, performances, and other career developments.

— Shereita Grizzle

World.title: US$18-m fuel shield
World.content:
STATE-OWNED refinery Petrojam has spent about US$18 million subsidising fuel costs to shield consumers from steeper price increases, with Chairman Metry Seaga saying the Government will eventually reimburse the company.

Seaga disclosed the figure during a panel discussion following Tuesday’s release of the second-quarter JCC/GK Capital Consumer Indices, while responding to questions about measures being taken to contain energy costs.

“To date, Petrojam has spent about US$18 million subsidising the cost of fuel,” Seaga said.

While acknowledging that the refinery has not done a good job of explaining how fuel prices are determined because of the complexity of the process, Seaga explained that Petrojam has been using a long-standing fuel price “smoothing mechanism” to cushion consumers from sharp swings in global oil prices. The mechanism was introduced to reduce volatility in fuel prices and lessen the inflationary impact of sudden increases in international oil prices.

According to Seaga, since the Middle East war began, domestic fuel-price increase reached as much as $40 per litre, leaving Petrojam to absorb significant costs rather than allowing domestic fuel price increases to immediately reflect international price movements which he said would have been “extremely inflationary”.

Under Petrojam’s pricing mechanism, weekly fuel price increases were initially capped at $4.50 per litre, before Cabinet approved an increase to $12.50. Petrojam calculates its prices using a US reference price and then applies costs within its control. When the calculated increase exceeds the cap, the refinery absorbs the difference rather than passing it on to consumers.

“The increase that the consumer saw last week of $12.50 is not a real number; the real number is significantly higher than that, but Petrojam has taken up any losses that are incurred,” he said. “Petrojam is doing everything it can, and the government by extension has to give us back that money, because the money has to come from somewhere.”

The JCC/GK Capital Consumer Indices found that rising energy costs continue to influence the behaviour of both businesses and households. Among businesses surveyed, 36 per cent said rising electricity costs were significantly affecting their operations, while another 29 per cent described the impact as moderate. In response, businesses said they were reducing energy consumption, investing in renewable energy solutions, increasing prices charged to customers, cutting operating expenses elsewhere, investing in energy-efficient equipment and delaying investment or expansion plans.

Seaga acknowledged not all businesses can pass higher energy costs on to customers. Pointing to Jamaica’s geography, and dependence on imported energy, he said businesses must accept that the country will remain exposed to global price shocks.

“We have to recognise from the get-go we are subject to price increases worldwide, and these are things businesses must plan for, including natural disasters,” he said. “What we have to do is know they are coming and be more efficient.”

Beyond businesses, consumers are also changing their behaviour in response to higher energy bills. The survey found that 51 per cent of respondents had reduced their electricity usage, while others said they were using fewer appliances or purchasing more energy-efficient appliances and light bulbs. Respondents also called for measures to reduce energy costs, with 56 per cent saying the government should lower electricity rates. Other recommendations included more stable fuel prices, lower taxes and duties on energy-efficient appliances, and easier financing for residential solar systems.

However, Seaga argued that households have viable alternatives to reduce their electricity bills.

“Majority of the people I know are telling me about their light bills being $12 and $15, so there’s no good reason that people should not be putting solar into their homes,” he said, noting that financing options are available.

Seaga also disclosed that Petrojam is exploring diversification into LNG, solar and potentially nuclear energy. He also hinted at the possibility of participating in oil development should commercially viable reserves be discovered in Jamaica, extending its involvement from production to the sale of fuel. However, Seaga noted that such plans would require significant investment.

World.title: Child’s body found in Trelawny; two injured by irate residents in mob attack
World.content:
TRELAWNY, Jamaica — Police are now on a scene where the body of a child was found with her throat slashed in Tyre district near Troy in south Trelawny, residents say.

Residents told the Jamaica Observer that about 6:00 pm, the child’s body was found in bushes and an alarm was raised.

Residents say the child was raped before her death.

“A farmer went to look for his cow when he stumbled on the little girl’s body,” a resident who requested anonymity said.

Another resident said following the gruesome discovery there was a mob attack on a man who citizens accused of killing the child. His father was also wounded in the attack.

The men were reportedly taken to hospital. Their condition is not known at this time.

Efforts to get a comment from the police late Tuesday were unsuccessful.

— Kasey Williams

World.title: JLP condemns ‘vile’ alleged NaRRA voicenotes featuring PNP executives
World.content:
KINGSTON, Jamaica — The Jamaica Labour Party (JLP) says it has taken note of voicenotes leaked on traditional and social media in which two PNP executive members are allegedly heard confirming the PNP’s preparedness to implement delay tactics and use baseless allegations to smear “patriotic Jamaicans”.

In a statement on Tuesday, the JLP said media reports have indicated that the voicenotes were sent in a PNP executive WhatsApp group on May 27, 2026, shortly after Major General Antony Anderson was announced to head the National Resilience and Reconstruction Authority (NaRRA).

In the first piece of leaked audio the statement quotes, a PNP executive member whom it says may be heard stating:

“Bear in mind that the NaRRA is what the JLP sees as its glory and its saviour for a fourth term. So they see NaRRA as a saving grace and they are going to do everything in their power to try to get things done, which means bypassing, like all parish council, which, you know, we probably would do delay tactics, and they don’t get it, which is why they did it that way. But safety standards and these things is a concern. So let’s continue to play our ball game of politics.”

In the second piece of audio, which has gone viral in the public domain, a member of the PNP executive is heard referencing Major General Anderson’s appointment to lead NaRRA and saying:

“The concern I’m raising is that Anderson’s track record is not one full of blemishes that it will be so easy to attach certain things to him. The corruption argument is not going to be attached to him so easily, right? In my humble opinion, I think they’ve outsmarted us and put in this man to be a CEO and whatever reality is, we need to ensure that the average Jamaican is saying we don’t care who he is and him could have full integrity like, whoa, he could have been whatever. He’s the man who sorted out all of the hurricane relief that got it to Jamaica, whether we know it or not. So I would love for us to be able to put that information together, package it for the ground so that the average Jamaican can get that information.”

JLP Officer Corps member, Daryl Vaz, who co-chairs the Melissa Recovery and Relief Committee, says the revealing voicenotes disclose the PNP’s preparedness to implement delay tactics to slow down or block important national projects which NaRRA will pursue and to use baseless allegations to smear patriotic Jamaicans.

“What is particularly shameful is that the audio reveals that, despite the unprecedented natural disaster which devastated thousands of Jamaican lives and despite lamenting that the recovery effort should be faster, the PNP, at the highest level in their party, at the level of their executive, has been caught discussing ‘delay tactics’, which their executive member confessed they would probably implement. This behaviour by the PNP is most disgraceful but not surprising because we have seen these delay tactics implemented by the PNP before, to the detriment of Jamaicans.”

Vaz described the PNP executive member’s commitment to continue playing the political ball game concerning NaRRA as scandalous.

“Let us pause for a moment and recall that the Government has fast-tracked legislation to help rebuild communities and Jamaican lives in the aftermath of the devastating Category 5 Hurricane Melissa, and here is a PNP executive member caught on tape committing to ‘playing the ball game of politics’ with the people’s livelihood and the wellbeing of their communities. The obstructionist posture of the PNP on the issue of NaRRA and the Government’s bid to assist Jamaica to recover strongly and in a speedy manner is an utter disgrace,” he said.

He noted that the lamentation by another PNP executive member that corruption cannot be easily attached to Major General Anderson is also despicable and revealing, and confirms the PNP’s willingness to weaponise corruption without a credible basis and attempt to smear patriotic Jamaicans.

World.title: ‘Highway robbery’
World.content:
New toll fees affecting motorists using the North-South Highway are expected to take effect at the end of the month.

“HIGHWAY robbery” is how Noel Williams, president of the Kingston Chapter of Jamaica Union of Travellers Association (JUTA) Tours, has described the impending toll road rate increases, which transport operators fear could impact their operations. The increases prompted more calls on Monday for the Government to step in.

JUTA representatives, in collaboration with Jamaica Cooperative Automobile & Limousine (JCAL) Tours Limited and other transport organisations, gathered at the Jamaica Pegasus hotel in New Kingston for a meeting on Monday, hoping to get an audience with representatives of the Ministry of Transport and the Toll Authority of Jamaica to share pressing concerns.

But despite being invited, according to Williams, there were no representatives from either group.

Williams told the Jamaica Observer that their no-show was a clear indication of the scant regard which they have for transport operators.

“We are saying to the Government and the Toll Authority, that we cannot any longer absorb this toll increase, because we are of the opinion that this is the most expensive toll anywhere in the world,” Williams said, expressing that many operators already find it difficult to pay fees for certain categories of vehicles on the toll and cannot manage any upward adjustment at this time.

The new toll fees, to affect motorists using the North-South Highway, are expected to take effect at the end of the month.

The Government has published the proposed new rates with a capped toll of $2,610 each way for Class 1 vehicles. Operators of Class 2 vehicles would pay $5,220 one way, while the proposed toll for Class 3 vehicles, including larger trucks, is $7,830.

Williams recommended that the move be put on pause for a year, to allow for consultation among stakeholders.

“I think this is highway robbery by the Toll Authority, and the Government sits there completely complacent and they do nothing about it. With that said, we are asking the Government to have dialogue with the Toll Authority. We are having a serious issue already with what we are paying for one coaster bus to go from Kingston to St Ann and back. One round trip [now] costs bus operators $15,000. We will be asked to pay $15,680 when the new rate is introduced. If we are to do that, then we have to keep on passing on these increases to the passengers, who already have been complaining about what we are charging now,” he said.

The president said that numerous letters have been written to policymakers, but they have never responded.

He specifically referred to some representatives of the Toll Authority as being very disrespectful.

“We sent letters to the Toll Authority about another bus we have in the system, which is the new type of Hiace bus. It has a longer front than the older one, and hence when these buses go to the toll, they have to pay the same money as what the coaster pays,” he said.

“And when you question it, they are telling you that it’s because of the length of the bus. Nothing is put in place to accommodate the service that we provide in terms of transportation. And also the toll road barely has any lights. With all of this, we have to be paying so much money…

“We are definitely calling on the Government to sit and have a look at the situation and to renegotiate the contract so as to benefit the Jamaican people. A lot more people would use the toll as well, if it was much cheaper, but these people are just thinking about collecting money… they’re not thinking about us.“

Williams lamented that those operators who opt to take the alternative route from Kingston to St Ann cannot do so because those roads are deplorable. He appealed to the Government to have these alternative routes fixed.

“Right now, I believe it is a breach of people’s constitutional rights because they have been literally forced to use the toll, which is costly. The original roads are there, but they are not comfortable for people to drive on.

Meanwhile, Lorraine “Oscar” Finnikin, president of the All Voice Taxi Association, was among transport association heads present at the meeting.

He told the Observer that he attended to show solidarity with the JUTA president.

“They have tried their best over the years to not pass on the cost to their passengers but as it is now, they don’t have any choice,” he said.

“There are a lot of overhead expenses facing the public passenger vehicle sector. One is the cost of gas due to the situation in the Middle East, then there are overall expenses through maintenance, operational costs and service parts. With the increase in the toll fees, it has reached a stage where it is just too much for the sector to bear anymore.”

In a statement last Thursday, Minister of Transport Daryl Vaz acknowledged the concerns expressed by motorists, but explained that the concerning toll rates were yet another example of the former People’s National Party Administration entering into a less than favourable toll deal, which does not yield any tangible advantages for the Jamaican populace.

Vaz said the toll agreement binds current and future governments to its terms, but said the Government was moving to have discussions towards arriving at a more favourable and affordable toll cost for Jamaicans.

“However, the binding agreement entered by the former administration has put us in a position where the concessionaire has to agree to whatever we suggest in order for it to be implemented,” Vaz said.

He also said suggestions that Government pay off the toll operators in an effort to discontinue the unsustainable rise in rates, were impractical.

The Concession Agreement for the North-South Highway (Caymanas to Ocho Rios) was executed in June 2012 under a 50-year Build-Finance-Operate-Transfer arrangement.

World.title: Sweltering heat threatens egg industry
World.content:
President of the Jamaica Egg Farmers Association Mark Campbell on his egg farm in Trelawny on Monday. (Photo: Horace Hines)

FALMOUTH, Trelawny — President of the Jamaica Egg Farmers Association (JEFA) Mark Campbell is urging members to protect their flock from an ongoing heatwave that is taking a toll on the industry, even as it recovers from the double whammy of hurricanes Beryl and Melissa.

Speaking with reporters on his farm in Trelawny Monday afternoon, Campbell noted that prolonged high temperatures have been especially hard on farmers along the island’s south coast, where laying hens have died from heat stress. He said farmers have reported losses of hundreds of birds, representing millions of dollars in replacement costs, plus income lost from reduced egg production.

“This year, 2026, the egg industry has come under sweltering heat, and a number of farmers, particularly those on the south side of the island — St Elizabeth, and Clarendon — they have suffered heavy losses. One farmer over there told me that he has lost over 700 chickens because of the heat that is on the land. And another farmer on the same south side of the island lost over 600 chickens. Now, those two figures run into millions of dollars just in the cost to purchase these chickens. And then the opportunity that has been lost is significant,” said Campbell, who is also operator of Campbell’s Egg Farm Limited in Trelawny.

He explained that laying hens perform best at temperatures between 60 and 70 degrees Fahrenheit and become increasingly vulnerable as temperatures approach about 106 degrees Fahrenheit, which is their body temperature.

The JEFA president is recommending that farmers install irrigation systems or lawn sprinklers on the roofs of bird houses to help reduce temperatures during the hottest part of the day, between 10:00 am and 2:00 pm.

“The heat that radiates off these roofs and goes down to the chickens is what really hurts them. Once the temperature comes up to the body temperature of the chicken, the bird is going to die,” he explained.

Campbell pointed out that while temperature-controlled poultry houses provide greater protection, many local producers may not be able to afford them. To compensate, he encouraged farmers constructing new poultry houses to incorporate adequate roof height and insulation.

Other advice provided by the JEFA president involve feeding birds during cooler hours of the morning, adjusting lighting schedules to encourage earlier feeding, and providing vitamin supplements to help maintain feed intake.

“We have to start looking at how we are going to prepare for periods of elevated heat because laying birds cannot deal with heat at all,” he urged.

Campbell said chickens experiencing heat stress often reduce their feed intake, resulting in lower egg production. He added that production losses could range from 50 to 70 per cent if birds remain exposed to excessive heat. He said farmers in cooler, mountainous areas have not reported similar levels of losses because of lower temperatures and stronger winds.

Despite the challenges being faced by some farmers, Campbell cautiously said he does not expect any scarcity of eggs this year as replacement birds are entering production.

“I hate to make forecasts about production because so many I have made in the past have been wrong. But this is the period between now and the end of the year where a significant number of new birds are going in the field, and if the farmers pay attention to good practices, I do not see a shortage because of the heat at the moment,” he said.

World.title: Is everyone on the Burnham bus?
World.content:
Andy Burnham wants to talk about his new bus fare cap but, as Sam Coates and Anne McElvoy point out, there isn’t much chance of talking about anything else without the Commons sitting.

They go through how the bus fare plan is funded. Chancellor John Healey says it will be “no burden to British taxpayers”, but the small print raises questions about how the scheme will be funded.

At the Farnborough Air Show, there is the opportunity to talk defence spending – and fresh questions about how to fill the funding gap from Keir Starmer’s pledges.

Plus, Sam and Anne round up the latest ministerial movements.

World.title: The EU’s Russia sanctions crunch
World.content:
Today is a make-or-break moment for the EU’s 21st sanctions package targeting Russia.

After EU countries failed to agree on the ins and outs of the agreement last week, ambassadors are meeting again today in Brussels to finally clinch the deal. But can they hash out the remaining thorny issues?

Next: European Parliament is trying to reengage with China after a seven-year diplomatic freeze. But despite the defrosting of relations, it’s clear lawmakers are unsure of what their stance toward Beijing should be.

And finally, as Christopher Nolan’s “The Odyssey” hits cinemas, a Hollywood culture war hits Greece.

World.title: Ukraine’s drone strikes pile pressure on Russian economy
World.content:
The central bank has had to keep interest rates painfully high to keep a lid on inflation, at a time when the budget deficit is widening sharply. Its key rate currently stands at 14.25 percent.

Businesses typically have to pay well above that rate for credit, and things aren’t made easier by the Kremlin competing for the same, limited pool of savings.

Moscow had originally budgeted to cut military spending this year, Janis Kluge, an analyst with the German Institute for International and Security Affairs, said. Instead, it has ballooned and accounted for nearly half of government spending in the second quarter, he estimates.

Kluge said the bond market standoff doesn’t herald any imminent collapse, but is consistent with other signs of strain in Russia’s financial markets. The benchmark stock index, dominated for years by the oil and gas industry, has fallen 30 percent in the last two months as Ukraine has shown its ability to hit important economic infrastructure as far afield as Omsk in Siberia.

Ukraine has broadened its drone offensive in spectacular fashion during that time. In addition to the refinery attacks that have caused long lines for fuel up and down the country, its armed forces claim to have struck 183 ships in the Black Sea and the Sea of Azov, severely disrupting Russia’s attempts to resupply a beleaguered Crimea with fuel, as well as hampering its exports of grain to world markets.

Wild fires

But even that has been overshadowed by attacks in recent days on the fulfillment centers of Wildberries, Russia’s biggest e-commerce company and an essential part of the supply chain for thousands of small businesses.

World.title: 7 times Andy Burnham flirted with Nigel Farage’s voters
World.content:
1) Staying out of the EU

Last year, the then-Greater Manchester mayor said he’d like to rejoin the European Union within his lifetime. But then reality struck.

At the outset of his by-election campaign in Makerfield — which voted heavily for Brexit — this May, Burnham said reentering the Brussels orbit is a battle he wouldn’t fight.

Despite calling Brexit “damaging,” he stressed “the last thing we should do right now is re-run those arguments.”

Burnham said his own calls to strengthen democracy would be undermined “if we don’t respect that vote.”

2) Slamming the Whitehall ‘blob’

Burnham has attacked the British state, arguing real power is vested in around 50 people with “London-centric views” at the heart of officialdom.

Though praising the civil service as “full of good people,” Burnham has said they’re held back by a “structure and the culture” which is “too adversarial.”

World.title: Post-Orbán sanctions showdown exposes EU capitals’ red lines
World.content:
A deal is still broadly expected, but more concessions may be needed before ambassadors can get it over the line. Seven people working on the package told POLITICO that several measures had already been weakened or dropped altogether.

The package, presented by European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen in June, is the 21st since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine. After 20 previous rounds, diplomats say the EU is running out of easy targets and increasingly colliding with powerful national interests. Sanctions require the unanimous backing of all 27 EU countries.

“There’s no more low-hanging fruit, with 20 packages done. You’ll bump into individual member state interests more, so you have to find a balance,” said an EU diplomat involved in the discussions, granted anonymity to discuss the confidential talks, like others in this article.

Greece has so far refused to support the 21st package because of a ban on EU companies shipping Russian liquefied natural gas to third countries. Athens oversees the world’s largest merchant fleet and is concerned about the impact on a Greek company that operates ice-breaking tankers that export Russian LNG.

Greece’s ambassador warned that the measure could prompt vessels to reflag and move to jurisdictions where the rules would be even harder to enforce, according to two further diplomats involved in the discussions.

“We’re trying to find a way out of this, but what this [issue with Greece] shows is that we’re starting to collide with some key economic interests,” said a fourth diplomat.

World.title: Lifting Russian athletes ban only helps Putin, Ukraine tells IOC
World.content:
“Why now? I have no answer on this question. I can’t see any reason for it,” said Bidnyi, a former bodybuilder. “Undermining the collective pressure that the international community has been building against the aggressor … it’s not a very honorable role for this organization.”

The IOC said that the reversal did not represent any change in its view of Russia’s war in Ukraine, which it still condemns. However, it said the ban was relaxed because the Russian committee removed regional sports organizations ​from Russia-occupied Ukrainian territories from its membership, which was the reason it was sanctioned.

Bidnyi said the IOC had fallen for a “primitive legal trick” and that Russia had simply restructured its Olympic committee to circumvent the IOC’s ban.

“We do not believe the IOC fails to understand this,” he said. “This is a deliberate decision to ignore reality, which completely ruins their own credibility.”

Moscow has repeatedly used international sport to maintain a foothold in Western institutions despite its broader diplomatic isolation since the war in Ukraine began. That has included influencing the world of chess, international fencing and lobbying for the gradual return of Russian athletes to global competitions.

European sport ministers have also reacted with anger to the IOC’s decision, with ministers from nine countries — Sweden, Estonia, the Netherlands, Lithuania, Latvia, Poland, Romania, Finland and Denmark — calling for the EU to cut funding for the Olympics.

World.title: Zelenskyy fires top army commander amid nationwide protests
World.content:
"We will jointly determine an updated strategy of our defense [and] steps to continue the reform of the corps system, to fulfill the supply requests of combat commanders," Zelenskyy said in an address to the nation on Tuesday evening.

He also expressed gratitude to Syrskyi for previous successful operations in 2022 in Kyiv and Kharkiv and the 2024 incursion into Russia's Kursk region.

Joint Forces Commander Maj. Gen. Mykhailo Drapatyi will become the Ukrainian Army's new commander-in-chief, Zelenskyy said in his speech.

Drapatyi is an experienced field commander who successfully organized the protection of Kharkiv in 2024 from a Russian counteroffensive. He was among the first of Ukraine's top commanders to openly support Fedorov last week.

Ukraine has seen nationwide protests since Zelenskyy ousted Fedorov, and it's far from certain that Syrskyi's ouster will suffice to quell them.

Fedorov has refused to take any post besides his old job as defense minister, two officials familiar with the talks told POLITICO. It's not clear whether he has accepted Zelenskyy's latest offer to return to government.

He congratulated Drapatyi, however, describing him as a "breath of fresh air." He also called Syrskyi to thank him for his successes in Kyiv and Kharkiv, calling them now "part of history."

"But we need to move even faster and write new chapters, correcting all previous mistakes," Fedorov said.
