World.title: Ukraine's Fire Point CEO: Germany can count on us for deep-strike deterrence
World.content:
In Norse mythology, Freyja is known as the goddess of war, love and beauty. "A strange combination, until you look at Ukraine today, where all three coexist," writes Iryna Terekh, CEO of Ukrainian defence company Fire Point, on X.

 

She continues, saying that those "shared values run across this continent, from the Baltic to the Black Sea", referencing the Joint Declaration on the Establishment of the Integrated Anti-Ballistic Missile Coalition, which names Freyja as its flagship programme, signed by the Coalition of the Willing in Paris on Monday last week.

The idea is to create a lower-cost, modular missile-defence system by combining Ukraine's combat and wartime experience with European technology and industry.

Instead of relying on a single manufacturer, different countries would contribute individual components – from interceptor missiles to radars and command systems – to build what participating governments describe as an integrated European missile-defence architecture that complements existing systems, such as the US Patriot air defence system.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, French President Emmanuel Macron and UK Prime Minister Keir Starmer in Paris. Teresa Suarez/Pool Photo via AP

Just a year ago, Freyja was little more than a concept put forward by Fire Point. The Ukrainian defence company rose to prominence with its long-range cruise missile FP-5 "Flamingo", which has been used by Kyiv to carry out deep strikes against targets inside Russia.

Euronews caught up with Iryna Terekh, the company's CEO and CTO, one day after the joint declaration's signing in Paris last week. Will Freyja thrive despite European bureaucracy, and what would the Flamingo's potential production in Germany mean for deterrence against Russia?

Euronews: Let's start with the latest Coalition of the Willing meeting and the signing of the Freyja initiative, which was initiated by Fire Point. How significant was last week's agreement, and what does it mean for the future of the programme?

Iryna Terekh: First of all, I'm completely amazed. I never expected that what started as a brief idea, one and a half years ago, with the first discussions taking place on a napkin, would come this far and end up in a room full of leaders, National Security Advisers, decision-makers, CEOs of prominent companies and all the supporters of the change that we all made together.

So, of course, it's very inspiring, and I do feel like this change was due for quite some time. We're very happy that we were able to inspire people to actually start implementing this technological and doctrinal shift that we're making with Freyja.

Euronews: Now that nine European countries have signed up to the Freyja initiative alongside Ukraine, how quickly do you think this change can actually be implemented?

Iryna Terekh: This is a very cool question because I thought, what's the difference between security guarantees promised and actual security guarantees executed? That's why on the first slide of a Freyja presentation, there is a phrase that says "security guarantees are written in steel and not in ink".

I consider this more important than the Budapest memorandum. And of course, the execution is the most important part of the job. But since we've been doing our homework on the b2b level already for quite some time, we see the commitment, the effort, the interest. I'm sure that with the support of the leadership, we will be able to overcome bureaucracy much faster.

The main task for leadership is to remove bureaucratic obstacles, because they sometimes make things worse and help the enemy.

We have to understand that this threat is no smaller than the threat from Russia, for example, because sabotaging critical processes can be extremely harmful – it can even be deadly. That's why we've seen a full commitment from political leaders to help us focus on technological development, while they have our backs in addressing the bureaucratic challenges.

Euronews: We often hear the argument that Europe is still at peace, and that if a war were to break out, production of tanks, missiles and other weapons could simply be ramped up. What do you make of that argument? Do you think Europe can afford to wait until a conflict starts before significantly increasing production?

Iryna Terekh: I would like to mention that it's completely normal for a human brain to avoid thinking about uncomfortable things. I recently saw statistics about human anxiety and how people react to threats. And the fact is that the closer you are to a threat, the more relaxed you are.

Why is that? Because the worst has already happened and you don't have to think about it, you just have to act.

The further away you are from the threat, the more you want to avoid uncomfortable things and hide in the normality of today.

Therefore, we cannot judge human brains for being designed in this specific way. But we need to know this and we need to consider this, take it into account while we're planning big defence things. And while the average time of a ballistic missile reaching the Ukrainian capital takes around two to five minutes maximum, it's seven minutes to Warsaw, eight minutes to Berlin, and a maximum of 12 minutes to Paris. The difference is not that big.

What we are trying to do is not to use threats as a motivation factor, but to build a whole ecosystem that would be able to react to threats in a correct way. And this is the major thing about Freyja, the whole rethinking of how air protection should work. And the system, the technology should outlive any political cycle, any changes that are happening because if the system is built correctly, it is very resilient. What we're trying to build is a resilient defence ecosystem.

Deutsche Soldaten feuern das Patriot-Waffensystem auf der NATO-Raketenabschussanlage in Chania, Griechenland, ab. Sebastian Apel/U.S. Department of Defense, via AP

Euronews: We've all seen the reports about dwindling stocks of Patriot interceptors and other missiles. How much did those shortages influence the development of Freyja?

Iryna Terekh: A big role, of course. I love Patriot Systems. As an engineer, I'm completely amazed. This is definitely an example to work with, but it was never designed to be consumed in such amounts as we do in Ukraine. We need to create a product that is relevant to the threat that we have.

Euronews: A few weeks ago, German company Diehl Defence announced an agreement with Fire Point to produce the Flamingo cruise missile in Germany. Can you say anything about the progress of these talks and the cooperation?

Iryna Terekh: I will say abstractly that there are a few layers of negotiations, one with a few German companies and with the German government on creating an industrial cooperation where we can share our Ukrainian experience and help Germany to have cheap and mass-produced weapons.

Euronews: In your point of view, what role is Germany playing at the moment? France and the UK have taken the lead with the Coalition of the Willing.

Iryna Terekh: I would say that in the end, it's humans talking to each other. As in any country, there are companies that are very like-minded and some that are completely different. We see this inconsistency within Germany and even within Ukraine. It's the same for each and every country.

And in general, I understand that it’s hard – especially for Germans – to overcome the narrative of never again, where war is something extremely toxic, something that should never happen again. I completely support this, until you are facing a completely unfair attack on yourself.

Freyja is not an offensive system. It is clearly a defensive system. We're thinking on defence, it's a completely different narrative, which makes it easier to adopt. In the end, these are all people, you have to find the people who share the same values as you, and then the work will go as smoothly as possible.

Euronews: Coming back to the Flamingo cruise missile. If you look at the European leg of NATO, there's this so-called deep strike gap. Ukraine seems to have solved that deep strike gap with the Flamingo. Is the Flamingo, in a sense, the deterrence Europe needs? Especially looking at Germany, where there was recently uncertainty about whether the US would station their Tomahawk long-range missiles in Germany after all.

Iryna Terekh: Let's say Germany can count on us in terms of providing them with deep strike deterrence. Of course, at the moment, the priorities are Ukrainian needs. But we have a very good memory of the good and the bad things and we will be forever thankful to our allies for supporting us during the hardest times.

And of course, as soon as this would be possible in terms of production capacity, we would be able to support Germany as well. With the Flamingo and the modernised version of FP1, we achieved another world record of a distance of 3,000 kilometres. We are rethinking the doctrine of 'Deep Rear' and kind of rewriting military vocabulary.

There is no such thing as a deep rear for our enemy at the moment. And that is a good thing for us.

Workers inspect Flamingo missiles a Fire Point's secret factory in Ukraine on Thursday, Aug. 14, 2025. AP Photo/Efrem Lukatsky

Euronews: Last year, the Flamingo was dubbed a "wonder weapon" and a gamechanger. Has it delivered?

Iryna Terekh: I do not believe in this concept, because if you cannot repeat your own result in a predictable way, you will not make a big change. Yes, you can have tactical success, but this is definitely not what changed the narrative.

We see now on a daily basis that at least 300 Ukrainian drones are flying every night and about the same number during the day, the big drones towards Russian territories. Not the one drone, but the possibility to make daily launches in a predictable way.

So, Flamingo is, of course, a very big card, an important one, a game changer in a way. But the most important part about the Flamingo is that we are increasing its production, that we are increasing its accuracy, that we are using this as a very heavy argument.

Basically, this is our pen to write our conditions for future peace negotiations.

Flamingo-missile Fire Point

Euronews: When it comes to unmanned systems, it's known that the advancement proceeds so fast that a drone needs an upgrade every few weeks. Do you adapt the missile after each use?

Iryna Terekh: At the moment, it's a constant loop. After each and every battlefield use, we change and adjust something to make it more efficient. Let's say it's a daily, weekly loop.

You mainly have to adapt the head (guidance unit), which contains the main computing power. The software still fits in the small part, whether it's a drone or a missile.

Euronews: Does that apply to other missiles, too? Or is Ukraine a sort-of front runner in this case?

Iryna Terekh: I think it's mostly a Ukrainian thing because we can afford this from a bureaucratic perspective at least. I don't know whether or not it's a common practice for Western weapons because the amount of paperwork behind every change is crazy. Therefore, I'm not so sure about this.

World.title: Mamdani says NYC lacks authority to arrest Israeli PM Netanyahu
World.content:
Zohran Mamdani, the mayor of New York City, has said the city lacks the authority to carry out the International Criminal Court's (ICC) arrest warrant for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, but urged US federal authorities to do so should he visit the United States.

 

"Benjamin Netanyahu is a war criminal," Mamdani said in a video statement posted to social media. "The architect of a horrific genocide against the Palestinian people".

The ICC issued a warrant for the Israeli PM's arrest in November 2024, alleging responsibility for war crimes including "starvation as a method of warfare" and "intentionally directing an attack against the civilian population." It also accused Netanyahu of a number of crimes against humanity.

In his video address, Mamdani said he agreed with the ICC that Netanyahu should be arrested and put on trial. But after reviewing "every avenue available under applicable law," the mayor said his administration had determined it did not have the "independent legal authority to enforce this warrant."

"The federal government, however, does," he continued, adding: "I call on them to join the ICC and execute this warrant."

Netanyahu's office has dubbed the ICC a "kangaroo court" and called the warrant against the Israeli leader "bogus."

On Monday, US President Donald Trump said Netanyahu "will not be arrested, in any way, shape, or form, while in the United States of America."

Netanyahu could attend the United Nations General Assembly summit in New York in September.

Mamdani, a Democrat, was elected as NYC mayor in November 2025, securing just over 50% of the vote.

Mamdani's bid for office centred on the cost-of-living crises. He vowed to freeze rent, make buses and childcare free, and to create city-owned grocery stores as part of his campaign.

Trump has been highly critical of Mamdani, branding him a "communist" and saying he was "destroying New York."

World.title: Ferran Torres sparks controversy with 'Make Spain Great Again' cap at World Cup parade
World.content:
Ferran Torres scored the goal that secured the 2026 World Cup title against Argentina, in the 106th minute of the final played at the New York/New Jersey stadium. A day later, during the victory parade through the streets of Madrid, the striker appeared bare-chested and wearing a red cap emblazoned with the phrase "Make Spain Great Again", a direct adaptation of Donald Trump’s campaign slogan, "Make America Great Again".

 

Images of Torres greeting fans from the open-top bus, cap on his head, spread rapidly on social media. The cap is not part of the official MAGA merchandise line, but a customised version of the slogan with a reference to Spain. Before the parade, the squad had visited King Felipe VI and Queen Letizia at the Zarzuela Palace, and also the prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, at Moncloa.

Mixed reactions

The gesture prompted very different interpretations among fans and media. Some took it as a joke with no deeper meaning; others saw it as an ironic nod to Trump, or even as a possible dig at Sánchez. It has also been pointed out that the formula "Make Spain great again" has been used in the past by the right-wing party Vox, which fuelled the political readings of the incident.

Torres has offered no public explanation for why he chose the cap or whether there was a specific intention behind the message, so for the time being the various theories remain open to each person’s interpretation.

Ferran Torres celebrating his goal Copyright 2026 The Associated Press. All rights reserved.

Sumar accuses Torres of being behind a vulture fund

The row was not just about the cap. Alberto Ibáñez, an MP for Compromís–Sumar, on Tuesday shared incorrect information when he claimed that Ferran Torres’s company was acting as a "vulture fund" and had acquired "20 homes in Valencia" to speculate. However, as ‘El Español’ (source in Spanish) reported and the player’s camp confirmed to the outlet, that claim does not reflect reality.

Sources close to the player explain that the main property asset of Eleven Future Invest, the company of Spain’s No 7, is a tertiary-use building located next to Mestalla, made up of 50 offices rented to businesses, and not a stock of residential properties intended for speculation.

As for his residential portfolio, Ferran Torres owns four homes: his residence in Barcelona, two properties in Valencia and another house in the town where he spends his holidays. He also owns a plot of land on which he plans to build in the future.

The controversy arose from information published by ‘Forbes’, which stated that the forward has "20 properties strategically spread" between the Valencian Community and Catalonia.

On the back of that reference, Ibáñez stepped up his criticism and called for legal reform to prevent "companies and vulture funds such as Eleven Future Invest, Ferran Torres’s company which, according to ‘Forbes’, already hoards 20 homes in Valencia, from buying houses to speculate".

Cucurella also in hot water with Argentina

The defender, a new Real Madrid signing, was one of the liveliest during the celebrations in Madrid. After the official receptions at the Zarzuela Palace and La Moncloa, the party moved on to Plaza de Cibeles. There, each player walked on stage to a song of his own choosing, and Marc once again chose ‘Malbec’, the track by Duki and Bizarrap which he had already used during the celebrations after Euro 2024.

The gesture did not go unnoticed in Argentina for two reasons. The artists behind the song are both Argentinian (Duki and Bizarrap) and the verses: "Llegué a la ciudad y me reciben como si fuera un boss. Cada vez más pegao y ni yo sé cómo pasó. Hoy festejamos y mi equipo salió campeón. Adentro del party, afuera en la calle, se escucha mi voz", which did not exactly help either...

Part of the fanbase and some media interpreted the choice of song as a provocation towards the Albiceleste after the outcome of the tournament. The daily ‘TyC Sports’, for example, went so far as to describe it as a "taunt" aimed at the Argentine national team.

World.title: Aerial footage reveals the scale of Spain’s La Mierla wildfire
World.content:
Aerial footage from Spain's Guardia Civil and the Spanish Air and Space Force shows the scale of the La Mierla wildfire in Guadalajara, central Spain.

 

Thick smoke rises over hillsides blackened by flames as helicopters fly above the fire, revealing the vast area affected by one of the country's largest wildfires this summer.

The blaze has been burning for six days despite a major firefighting operation involving more than 600 firefighters and troops, supported by 29 aircraft. Authorities say it is one of the most challenging wildfires they have faced.

More than 26,000 hectares have burned, while other official estimates put the affected area at around 30,000 hectares. Around 1,200 residents have been evacuated as crews continue to battle the flames north of Madrid.

World.title: Countdown to the ballot: Zambia gears up for August elections
World.content:
This week on Spotlight on Africa, we're heading to Zambia, where general elections are set to take place on the 13th August. Voters will go to the polls to elect a president, members of the National Assembly, councillors and council chairs. Incumbent President Hakainde Hichilema has already picked up endorsements from within his own camp, the UPND Alliance, the coalition that's held power since 2021. So what's at stake, and who's in the running?

Advertising

This week on the podcast, we're heading to Zambia, which is gearing up for elections next month and is now in full campaign mode. Two of our RFI colleagues, Yang Mei and Igor Strauss, travelled to Zambia recently for in-depth reporting on four years of Hakainde Hichilema's rule, and his chances of re-election.

In power since August 2021, "HH", as he's most often called, is a businessman, farmer and politician, and the seventh president of Zambia.

General elections are due to be held in the country on 13 August 2026 to elect a president, members of the National Assembly, councillors and council chairs.

The year ahead for African democracy: who is going to the polls in 2026?

Hichilema has received endorsements from some members of the UPND Alliance, including from the leaders of the Party of National Unity and Progress and the Movement for Multi-Party Democracy.

According to an opinion poll conducted by a University of Zambia demographer, Hichilema is set to be re-elected, leading with 60 percent of the vote, while the combined opposition would take 35 percent.

Zambia's Hichilema sworn in, becoming rare opposition president in southern Africa

Our colleagues Yang Mei and Igor Strauss bring us some of the interviews they gathered on the ground, so join us as we hear from ordinary Zambians, as well as from leading journalist Joseph Mwenda, editor-in-chief at News Diggers, who has led multiple investigations into the current government's relations with China; and from Robert Mwale, an economist and Lead Public Finance and Economic Governance Researcher at the Centre for Trade Policy and Development (CTPD).

Among the issues at stake are a lack of freedom of expression, but also a legacy of economic growth, driven in no small part by China's heavy involvement in the economy.

Thanks to our reporters, Igor Strauss and Yang Mei, for their work and insight, and thank you for listening.

This is the last episode of the 2025–26 season. We'll be back in September with another one.

Spotlight on Africa is produced by RFI's English language service. This episode was mixed by Erwan Rome.

World.title: Turkey marks a decade since the coup that never was, but never really ended
World.content:
On 16 July, Turkey marked a decade since the failed coup that shook the nation. Its defeat is widely viewed as the final curtain on military meddling in politics and as the moment when President Erdogan cemented his grip on power, yet the aftershocks for human rights and foreign relations still reverberate.

Advertising

On 16 July, Turkey marked a decade since the failed coup that shook the nation. Its defeat is widely viewed as the final curtain on military meddling in politics and as the moment when President Erdogan cemented his grip on power, yet the aftershocks for human rights and foreign relations still reverberate.

A decade ago, factions within the Turkish military, composed of rebellious officers and followers of the Islamic cleric Fethullah Gulen, launched a dramatic attempt to topple President Erdogan.

"I remember, as a soldier, those who started the coup," recalls Murat Aslan, an army officer at the time. "I had no idea that there were members of this organisation (Gulen followers); they were very secretive."

Erdogan tightens his grip

Now a security analyst at SETA, a pro-government think tank, Aslan describes the failed coup as a turning point that reshaped the course of Turkish democracy.

"The message was very clear. Turkish society collectively rejected it," said Aslan. "Thousands took to the streets; that's more than challenging, because you see tanks rolling and people trying to stop them, trying to capture the soldiers with their rifles. It takes more than courage." More than 250 people died resisting the coup.

In the aftermath, Erdogan imposed emergency rule and expanded his presidential authority through a sharply contested national referendum. "This military intervention actually consolidated the Erdogan-led government," Aslan added.

Turkey's military, relations with US to survive failed coup, ruling party vice-president

Hundreds of soldiers and officers faced prosecution as the government declared an end to the army's long history of political interference. Since 1960, the military had orchestrated three coups, the most recent in 1980.

A decade of purges and closures

In the wake of the failed takeover, tens of thousands were purged from state institutions, many never returning even after being cleared.

More than a thousand NGOs were shut down during two years of emergency rule. Milena Buyum, senior Turkey campaigner for Amnesty International, acknowledges the grave threat to democracy posed by the attempted coup: "The state has a responsibility to ensure the safety and security of its citizens and to investigate criminal acts like the ones carried out that night," said Buyum.

Turkey's Erdogan warms to Russia after West coup response

However, Buyum warns that many of the measures introduced under the state of emergency have since been written into ordinary law, permanently curtailing fundamental freedoms: "The right to freedom of expression, freedom of assembly and association: the impact on civil society was felt very sharply and starkly in the immediate aftermath of the coup, but that impact continues," said Buyum.

Ankara's alliances

The failed coup also drove a wedge into Turkey's long-standing alliance with the United States. "Ankara saw the hand of the United States behind the failed coup attempt," claims Ozgur Unluhisarcikli, who leads the Ankara office of the German Marshall Fund.

Even before the attempted coup, Erdogan's relations with President Barack Obama had been tense. Obama's belated support, offered only after the coup had failed, fuelled Ankara's suspicions of US complicity, particularly as Washington refused to extradite Fethullah Gulen, whom Erdogan blamed for orchestrating the plot. Gulen denied the accusation until his death in 2024.

Turks in France divided on failed coup

Unluhisarcikli observes that US-Turkish relations remained strained for years, while Erdogan gravitated towards Russian President Vladimir Putin, whose rapid show of support stood in sharp contrast to Washington's hesitation.

"Putin was among the first leaders, I believe even the first, to extend political support to the elected government in Ankara, and in those days I believe that support mattered greatly to President Erdogan," Unluhisarcikli said.

Rumours still persist in Turkey today that Moscow warned Erdogan on the day of the failed coup. Unluhisarcikli says it was only with the election of President Donald Trump, who shared Erdogan's animosity towards Obama and Joe Biden, that US-Turkish relations began to thaw, a shift highlighted at this month's NATO summit in Ankara. Yet the wave of mass arrests during the summit, enabled by post-coup emergency powers, served as a stark reminder that the shadow of the failed takeover still looms over Turkey.

World.title: India news: Opposition steps up pressure amid 'Cockroach' protests
World.content:
07/22/2026 July 22, 2026 India's education minister breaks silence as protests press for resignation

India's Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan said that Prime Minister Narendra Modi's administration was committed to addressing the concerns of youth protesters and examination reforms, as he broke his silence amid intensifying calls for his resignation.

Protesters have asked Pradhan to step down, angered by a slew of entrance test paper leaks, including those of a major medical school entrance exam called National Eligibility cum Entrance Test (NEET).

The NEET paper leak in May forced over two million students to resit the highly-competitive exam, leading to some young applicants taking their own lives.

"Our Government remains 100% committed to discussing NEET and addressing every genuine concern of our youth on the floor of the House," Pradhan said on X.

He criticized opposition leader Rahul Gandhi and his Congress party's Tuesday protest outside Modi's residence, describing it as a "political spectacle," and saying that the government conveyed its readiness for a comprehensive discussion on the students' issues.

"The students of India deserve far better than being treated as props in a political campaign. They deserve certainty over chaos, solutions over slogans and responsibility over disruption," Pradhan said, referring to Gandhi's demonstration.

He said that students were owed "answers, reforms and accountability" and the Modi government "remains committed to delivering".

The statement is Pradhan's first on the youth protests led by the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) that started as a sit-in demonstration at New Delhi's Jantar Mantar on June 20 and quickly snowballed into a protest march on Monday, drawing thousands of protesters into the streets of central Delhi — India's main corridor of political power.

Police had denied permission for the march to the Indian parliament but the 'Cockroach' protesters pushed ahead, clashing with police who used tear gas and batons to push them back.

According to official figures, nearly 180 people — including 118 police personnel and 60 protesters — were injured.

World.title: Can VR help you achieve your goals?
World.content:
A Max Planck researcher has developed VR and smartphone tools that let you "meet" your future self. The science behind it is more powerful than it sounds.

Imagine sitting in a virtual room and coming face to face with yourself — ten years older, slightly grayer, but unmistakably you. Not a fantasy. Not a filter. Just you, aged by a decade, staring back.

That's the core of an experiment developed by Jean-Louis van Gelder, a criminologist and psychologist at the Max Planck Institute for the Study of Crime, Security and Law in Freiburg, Germany. His team has just published findings showing that confronting people with a digitally aged version of themselves —their "future self" — can sharpen long-term thinking and help them act on their own goals .

The science of the future self

The setup is deceptively simple. Participants come into a lab, where they have their photo taken. After software has aged the respective face by ten years, they enter a VR environment, look into a virtual mirror and see their present self — while the older version sits across the room. They interact with their future self and ask it questions. They hear their own voice played back, slightly lowered to match the aging effect.

The result, van Gelder says, is that the future becomes more concrete rather than abstract. "When future states or future events become more vivid in our minds, we're also more likely to actively work towards them," he tells DW. A clear mental image of who you're going to be makes it easier to divide a goal into actionable steps — and gives you stronger motivation to take them.

In the study, participants set their own goals: better health, improved academic performance, less procrastination, reduced screen time.

The VR edition outperformed a parallel smartphone-based version. Both tools helped people feel more connected to their future self, but only the VR one demonstrably helped them achieve their goals.

Why a criminology institute is studying self-improvement

The link to the Max Planck Institute for crime research is not incidental. Van Gelder's original target group was not university students. It was young delinquents.

Impulsivity and short-term thinking are among the most robust predictors of juvenile delinquency, he explains. Crime almost always involves immediate benefits — quick cash, status, gratification — but also long-term costs that tend to far outweigh them. From this perspective, delinquents are not irrational; they are simply disconnected from their later lives, discounting the future so heavily that it barely registers.

"If you talk to some of them, you realize they actually know that what they're doing is not good for them," van Gelder says. The aim, then, is not to lecture but rather to help people to persuade themselves — using their own face, their own voice and their own imagined future.

What you can try right now

No VR headset is required. Van Gelder's team is currently developing a smartphone application to broaden access. In the meantime he suggests a lower-tech version: simply ask yourself how your future self will look back on a decision you're making today. This practice — sometimes called episodic future thinking, or mental time travel — is something he incorporates into his own daily life.

Van Gelder believes the technology could go even further. He envisions a personalized AI avatar — fed with data about how you speak, think and write — acting as a daily coach from five or ten years in the future. "I can see your future self being your present-day coach," he says.

For now, there's the extremely accessible option of one of the oldest tools available: a piece of paper, a pen, and a question worth pondering. Where do you want to be in ten years' time — and what would that future individual tell you to do today?

This article is an excerpt from our podcast Science Unscripted. You can subscribe to the podcast here .

World.title: Chile: Several dead, missing in severe rainstorm
World.content:
President Jose Antonio Kast has declared a state of emergency in the affected areas of the country.

At least 13 people have died and seven others went missing after heavy rains lashed Chile, authorities said on Tuesday.

The rainstorm has hit Chile's central region down to the south which has led to widespread flooding, road closures and damage to homes.

President Jose Antonio Kast declared a state of emergency in the affected areas on Monday.

What is the extent of the damage?

"We have 13 dead and seven missing," Alicia Cebrian, director of Chile's SENAPRED national emergency service, told reporters.

In addition to the casualties, 2,281 people have been displaced, 81 homes have been destroyed with 2,761 more sustaining major damage, while 87,000 people remain without electricity, according to Cebrian.

Swollen rivers have blocked roads, cutting off several houses Image: Alejandro Pizarro/Aton Chile/IMAGO

The power supply was disrupted due to washed out roads, government officials said, adding that they are seeking sanctions ‌on ⁠electricity ⁠distributors for sustained power outages.

School classes were suspended across several municipalities in four regions.

Interior Minister Claudio Alvarado said the rains were expected to ease, but that risks still remain due to "swollen riverbeds and ravines."

"Waterways, streams, ​and riverbanks have been weakened by the rainfall ​over ‌the past few days; there is still a risk of rising water levels in some of ‌them," Cebrian said.

Edited by: Rana Taha

World.title: Hegseth says Iran war has cost $37.5 billion so far
World.content:
07/22/2026 July 22, 2026 Rubio says US open to talks, warns against Iranian control of Hormuz

Rubio has stressed that Iran cannot maintain control over the Strait of Hormuz Image: Eloisa Lopez/REUTERS/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

US Secretary of State Marco Rubiosays Washington remains willing to negotiate with Iran but doubts Tehran is serious about finding a diplomatic solution to the conflict.

"The problem we're having right now is that they're not serious about talks," Rubio said during a meeting of Southeast Asian foreign ministers in Manila, in reference to Iran. "If they're serious, we're serious. If they're not, then we will do what's necessary to protect our interests, and also the interests of our allies."

His remarks came as the US military launched an 11th consecutive night of strikes on Iranand concerns grew over disruptions to global energy supplies.

Rubio warned that Iran must not be allowed to control the Strait of Hormuz, arguing that such a move would have implications far beyond the Middle East.

"If we create a precedent in the Middle East where a nation state can decide that they are going to control an international waterway, charge a toll, and if you don't pay them blow up your ships, we have created a very dangerous precedent, which will repeat itself in other parts of the world, including in this region," Rubio said.

Despite the fighting, Rubio said the US remains "open and willing to engage in positive and constructive negotiations and discussions" if Iran honors its commitments.

World.title: Trump allows direct US flights to Lebanon in historic move
World.content:
It comes over 40 years after the US suspended the direct route with Lebanon. The announcement was made after US President Donald Trump met with Lebanese President Joseph Aoun.

The US will allow direct flights to Lebanon, President Donald Trump announced on Tuesday.

It comes over 40 years after the US suspended direct flights between the two countries in 1985, during US President Ronald Reagan's administration, in the wake of the hijacking of TWA Flight 847.

"I am hereby directing my Administration to allow all US airline carriers to fly directly to Lebanon so that Americans can easily visit this beautiful land," Trump said in a post on his Truth Social platform.

Lebanese Prime Minister Nawaf Salam hailed Trump's announcement. Salam said it "represents a significant opportunity to enhance travel and connectivity between Lebanon and the United States, and to support the Lebanese economy."

What did Trump say about the resumption of direct flights between the US and Lebanon?

The announcement comes after Trump hosted Lebanese President Michel Aoun at the White House on Tuesday.

During that meeting, Trump told Aoun that Lebanon had "been a very badly treated place and country and we’re going to have it properly treated and treated with the respect it deserves."

"We’re gonna help it a lot," he said, without providing specific details.

Lebanon appeals to US, Trump to help secure lasting peace

Washington has been mediating rare talks between Israel and Lebanon, but has become distracted in recent weeks by the resumption of full-scale hostilities between the US and Iran.

Could US-backed Israel-Lebanon deal lead to civil war? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Aoun, who was making the first visit to the US capital by a Lebanese president since 2009, had traveled to Washington, D.C. to appeal for a longer-term, more stable peace in his country, which has been plagued by months of war between Israel and the Iran-backed, Lebanon-based militant group Hezbollah.

Aside from the resumption of direct flights between the US and Lebanon, authorities in Beirut will be hoping that this week's talks in Washington yield an Israeli withdrawal from southern Lebanon, where Israel's ground forces have occupied swathes of territory as part of its campaign against Hezbollah.

Trump claimed Israel's military was "in the process of doing that. They’re in the process of redeploying," he said, without elaborating.

Israel is occupying southern Lebanon in what it says is an effort to protect northern Israeli communities from Hezbollah attacks. Israel, along with the US, Germany and some other countries, recognize Hezbollah as a terror group.

Aoun hails Trump as 'great president'

Aoun, for his part, heaped praise on Trump, whom he called a "great president" whose "vision is peace."

Aoun met with Trump at the end of a 4-day visit to Washington Image: Evelyn Hockstein/REUTERS

"I do agree with that," Trump jokingly replied, calling Aoun handsome and someone who "knows how to get to me."

"Now he can have anything," Trump added.

World.title: Spain: Firefighters battle major wildfire north of Madrid
World.content:
Officials say the blaze, which has forced about 1,200 people to evacuate and has burned at least 30,000 hectares of land, is one of the most complex to affect the country in years.

Hundreds of firefighters and soldiers were battling a massive wildfire northeast of Madrid on Tuesday that has been raging since last week.

Authorities say the blaze, which broke out on Thursday in Guadalajara province about 100 kilometers (60 miles) north of Spain's capital, is one of the most difficult they have faced and is considered the most significant wildfire to affect the country this year.

What do we know about the fire north of Madrid?

"It is the most complex of those that have been tackled in recent years in Spain," Castilla-La Mancha regional president Emiliano Garcia-Page told reporters.

The fire has been raging in an area just 100 kilometers from Madrid Image: Ana Beltran/REUTERS

Garcia-Page added that more than 600 firefighters and nearly 50 aircraft and helicopters had "practically stopped" the blaze from spreading toward the provincial capital of Soria, but that it was not yet under control.

"We can now see light at the end of the tunnel," he said.

The blaze has forced some 1,200 people to evacuate from their homes across the region of Castilla-La Mancha, while at least 30,000 hectares (74,000 acres) of land have been burnt, officials said.

The fire has been so difficult to bring under control because the area is made up of scrubland and has been under prolonged, severe drought conditions. High winds have also complicated the situation.

At least 30,000 hectares have been destroyed Image: Nacho Valverde/Europa Press/IMAGO

Spain's risk of more fires 'remains high'

Spain on Tuesday entered the third heatwave of the summer so far, with temperatures expected to soar above 40 degrees Celsius (104 Fahrenheit) in much of the country, hindering firefighting efforts.

According to Spain's national weather agency AEMET, the heatwave is expected to only last about three days.

Spain is still reeling from one of the deadliest wildfires in modern times that killed 13 people and destroyed 7,000 hectares in southern Almeria province earlier this month.

According to the European Forest Fire Information System (EFFIS), wildfires have destroyed over 115,000 hectares of land in Spain this year.

"We are going through particularly complex weeks, and the risk of fires remains extremely high," government spokeswoman Elma Saiz told a press conference.

Last year, the EFFIS said more than 393,000 hectares were destroyed by wildfires, the most in Spain's history.

Spain has been fighting multiple fires in recent weeks and is already in its third heatwave this year Image: Ricardo Rubio/Europa Press/IMAGO

France also battling major fires

In southwestern France, two firefighters were killed near an airport in Gironde, Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said Tuesday.

On Monday, firefighters tackled a fire at a Roma camp on the outskirts of Nantes in western France.

Around 200 people were evacuated after the blaze, which began after a car caught fire, spread to nearby woodland and to caravans belonging to people living in the settlement.

Human-driven global heating is making heatwaves longer, more intense and more frequent, most scientists say, which creates dry conditions that increase the likelihood of destructive wildfires.

World.title: Ukraine's Zelenskyy fires military chief after days of protests
World.content:
Mass protests in recent days in Kyiv and other Ukrainian cities had called for the removal of commander-in-chief Oleksandr Syrskyi. Volodymyr Zelenskyy has named Mykhailo Drapatyi as the army's new chief.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy announced on Tuesday that he was removing Oleksandr Syrskyi, the army's commander-in-chief, from his post.

"I have decided that the new Commander-in-Chief of the Armed Forces of Ukraine will be Mykhailo Drapatyi... I am grateful to Oleksandr Syrskyi and to each of our warriors for Ukraine's strong front-line positions," Zelenskyy said in a post on Telegram.

"Our shared wish is one — victory over the enemy and conditions at the front and in pressure on Russia that would force Russia toward peace," Zelenskyy said. "A significant path has been traveled, the defense of Ukraine continues, and every warrior deserves dignified treatment."

Why did Zelenskyy sack his commander-in-chief?

The move comes as Zelenskyy has been facing mounting criticism over the dismissal of Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov last week.

Following his sacking, Fedorov, 35, went public with his conflict with Syrskyi. Their dispute was mainly over a disagreement about the direction of Ukraine's war effort against Russia's ongoing invasion.

Fedorov had accused Syrskyi of blocking his attempts at reforming and modernizing the army.

Fedorov's removal triggered massive, nationwide protests that saw several thousand, mostly young people demonstrate in Ukraine's capital, Kyiv and other cities. They demanded that Syrskyi be removed and that Fedorov be reinstated.

Zelenskyy, who had initially sided with Syrskyi, eventually bowed to public pressure on Tuesday, after days of meetings with dozens of Ukraine's top military figures.

Zelenksyy's sacking of Fedorov triggered massive protests across Ukraine Image: Oleksandr Savytskyj/DW

Who is sacked Ukrainian general Oleksandr Syrskyi?

Syrskyi, 60, was born in Russia and was trained in Moscow during the Soviet era.

He had led some of Ukraine's most decisive campaigns, including halting Russia's initial advance towards Kyiv in 2022 and leading Ukraine's incursion into Kursk, Russia in 2024.

"It is a fact that Oleksandr Syrskyi ensured Ukraine's successes in the defense of Kyiv, in the Kharkiv offensive operation, and in the Kursk operation," Ukraine's president said on Tuesday when announcing the change.

But the military veteran had clashed with reformers over a range of issues, including the use of drones and technology.

His dismissal caps a dramatic week in Ukrainian politics, which has seen Zelenskyy botch a leadership reshuffle that has triggered some of the largest protests the country has seen since Russia's full-scale invasion began in 2022.

Critics had called Syrskyi the 'butcher' for not caring about the number of his troops who were killed Image: Valentyn Ogirenko/REUTERS

How has ex-Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov reacted?

Fedorov, a reformist, was associated with Ukraine's drone strikes against targets in Russia, which have helped turn the tide of the war and garnered wide praise in the West.

Fedorov said Syrskyi's replacement as Ukraine's commander-in-chief by Drapatyi brings "fresh hope" to the country.

"This is a breath of fresh air and a new hope in the struggle of free people for freedom and justice," Fedorov said on social media.
