In his view, Georgia’s greatest asset is its integration with the Western system. The country can become a reliable legal, financial and transit platform for Central Asia, but only if it remains connected to European rules and standards.

“What matters to Central Asian markets is Georgia’s geopolitical role, not simply its geographical location. They fully understand that geography alone offers them nothing. By contrast, Georgia’s geopolitical weight allows them to integrate their economic model, culture, legal framework and institutions more smoothly with major Western markets. Asia needs a connection to Europe, just as Europe needs a connection to Asia. If we limit ourselves to serving only as a geographical corridor, we will gain nothing, remain merely a transit route and ultimately be left with little more than environmental or infrastructure-related costs alongside short-term benefits,” Alavidze said.

Economist Elguja Khokrishvili also sees Georgia’s geographical advantage as only a temporary opportunity. In his view, cargo owners will continue to use the Georgian corridor only as long as it remains competitive.

Khokrishvili also notes that the Central Asian countries possess other sources of leverage. Kazakhstan offers partners oil, uranium and a large market. Uzbekistan has gold, copper, uranium and a growing economy. Georgia’s main advantage, by contrast, is its geographical location.

“But geographical advantages quickly lose their value once alternative routes are developed,” Khokrishvili wrote.

Zaza Shengelia, a researcher at EPRC, highlights the financial and institutional support associated with Georgia’s EU candidate status. In his view, partnership with Central Asian countries cannot replace that resource.

“It would be a mistake to suggest that this partnership is an alternative or a substitute for the enormous institutional support that was practically within our grasp thanks to EU candidate status,” Shengelia said.

Taken together, the experts reach a similar conclusion: Central Asia is an important market and transit partner for Georgia. However, the economic value of these relationships depends to a large extent on Georgia’s connection with Europe.

Georgia can serve as Central Asia’s gateway to the West. But to do so, it must itself remain integrated into the West’s economic and legal space.

Otherwise, the country will be left with little more than a favourable geographical location. And a good place on the map is not an economic policy.

Georgia’s Asian pivot

World.title: ‘The whole village knew’: Harrowing story of Nata Vibliani, who survived childhood sexual abuse
World.content:
Nata Vibliani’s story

Forty-three-year-old Nata Vibliani says she was just nine years old when she was repeatedly sexually abused by four men from her village of Sgurishi in the mountainous region of Svaneti.

Nearly 35 years have passed since then. Nata now lives in Germany, far from Georgia. She has cut all ties with her family, relatives and her home village, but says she has never been able to leave the past behind. Three months ago, she posted a video on social media in which she recounted her story, identified the alleged perpetrators by name and accused the entire village of turning a blind eye.

Nata Vibliani’s harrowing account shocked Georgian society.

But the reaction did not stop on social media. About a month ago, police contacted Vibliani and opened an investigation into allegations of rape. The authorities must now establish not only what happened to a child 35 years ago, but also why her family, fellow villagers and law enforcement authorities failed to protect her.

Videos that prompted investigation

The 1990s, Svaneti. At the time, Georgia was being torn apart by several armed conflicts. Chaos and lawlessness prevailed, with armed men controlling the streets. The state existed largely on paper and was unable to protect its citizens.

Nata Vibliani. Photo: Formula

In a mountain village in Svaneṭi, Georgia, the story of a nine-year-old girl was unfolding.

The first video appeals by Nata Vibliani appeared on social media three months ago, but the broader public learned of her story after she appeared as a guest on a popular podcast hosted by journalist Tamuna Museridze.

Speaking from exile in a video recording, Vibliani recounted a childhood she says was destroyed by systematic sexual and physical abuse.

Vibliani publicly named four men, stating they were her relatives and fellow villagers. According to her, one of them—the brother of her godfather—raped her for several years. The other three, the woman says, are relatives of the first alleged abuser.

The videos have sparked mixed reactions. The majority of the public is demanding an investigation and the punishment of those responsible. However, some accuse her of damaging the reputation of Svaneti and the Svan people.

The case is being investigated by the Samegrelo-Zemo Svaneti Police Department under the Ministry of Internal Affairs. Police have already questioned several individuals who may possess vital information.

On 21 July, Nata Vibliani herself was also questioned via video link.

According to publicly available information, no charges have been brought against anyone at this stage. Consequently, the individuals named by Vibliani are legally presumed innocent until proven guilty in a court of law, which is why we are not disclosing their names in this article.

Nata Vibliani’s childhood after her father’s death

Nata Vibliani struggles to recall the exact years the events took place, but she vividly remembers individual episodes of violence.

In Svaneti, she lived with her father, mother, and three siblings. Nata was the eldest of the children.

She was seven years old when her father died under mysterious circumstances, leaving four children with their mother. According to Vibliani, the abuse began shortly thereafter.

“I have a fourth-grade education. I remember the facts well, but I struggle to pinpoint the exact years. This nightmare began a year after my father’s death, just a few days after the anniversary of his passing. My father died in my arms when I was seven years old, leaving four of us children behind.”

According to Nata, a man close to the family—the brother of her godfather—raped her for the first time in a cowshed. The young girl was milking a cow when the man entered.

“He put his hand on my head and told me not to be afraid… I passed out from the pain, and I don’t know how long I lay in that cowshed in that state. When I regained consciousness, the man was no longer there. He had left me and run off.”

Vibliani says that after this incident, the abuse became systematic. While the location changed, the perpetrator’s control over her never wavered.

“He raped me in the bushes, at home, in the field,” Nata Vibliani told Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty.

According to Vibliani, the man also threatened her at gunpoint. He directed the firearm at her younger siblings as well, using terror to keep her silent: if she spoke about the abuse, he would kill her brothers and sister.

“I fought back until he took out a gun and pressed the barrel to my mouth. He raped me like that. He also aimed the gun at my younger brothers and told me that if I made a single sound, he would kill them.”

Vibliani recalls another ordeal. According to her, the abuser tied her to a horse and dragged her to a pasture. The woman says this was done as punishment and a warning never to tell anyone about what had happened.

Pregnancy and unknown fate of her child

One of the most painful aspects of Vibliani’s story involves her pregnancy. She says she became pregnant by her abuser around the age of 14 and went into premature labor.

According to Vibliani, she was taken to give birth in the neighboring Samegrelo region. The child was born alive at a maternity hospital in Zugdidi. She says she saw the newborn’s dark hair and heard his voice, yet to this day she does not know what became of him.

“I know he was born alive—I saw him and I heard his voice. Based on my information, the doctor who delivered the baby is no longer alive. I remember a dialogue where a doctor or nurse asked what should be done with the child, and he [the man Vibliani accuses of sexual abuse] replied, ‘Kill him.’ I don’t know what happened after that.”

Nata Vibliani named fellow villagers who accompanied the abuser to Zugdidi and witnessed this conversation.

Corroborating this account will be one of the investigation’s most challenging tasks. It will require locating medical records, potential witnesses, and archival investigative files. It remains unknown whether these documents have survived after three decades.

“I Want to rid Svaneti of paedophiles”

Vibliani states that her pregnancy was no secret and that everyone was aware of it. For this reason, she directs her most painful questions not only at her alleged abusers, but at her fellow villagers as well:

“The whole village knew I was pregnant. Why didn’t they stand up for me when they heard what was happening in my grandfather’s house? Where were those Svan men who are now accusing me everywhere of wanting to tarnish Svaneti’s name? I want to rid Svaneti of paedophiles. They have no right to build a house on my land, mock my father’s memory, throw stones at me like a criminal, or drive me out of Svaneti in disgrace. They killed my child.”

According to Vibliani, the man who fathered the child spread rumors throughout the village claiming the baby was not his. She says he threatened a local boy and forced him to confess to having had sexual relations with Nata and claiming paternity of the child.

However, Vibliani believes everyone in the village knew the truth full well, but remained silent out of fear, as the man and his brothers were local criminal figures.

When entire village blames the victim

According to Vibliani, family members, relatives, and fellow villagers were aware of the abuse. Yet instead of support, she faced humiliation.

She recalls attending a fellow villager’s christening while pregnant. She was driven out of the event, called a “whore,” and children threw stones at her in the yard.

For Vibliani, this episode clearly demonstrates how the entire village shifted the blame for the abuse from the perpetrator to the child.

Vibliani also stresses that she was abused by multiple men. She alleges that subsequent assaults were carried out with the involvement of the first abuser in an effort to intimidate her and ultimately silence her forever.

“All three are relatives of this man. They raped me with his involvement to cover up his atrocity, so that I could never speak out as a woman, so that I could never say I had been raped by so many men.”

According to Vibliani, one of the three additional abusers was the primary perpetrator’s brother—a criminal figure who had just been released from prison.

First investigation closed in a week

Vibliani says that in the mid-1990s, her grandfather filed a police report regarding the sexual abuse. A case was opened by the regional police department in Zugdidi, and the child underwent a forensic medical examination.

“They even sent me the results of the examination. But this man [the abuser] had connections in the police and was able to cover up a lot. About a week later, my family withdrew the complaint, and that’s how the case ended.”

This detail could prove crucial for the ongoing investigation. If the original case files have survived, they may contain expert medical findings, witness statements, and other official records.

The Ministry of Internal Affairs has not yet publicly confirmed whether the 1990s case file has been located, nor has it commented on why the investigation was halted at the time.

Sale of family home and departure from Svaneti

According to Vibliani, as a result of the abuse and public condemnation, her family lost their ancestral home. In the late 1990s, under pressure from the community, they left the village.

In exchange for their house and land, the family was paid 22,000 GEL, a sum Vibliani considers symbolic. The children then moved with their mother to Zugdidi, where they were forced to live in hardship.

“I was still a minor at the time, and I even attempted suicide, but I survived. As soon as I recovered and regained my strength, I left home for Kutaisi. After that, I never spoke to my family members again—not to my brothers and sisters, not to my mother, not to anyone. When I needed help, nobody supported me, not even my mother.

It is true that I later re-established contact with my relatives, but they treated me like a criminal, so I no longer wanted to communicate with anyone,” Vibliani recalls.

In the interview, Nata Vibliani speaks of her mother with bitterness. In the victim’s view, her mother failed to protect her properly. At the same time, Vibliani notes that following her father’s death, her mother herself became a victim of sexual violence at the hands of fellow villagers.

Father factor

Nata remembers her father with tears in her eyes, saying that her life turned into a living hell after he died.

Vibliani says she began her fight for justice largely to honor her father’s memory.

Her father died in seven-year-old Nata’s arms from a gunshot wound to the heart; the origin of the shooting remains unknown, as no autopsy was ever performed.

Vibliani does not rule out suicide, as her father was in conflict with the community. The dispute stemmed from the fact that her father was adopted, rather than a biological descendant of the Vibliani lineage.

Her grandfather’s family did not want the extensive Vibliani lands to pass to an adopted son, and they persecuted the young girl’s father as a result. After his death, his wife and children were subjected to abuse, and the family was ultimately driven from the village.

What does Nata Vibliani demand?

Vibliani maintains that she began speaking out publicly about the abuse not out of revenge, but to seek justice.

She is represented by lawyer Mariam Barsonidze. On 15 July, Vibliani officially petitioned the Ministry of Internal Affairs for the assignment of legal counsel to the case.

The defence team’s primary demand was a timely and thorough interview of Vibliani. Her lawyer is now requesting that she be granted official victim status, which would allow Vibliani and her counsel full access to the case files.

“The horrific facts recounted by Nata Vibliani must be detailed comprehensively. Following this, she must be granted victim status, and as the victim and her legal counsel, we will have the full right to examine the investigative materials.”

According to the lawyer, this is not an isolated case. Its outcome is equally vital for other women who remain silent about the abuse they suffered during childhood.

Today, Nata lives in Germany and is a mother to an adult son and a grandmother. She has partially reconciled with her relatives; however, according to Vibliani, her family continues to treat her as though she herself were to blame for what happened.

Is justice possible 35 years later?

In interviews, Nata says that over these 35 years, not a single day has passed without her thinking about what happened to her.

Time poses the primary challenge for the investigation. Potential crime scenes have altered, some witnesses may have died, and memories face rigorous scrutiny in court.

At the same time, the statute of limitations does not automatically preclude prosecution.

In 2020, the law was amended so that the statute of limitations no longer applies to certain sexual offences committed against minors. However, in Vibliani’s case, investigators must first determine the exact timeframe of the last alleged act of abuse.

The legal classification of the offences must also be clarified in light of current legislation and recent amendments. The final assessment will depend on specific dates and circumstances.

Mari Varamashvili, a lawyer with the human rights organization Sapari, explains that the 2020 amendment will apply to the case provided the 30-year statute of limitations had not expired by that time.

“If it turns out that the 30-year statute of limitations had not lapsed by 2020, it means that no statute of limitations will apply to Nata Vibliani’s case.”

Under current law, rape is defined under Article 137 of the Criminal Code as sexual intercourse involving physical force, threats of violence, or taking advantage of a victim’s helpless state.

However, when evaluating actions allegedly committed in the 1990s, investigators will also need to examine the legislation in force at that time.

According to Varamashvili, investigators must also interview all potential witnesses and locate historical case records. Psychological evaluations could also prove highly significant.

Georgian courts have previously heard cases involving historical sexual abuse. In 2022, a court found a man guilty of raping a minor 25 years prior.

In 2024, another man was sentenced to 20 years in prison for raping his sister’s underage children.

While these precedents offer no guarantee of a favorable outcome in Vibliani’s case, they demonstrate that while passage of time complicates evidence gathering, it does not render an investigation impossible.

Danger even in exile

Vibliani fears persecution despite residing in Germany.

On 14 July, she told Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty that she had not left her house for four days.

“I have exposed five families in Svaneti. Five families hate me and are coming after me, and I don’t know which of them might decide to take revenge. Even though I am not in Georgia, I do not feel safe.”

For this reason, the investigation must extend beyond uncovering historical evidence; authorities must also assess the risk of potential intimidation and retaliation.

The Women’s Movement has called on law enforcement agencies to conduct an independent and effective investigation. The organization demands a trauma-informed approach, measures to guarantee Vibliani’s safety, and that she be kept fully informed of developments.

Vibliani’s public account highlights a critical issue: the true scale of child sexual abuse in Georgia remains unknown, as the country still lacks a comprehensive system for prevention, detection, and victim support.

World.title: Transparency International Georgia: ‘Georgia now has 90 political prisoners under PACE criteria’
World.content:
List of political prisoners in Georgia

According to Transparency International Georgia, there are currently 90 political prisoners in Georgia. The organisation has published a list of their names.

The list was compiled using the criteria set out in Resolution 1900 (2012) of the Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe.

How were the cases assessed?

Transparency International Georgia said each case was assessed individually, based on the circumstances of the case, court decisions and international human rights standards.

The organisation said the list is based on legal criteria established by the Council of Europe rather than politically motivated assessments.

Under those criteria, a person may be considered a political prisoner if their detention is linked to:

violations of fundamental rights;

detention for political reasons where the alleged act does not constitute a criminal offence;

a punishment that is clearly disproportionate;

discriminatory treatment; or

judicial proceedings that fail to meet the requirements of a fair trial.

The list specifies which of these criteria are considered to apply in each individual case.

“The large number of political prisoners once again demonstrates the existence of politically motivated justice in Georgia and the deterioration of the human rights situation,” Transparency International Georgia said in a statement.

Who is on the list?

The list published by Transparency International includes several high-profile figures, among them journalist Mzia Amaghlobeli, the founder of the media outlets Batumelebi and Netgazeti.

Amaghlobeli was arrested overnight on 11-12 January 2025 in Batumi after being accused of slapping the city’s police chief. The incident followed what her supporters say was an insult by the police officer. She was sentenced to two years in prison.

Another person on the list is opposition politician Elene Khoshtaria, the leader of the Droa party. She was sentenced to 18 months in prison for painting graffiti on an election poster of Tbilisi Mayor Kakha Kaladze.

Opposition politician Levan Khabeishvili, one of the leaders of the United National Movement, was also sentenced to prison. He received a sentence of two years and six months on charges of “promising a bribe to a public official” and “calling for the overthrow of the government”.

Opposition politician Nika Melia, one of the leaders of the Ahali party, is facing several criminal cases. Among them is the so-called government sabotage case, which is still pending and carries the possibility of a lengthy prison sentence.

Singer and activist Paata Burchuladze was arrested over the alleged “failed coup” of 4 October and sentenced to seven years in prison. He was convicted of attempting to seize a strategic facility, organising and leading group violence, and publicly calling for the overthrow of the government.

Poet Zviad Ratiani was sentenced to two years in prison for insulting a police officer.

The full list of political prisoners is available at the link below.

List of political prisoners in Georgia

World.title: Armenia sets new tourism record as visitor numbers hit all-time high
World.content:
Tourist arrivals in Armenia reach record high

Armenia‘s tourism sector has reported a new record. The country welcomed 1.042 million tourists in the first half of 2026. According to Sona Hovhannisyan, head of the International Cooperation Department, the number of tourists who visited Armenia between January and June was 14.8% higher than during the same period last year.

Although this is the highest figure on record, the Tourism Committee expects to break the record again by the end of the year. Officials expect the number of tourists to surpass last year’s total of 2.2 million visitors.

Main sources of tourist arrivals

According to the Tourism Committee, visitors from Russia, Georgia and Iran have made up the largest share of tourists travelling to Armenia for many years. As of June this year, that pattern had not changed. The figures are as follows:

Around 40% of all visitors came from Russia,

15% from Georgia,

8% from Iran.

Compared with the three leading source markets, visitor numbers from other countries remain relatively low. According to Sona Hovhannisyan, head of the International Cooperation Department, several factors explain why tourists from these countries account for the largest share of arrivals:

“Iran and Georgia are Armenia’s closest neighbours, while Armenia has historical ties with Russia. It is also important that people can travel to Armenia from these countries relatively quickly. The presence of Armenian diaspora communities in these countries also plays a role.”

Hovhannisyan said countries with direct flights to Armenia, as well as those whose citizens benefit from simplified visa rules, have seen growing numbers of visitors. She cited China as an example, saying the sharp increase in Chinese tourists followed the launch of direct flights between Urumqi and Yerevan, along with the introduction of a visa-free regime.

Hovhannisyan also explained what has driven growth from other countries:

“The significant increase in the number of tourists from Italy is due to the expansion of flights between our countries. The same factor has influenced arrivals from Germany, where visitor numbers had previously declined. The launch of a direct flight from Kazakhstan has also boosted tourist flows.”

Armenia has also recently become a more popular destination for tourists from Spain, the Czech Republic, the Netherlands and the United Kingdom.

Hovhannisyan said visitor numbers from those countries remain well below the figures for Russia. However, she added that the recent launch of direct flights between London and Yerevan gives reason for optimism.

“The peak tourism season is gradually getting longer”

Armenia usually sees the highest number of tourist arrivals during the summer and in September and October. Activity typically begins to slow towards the end of November. According to Hovhannisyan, however, the peak season is gradually becoming longer. She said more tourists are now choosing to visit the country during the winter months.

“It is encouraging to see growing activity during the winter as well. The government is taking steps to support this trend. If this January’s record figures are sustained and become the norm, we can expect strong tourism for almost the entire year.”

Trade fairs and other PR efforts to attract tourists

The Tourism Committee is running a number of programmes to make Armenia a more attractive destination on the international tourism market.

According to Diana Karapetyan, head of the Marketing Department, Armenia showcased national pavilions at major tourism fairs in Spain, Germany, Romania and Russia this year.

“By the end of the year, we plan to take part in several more international events. Armenian tourism companies attending these exhibitions present highly attractive offers. They promote our country’s cultural events, cuisine and tourist attractions. They also offer tastings, distribute brochures and show promotional videos.”

The committee also works with international media outlets, PR agencies, well-known bloggers and influencers. It organises familiarisation trips to Armenia and runs promotional campaigns. Karapetyan said these efforts have led to more frequent coverage of Armenia in the international media, with growing attention to its tourism appeal and potential.

“Armenia has established itself on the global tourism market as a safe and reliable destination,” she said.

Tourist arrivals in Armenia reach record high

World.title: Aleksandre Kartozia to receive accreditation as Georgia’s ambassador to Germany
World.content:
Accreditation of Georgia’s ambassador to Germany

Aleksandre Kartozia, who was appointed Georgia‘s ambassador to Germany in September last year, is set to present his credentials to German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier on 23 July.

The information was published on the official website of the German president.

The website lists the ambassadorial accreditation ceremonies scheduled for 23 July. Seven ambassadors are due to present their credentials, with Kartozia first on the programme. According to the schedule, his accreditation ceremony is set to begin at 10:30.

Ambassadors from Chile, Honduras, Nigeria, Mauritania, Madagascar and the Vatican’s Apostolic Nuncio are also scheduled to be accredited on the same day.

Why is the accreditation important?

Aleksandre Kartozia was appointed Georgia’s ambassador to Germany in September last year, succeeding Levan Izoria, who had served in the post since 2020.

Before an ambassador can officially take up their duties in Germany, they must present their credentials to the country’s president. Only after this ceremony are they formally accredited and able to carry out the full responsibilities of the role. Until now, Kartozia had been awaiting an invitation to present his credentials.

Letters of credence are official documents by which one head of state appoints a diplomat as their representative to another country.

The documents identify the appointed diplomat and their diplomatic rank. They also contain a formal request from the sending head of state to the receiving head of state to “give credence” to everything the diplomat says or does on behalf of their country.

The accreditation also carries added political significance given the strained relationship between Georgia and Germany.

Relations between Tbilisi and Berlin have been tense over the past two years. Senior Georgian officials have repeatedly criticised Germany’s ambassador to Georgia, Peter Fischer, while Germany has voiced concern over developments in Georgia.

There have also been several occasions when the German ambassador was summoned by the Georgian authorities.

On 31 December 2024, Germany imposed entry bans on nine people it said were responsible for violence against protesters and opposition figures in Georgia.

Who is Aleksandre Kartozia?

Aleksandre Kartozia served as Georgia’s education minister from 1998 to 2004 under President Eduard Shevardnadze.

He has worked as a researcher and taught courses and seminars at leading universities in Berlin, Frankfurt and Bremen. In 2022, he was awarded the Order of Merit of the Federal Republic of Germany.

During his tenure as education minister, Kartozia faced corruption allegations. In 2002, Givi Targamadze, a member of Georgia’s Anti-Corruption Council, publicly accused him of corruption. In 2004, prosecutors charged Kartozia and his deputy, Vladimir Sanadze, with abuse of office and the embezzlement of public funds.

Accreditation of Georgia’s ambassador to Germany

World.title: President Aliyev’s visit to Germany: Pragmatism, energy and changing South Caucasus
World.content:
President Aliyev’s visit to Germany

President Ilham Aliyev of Azerbaijan arrived in Berlin on Sunday evening for an official visit. An official welcoming ceremony was held at Berlin Brandenburg Airport, where the Azerbaijani leader also met Michael Harms, chairman of the German Eastern Business Association.

As the visit has only just begun, few details have emerged about its outcomes. However, information released so far, together with the broader context, suggests the trip could mark a new phase in relations between Baku and Berlin, driven by pragmatism, closer economic cooperation and a shared interest in regional stability.

What is known so far?

According to official information, Aliyev’s meeting with Michael Harms highlighted growing interest among Azerbaijani and German businesses in expanding cooperation. The two sides also discussed ways to institutionalise that cooperation. They exchanged views on opportunities in both conventional and renewable energy, as well as on developing transport, logistics and communications links, including the Middle Corridor.

Officials also noted that Azerbaijan has adopted a new state programme for agriculture. The two sides discussed the potential for introducing German technologies, particularly in the field of smart farming. Tourism development and other issues of mutual interest were also on the agenda.

The groundwork for the visit had been laid well before Aliyev arrived in Berlin. On 4 December 2025, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz called President Aliyev to congratulate him on progress in the peace process between Azerbaijan and Armenia. He reaffirmed Germany’s support for regional stability and invited the Azerbaijani leader to visit Germany. Aliyev accepted the invitation and, in turn, invited the chancellor to visit Azerbaijan.

On 15 June 2026, Germany’s ambassador to Azerbaijan, Ralf Horlemann, said during a farewell meeting that the visit was expected to take place later in the year.

Bilateral trade reached around €1.7 billion in 2025, while more than 250 German companies operate in Azerbaijan. Since the beginning of 2026, Azerbaijan has also started direct gas exports to Germany and Austria. These figures, together with recent economic initiatives, underline the visit’s strong commercial focus.

The broader trajectory of bilateral relations is also noteworthy. In April 2025, German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier paid an official visit to Azerbaijan—the first official visit by a German head of state to the country. Aliyev, for his part, has travelled to Germany on several occasions to attend the Munich Security Conference and other international events.

Why is this visit taking place?

The visit reinforces the pragmatic nature of relations between Azerbaijan and Germany, which are increasingly centred on expanding economic cooperation. As Europe continues to diversify its energy supplies and reduce its dependence on Russian gas, Azerbaijan has strengthened its position as a reliable and predictable energy supplier.

The start of direct gas exports to Germany and Austria in 2026 marked a significant step in that process. But the visit’s agenda extends beyond energy. Discussions are expected to focus on a broader “energy-plus” framework, encompassing cooperation in logistics, the Middle Corridor, industry, agricultural technology and tourism. German businesses, supported by the German Eastern Business Association, have shown growing interest in these sectors.

Germany also attaches considerable importance to stability in the South Caucasus, particularly the peace process between Azerbaijan and Armenia. This was reflected in Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s phone call with President Aliyev in December 2025, during which he highlighted the importance of the peace agenda. From Berlin’s perspective, Azerbaijan’s multi-vector foreign policy has therefore taken on additional significance, with Baku seen both as an energy supplier and as a participant in efforts to strengthen regional stability.

The Berlin visit also comes against the backdrop of growing tensions between Azerbaijan and the Council of Europe, following President Aliyev’s remarks at the Shusha Global Media Forum that the country could fully withdraw from the organisation. In that sense, the trip highlights the tension between Europe’s values-based agenda and its pragmatic interests. At the same time, current developments suggest that relations between Germany and Azerbaijan continue to be shaped primarily by economic interests and a shared commitment to regional stability.

Europe’s approach to Azerbaijan remains far from uniform. While some European institutions have taken a critical stance towards Baku, bilateral relations with individual partners continue to be driven largely by pragmatic considerations. This reflects Azerbaijan’s continued pursuit of a selective and multi-vector foreign policy.

What outcomes can be expected?

As the visit has only just begun, few official details have been released. Even so, the main areas of cooperation are already becoming clear. One of the central themes of Aliyev’s meeting with Michael Harms was the institutionalisation of business ties, including the creation of new mechanisms for cooperation, business councils and joint working groups.

Among the most likely outcomes are progress in talks on increasing energy exports, broader involvement of German companies in Middle Corridor projects, greater technology transfer and investment in agriculture, as well as new joint initiatives in tourism.

Meetings with Chancellor Friedrich Merz, other senior government officials and representatives of the German business community are also expected to take place during the visit. The agenda may include the signing of cooperation agreements and the adoption of roadmaps for future collaboration.

The longer-term outlook extends well beyond the immediate visit. Both sides are seeking to diversify Azerbaijan’s ties with Europe, expand investment, strengthen the Middle Corridor’s role in Eurasian logistics and increase bilateral trade, which currently stands at €1.7 billion. At the same time, risks remain. Future cooperation could be affected by fluctuations in energy prices, differing approaches among European governments towards Azerbaijan and the overall stability of the South Caucasus.

The visit therefore reflects the pragmatic and multi-vector nature of Azerbaijan’s foreign policy. Baku is seeking to move beyond its role as an energy supplier and position itself as a broader economic and logistics partner. Berlin, for its part, has an interest in strengthening cooperation with a reliable partner while supporting stability in the South Caucasus. The full results of the visit will become clearer in the coming days, but it is already evident that relations are evolving towards an “energy-plus” partnership from which both sides expect tangible economic benefits.

President Aliyev’s visit to Germany

World.title: Doctor reveals injuries of woman allegedly sexually assaulted by Yung Filly
World.content:
WARNING: This story contains details some readers may find distressing, including descriptions of alleged sexual assault.

Graphic photographs of injuries allegedly inflicted by an internationally renowned YouTube star on an infatuated fan in his hotel room after a concert have been shown to a jury at his sexual assault trial in a Perth court.

Andres Felipe Valencia Barrientos, known to his millions of fans as Yung Filly, is on trial in the Perth District Court, accused of the brutal rape and assault of a 20-year-old woman at the Intercontinental Hotel in Perth's CBD in September 2024.

The 30-year-old rapper had been in Perth performing at Bar1, a waterfront venue in Perth's northern suburbs, and after the show had taken the young woman back to his hotel.

The pair had consensual sex in his room at the Intercontinental, before he allegedly violently raped her and repeatedly assaulted her, including biting and slapping her on the face, neck and breasts, strangling her, spitting in her mouth and forcing her to perform oral sex.

Andres Felipe Valencia Barrientos's social media profiles have garnered millions of followers. (ABC News: David Weber)

Mr Barrientos denies all the charges against him, which include sexual penetration without consent, impeding a person's breathing and assault.

Today the court heard evidence from sexual assault specialist Geraldine Hoy, who examined the young woman at the Sexual Assault Resource Centre two days after her alleged ordeal.

Multiple bruises

Dr Hoy took a series of close-up photographs of the 20-year-old's face, neck and breasts that were shown to the jury, depicting multiple large bruises and swellings.

The 21 photos included what Dr Hoy described as a "green purply" bruise on her neck, a linear bruise on her neck and a "large … yellow bruise just above the right areola area of the breast".

Court hears Yung Filly choked, sexually assaulted young fan A Perth court hears disturbing details of the YouTube personality's alleged sexual assault of a young woman who had a "celebrity crush" on him.

Nearby on the same breast was another bruise measuring 4 centimetres x 8 centimetres, as well as a bruise that Dr Hoy described as yellow in colour.

Describing the photos in detail as they were displayed in court, Dr Hoy said the bruises on her face included two linear red swollen bruises on her right cheek, and bruising on the left side of her face that extended to her neck.

Earlier the trial heard the 20-year-old woman had a "celebrity crush" on Mr Barrientos and had spoken of him as "her future husband".

She had worn her "lucky" white top to the gig in the hope of gaining access to the VIP area of the venue to get close to him, the court heard, which she was ultimately able to do late in the evening, before leaving with the rapper and his entourage in a van, back to his hotel.

World.title: Jail for acccountant who gambled away $878,000 stolen from IGA
World.content:
An accountant for a network of IGA supermarkets in New South Wales has been jailed for defrauding $878,000.

Narelle Labuts, 61, worked with the Singh Group, which owns 10 IGA stores in the Hunter Valley.

She was sacked in 2021 after a bank flagged an unusual transaction.

Labuts stole the company's money by using white font on 522 transactions to hide her misconduct over a four-year period, the Newcastle District Court heard.

In October 2024, police charged her with obtaining financial advantage by deception and making a false document to obtain a financial advantage.

Labuts pleaded guilty at the end of last year.

Today she was sentenced to three and a half years in prison with a two-year non-parole period.

Judge Tim Gartelmann SC said what began as an opportunistic crime spiralled into something "that required significant planning and organising".

"The sentences for fraud offences must deter others to commit them," he said.

" They are easy to commit and hard to detect. "

Narelle Labuts was sacked after an irregular transaction was flagged. (Facebook)

The court heard Labuts had only returned a fraction of the stolen money, repaying $3,500 while the IGA network clawed back a further $9,000 by refusing to pay her entitlements.

At the sentencing hearing Labuts said she was addicted to gambling and that 90 per cent of the embezzled funds had gone into poker machines.

Labuts said she knew that what she was doing was wrong thing but was "praying for a big win to return it all back".

"The house always wins, so it never eventuated," she said tearfully.

Labuts said she was "so incredibly sorry" and acknowledged she had "destroyed the trust [her employer] put in me".

Narelle Labuts said she gambled most of the money. (ABC Newcastle: Alex Turner-Cohen)

The court heard she has since worked as a bookkeeper at a transport and a concreting company, but did not disclose why her employment at the IGA network came to an abrupt end.

She said she would "probably" tell future employers about the conviction because it was now common knowledge.

Defence barrister Stephen Hopper emphasised that Labuts was addressing her gambling addiction and had been getting counselling since June 2022.

Labuts disagreed with a suggestion from the Crown that she only sought help for her gambling problem because she had been caught.

She will be eligible for parole in July 2028.

World.title: The Aussie tech guru pardoned by Trump after Secret Service arrest
World.content:
Chris Wade has been unsuccessfully sued by Apple, arrested by the Secret Service and summoned to the White House to troubleshoot with Elon Musk and Donald Trump.

He is probably the most successful Australian entrepreneur you've never heard of, and is certainly the only Australian tech executive to be pardoned by the current US president.

Despite decades spent in the US that took him from convicted hacker to the White House he is back in his hometown of Murwillumbah on the NSW north coast.

Last year, the cyber security startup Mr Wade co-founded, Corellium, was bought by tech firm Cellebrite for $285 million.

Soon after the sale of his business, one company executive called him to ask him which supercar he bought.

He responded: "I didn't buy a supercar, I bought a pub". Wade paid $17.8 million for Murwillumbah's Riverview Hotel in December last year.

Chris bought Murwillumbah's Riverview Hotel for $17.8 million. (ABC News: Chris Gillette)

His American colleague was stunned.

"He said, 'Only an Australian would buy a pub instead of a Ferrari or a Lamborghini or something'," Wade said.

"But I tell you what, I get way more value out of the pub, and it gives back a lot more. I get to meet a lot of new people and I get to share in experiences."

Wade's current project is teaching a three-tonne welding robot to shake a cocktail, that passion for tech started when he was a child, when his father Peter says Chris was always tinkering with electronics.

As well as working at the pub, Chris Wade has a keen interest in robotics. (ABC News: Chris Gillette)

"We used to go to the local dump and he'd bring home all the electronic stuff he could find," Peter Wade said.

"This is when he was four or five and he'd pull it all apart and make things work and play around with stuff. And he was into high voltage before he was even 10. That's what worried me — but yeah, he managed to survive."

As a child, Chris would work on his own DIY projects. (Supplied)

Having learned to code on a Commodore 64, by the time Wade was a teenager he was assembling computers, selling them to friends and teachers.

Spams, scams and the Secret Service

At age 21, in the he early 2000s, Wade moved to the United States, where he got himself into trouble while awaiting his working visa.

"A guy that I knew approached me and said, 'Could you write a piece of software that allows me to proxy through other computers?' I said, 'Yeah, easy. No problems. A couple of thousand dollars, I'll do it.' And he took the software and plugged it into a spamming engine."

Chris Wade moved to the States at the age of 21. (Supplied)

The spams promoted financial scams, and because the emails crossed state borders, they were investigated by a federal authority — the US Secret Service.

In 2005, armed agents raided Wade's home in Dallas, Texas. Wade was arrested at gunpoint, handcuffed, and charged with federal crimes.

Foreign citizens convicted of crimes in the US are usually deported once they have served their sentence.

But the authorities realised that Wade was no hardened criminal, and had some very useful skills.

He was given a choice.

"I could help them with cases that they struggled with, where they didn't have the technical know-how to solve the cases, and in exchange, my time would be cut down," Wade said.

He was fined approximately US$70,000 ($99,800) and sentenced to two years' probation.

Cracking passwords for the FBI

In that time he began working with Chris Tarbell, an FBI Special Agent who specialised in cyber crimes.

"When I first met Chris, man, I under-utilised him," Tarbell told 7.30.

"I didn't realise how smart he was.

"If some technical question came up in some sort of strange investigation, he would be my go-to. I'd ask him, and everything I'd ask him to do seemed kind of stupid to him."

Chris's technical skills became an asset to US authorities.

Wade worked with authorities for more than 10 years and helped on some of Tarbell's biggest cases, including investigations into the Silk Road drugs marketplace and the Anonymous hacking group.

"I would do my piece of it," Wade said.

" Which was to solve a puzzle or understand the data that they couldn't figure out ... or crack some passwords or things like that. "

In return, Wade got to stay in the US.

Chris Wade went on to build his career in the US and eventually created a cybersecurity company. (ABC News: Chris Gillette)

He developed software which allowed app developers to emulate Androids and iPhones inside a computer.

His startup, Corellium, was feted by software engineers but targeted by Apple, which sued Corellium for infringing its copyright in 2019.

Despite his business success and work with the FBI, Wade's felony convictions remained a problem when his probation finished. He would be questioned, extensively, every time he entered or left the United States.

"It certainly made it uncomfortable to travel internationally," Wade said.

"It always weighed on me knowing that at some point the immigration and customs could show up at my door and escort me to the border and put me on a plane and I'd never be allowed to come back to the US, which is where my business was."

A sick fish and a Marvel-lous pardon

One way around the problem would be executive clemency — a presidential pardon.

"You need a sponsor, someone to advocate for you. And that could be a senator, someone famous, one of the Kardashians. And I didn't have anyone," Wade told 7.30.

That was until Gemmy, Wade's tropical Gem Tang, fell ill.

Wade collected coral and saltwater fish.

Chris Wade's aquarium at home. (Supplied)

"I got really into it," he said.

"I think at one point I had nine or 10 fish tanks in the house and eventually I reduced that to one big one."

A specialist went to his Florida home to treat Gemmy.

Gemmy is a tropical Gem Tang, a highly prized specimen known for its rarity. (Supplied)

"The fish doctor came over and saw all the fish tanks I had and said, 'There's only one other person in the world that I know that's as crazy about fish as you are,' and he introduced us, and that was 'Ike'," Wade said.

'Ike' turned out to be Isaac Perlmutter, the publicity-shy chairman of Marvel Entertainment.

The pair met outside Miami Seaquarium. At the time, neither man had any idea what the other did for a living.

"We hit it off," Wade said.

Chris Wade and Isaac 'Ike' Perlmutter developed a close bond. (Supplied)

After their first lunch, Perlmutter came back into the restaurant and said his car was showing a flat tyre alert.

"It was pouring rain outside … I remember going out and getting a tyre pump out of the back of my car and standing in the rain pumping his tyre up. And I think from that point on, he would always be there if I needed it," Wade said.

The pair became friends and Perlmutter, a member of Trump's Mar-a-Lago club advised Wade to seek a presidential pardon.

Ike Perlmutter was a member of the Mar-a-Lago club and had connections to Donald Trump. (Supplied)

"Ike definitely put in a word for me," Wade said.

"And I think they looked at my file. Others like Chris Tarbell … they wrote letters for me. And I think that made an impact."

Tarbell confirmed his contribution.

"I more than happily wrote a letter to President Trump telling him how great Chris had been," the former FBI agent told 7.30.

Chris Tarbell's letter to the president described Chris Wade's "positive conduct and stellar reputation." (Supplied)

'World's greatest hacker' and Elon Musk

Perlmutter soon invited Wade to Mar-a-Lago.

Eventually, Wade met Jared Kushner, Ivanka Trump and even Donald Trump himself. Trump, in turn, introduced Wade to Elon Musk as "the world's greatest hacker".

Chris would go on to meet Jared Kushner, Ivanka Trump and Donald Trump at Mar-a-Lago. (Reuters: Kevin Lamarque)

Musk called Wade after the meeting, beginning a relationship that is still in place today.

Wade says he has been called to the White House for late-night meetings with Musk.

"It's just like anything, he runs into issues and he has a lot of smart people … and sometimes they bring me in on things to help," Wade said.

Chris was introduced to Elon Musk through the president. (Reuters: Chip Somodevilla)

In December 2020, Kushner called Wade with some good news.

The Australian had been granted a presidential pardon.

"I'd met maybe once in passing to shake their hand or something, both Ivanka and Jared, but I'd never spent any time with them," Wade said.

"It always struck me how amazing it was that Jared took an interest because I have no value to him, but they treated me unbelievably and I really appreciate that they did that for me because it changed my life."

In December 2020, the same week he received the pardon, there were two more pieces of good news.

Forbes magazine said Wade's company Corellium had created the cybersecurity product of the year; then a US court dismissed Apple's lawsuit against the company.

The president's man

Since then, Wade has become a US citizen, and continues to help both Musk and Trump.

"[Donald Trump] has called me before, but normally there's a PA, or someone will call me, or Ike will call me and say, 'I just talked to the president. He needs your help with this'," he said.

He says the White House is on his list of allowed callers, "so that they wake me up even if I have do not disturb on," he told 7.30.

Chris Wade has become a US citizen and continues to help Donald Trump when called. (Supplied)

" I always told the president that he literally saved my life and if there was anything I could ever do to help ... I would show up and help him out. "

As part of the sale of his business, Wade was required to stay on to work for the parent company Cellebrite, something he wanted to do.

"I believe in the company ... and I wanted to make sure they didn't screw up my technology," Wade said.

Cellebrite is one of the world's biggest "mobile forensics" companies, with over 1,000 employees.

Its products are used by law enforcement in both the US and Australia to unlock and extract information from suspects' devices, once court approval has been granted.

"Cell phones have become like the storage locker of our lives," Wade said.

"So ... if you have criminal investigations and you can't get into the phones, it hinders them immensely."

The technology is used to unlock phones on major investigations, like the attempted assassination of Trump.

"The FBI and Secret Service will bring the phone in and they will plug it into a Cellebrite machine, which will extract all the data from the phone and it unlocks the phone as well if there's a password on it so that they can do the criminal investigation," Wade explained.

As Cellebrite's chief technology officer, Wade is focused on the tech staying ahead of criminals.

Now free to travel to and from the US, Chris Wade has returned to the Northern Rivers. (ABC News: Chris Gillette)

"I'm heavily focused on what's next. How do we stay ahead of the criminals? How do we get better at solving cases?" Wade said.

"So my focus is on the next three to five years of where a criminal's going, what technologies they're using, how do we keep up with them, and how do we take all that information and give it to AI in such a way that cold cases can be solved or even new cases are solved faster."

And while International time zones make his working day quite tricky he is still making time for the pub and his hobbies.

"I work from 10 o'clock at night until five o'clock in the morning. And then, not every day, but some days, I'll be at the pub from about 9am til about 3pm.

" I do sleep in there a little bit, which leaves some time for robots and trains. "

Watch 7.30, Mondays to Thursdays 7:30pm on ABC iview and ABC TV

World.title: Eels defend Luai's 2027 signing ahead of Chiefs move
World.content:
Parramatta coach Jason Ryles says he is unapologetic about agreeing to Jarome Luai's one-season stopover at the Eels.

A four-time premiership winner with the Panthers, Luai was released by Wests Tigers, which want to give their younger halves opportunities in first grade.

Ryles said he had no concerns Luai's arrival would discourage Parramatta's halves prospects.

Luai joins Parramatta, Marshall slams relationship breakdown rumours Benji Marshall has slammed "bull**** rumours" claiming a fractured relationship with Jarome Luai contributed to the star five-eighth's early exit from Wests Tigers.

He said signing Luai was a win for the 15th-placed Eels' stable of younger halves options, which includes Joash Papalii, Lincoln Fletcher and Lorenzo Talataina.

"We're sitting in a spot on the ladder that we don't want to be," Ryles said.

"It's no-one's fault directly but we need more experienced players. Jarome fits that bill at the moment.

"We have got younger players that are coming through our pathways and our system that may be ready in 12 months.

"But this gives them an extra bit of time to … learn off a true pro that's won a lot of premierships."

Amid a season of injury concerns for the Eels, centre Will Penisini could return from osteitis pubis via reserve grade this weekend.

Ryles said he was hopeful veteran prop Junior Paulo and outside back Bailey Simonsson would be back from their long-term injuries in "the next one or two weeks".

AAP

World.title: Private 'space port' to test guided weapons in Queensland outback
World.content:
A small outback town will host a private weapons and aerospace testing facility in its backyard as part of the Queensland government's efforts to bolster local industry.

The 1.2 million-hectare MaxQ range will test horizontal-launch equipment and guided weapons on leased grazing land near Thargomindah, 11 hours west of Brisbane.

Due to enter operation in mid-2028, phase one of the project will be available to "domestic and allied" users, according to the state government.

The new launch infrastructure, explosives storage and a 2.5-kilometre runway are expected to create 60 construction and operational jobs.

The range, operated by Black Sky Aerospace, has been known as the Outback Space Port and used for sub-orbital rocket launches.

State push for sovereign defence capability

Loading...

Attending a missile launch at the range, Deputy Premier Jarrod Bleijie said the government would be funding half of the $15 million project.

"This is going to go 'boom' for the Queensland economy in the defence space, literally," Mr Bleijie said.

He said weapons manufacturers currently had to look interstate or overseas for testing sites.

"This is the sort of facility you can't do in South East Queensland," he said.

"I don't think Brisbane would be particularly happy with rockets being launched and missiles being launched from their backyards."

Deputy Premier Jarrod Bleijie says the outback is better suited for defence testing than the city. (Supplied: 9News)

The state's contribution is drawn from its $180 million Sovereign Industry Development Fund launched last year to invest in defence, biomedical and biofuel capabilities.

"It is so uncertain in the world at the moment, and the dynamics the world has at the moment in defence and security," Mr Bleijie said.

" We've got to look at sovereign capability, we've got to look at national security. "

Queensland sets sights on space industry with outback rocket launch A rocket carrying Australia's first commercial payload is launched skyward in the state's southern outback.

Expanded industry an 'oil boom' for community

Bulloo Shire Mayor John 'Tractor' Ferguson said he welcomed the employment the project would bring to the region.

"I'm over the moon with it," Cr Ferguson said.

"Most people in Thargo are pretty positive about new industries coming to town because, you know, most of these little towns are crying out for other industries other than council work."

Bulloo Shire mayor John 'Tractor' Ferguson is welcoming the announcement of a weapons testing facility near his town of Thargomindah. (ABC News: Laura Lavelle)

The outback mayor compared the expansion of defence industries to the oil boom decades prior.

"I remember when they first [established] Jackson's oil fields back in the 80s. Straight away there was a new motel built in Thargomindah used to accommodate the throughput of traffic," Cr Ferguson said.

" That's more people in the town, that's more families, that's more kids at the school. It's all good stuff. "

Cr Ferguson said Black Sky had been "mucking about" at the site for several years.

"I don't know where else they've looked in Queensland but this seems to be the [one]. They're very excited about this site," he said.

Black Sky offers its outback launch range for sub-orbital missions. (Supplied: 9News)

Queensland-based Black Sky Aerospace was founded in 2018 and develops propulsion technology including rocket motors and fuels.

Headquartered in Logan it also operates a launch and production facility near Goondiwindi.

The federal government has previously invested in the company's manufacturing capability.

World.title: Gold Coast council chief executive abruptly resigns
World.content:
The boss of the Gold Coast City Council has abruptly resigned.

Tim Baker was appointed as chief executive of Australia's second largest council in 2021 and announced on Tuesday that he would leave the role early in December.

"Over recent months, my wife and I have been considering the next chapter for our family and what that means for our future," he said in a statement.

"After careful reflection, I determined that I was unlikely to be in a position to make the longer term commitment required of the role beyond my current contract.

"Serving as Chief Executive Officer of the City of Gold Coast for the past five years has been a privilege."

In 2024 councillors voted unanimously to extend Mr Baker's contract, worth about $700,000 a year, for another four years.

A council spokesperson said he would take leave after council's next full meeting on July 28.

Scrutiny over travel expenses

Mr Baker urged the Gold Coast to embrace growth during his tenure and described the city's light rail project as "the envy of the country" before it was scrapped by the state government last year.

But his use of ratepayer funds for overseas travel was described as "exorbitant" and "disproportionately high" by some councillors.

Mr Baker and one his staff members spent $54,000 during a week-long trip to the United Kingdom last year.

In February, it was revealed that an extra $46,000 had been spent on staff travel beyond what was disclosed in a public expense report.

Individual costs were withheld due to privacy concerns, according to council documents.

Earlier this month, Acting Mayor Mark Hammel announced he would ask councillors to back an independent review of the city's senior executive team, including Mr Baker, at council's next full meeting.

Gold Coast deputy mayor Mark Hammel at the council's adoption of the 2026 budget. (ABC Gold OCast: Dominic Cansdale)

Councillors held a late-notice meeting behind closed doors on Tuesday afternoon to discuss a confidential legal matter.

"Legal matters being consider have to be done in confidential, especially if there's any staffing matters involved we don't discuss those in public," Cr Hammel said.

Councillor Nick Marshall said the meeting was "high-level, to do with specifics around roles".

"I'm going to leave the story-telling to the CEO to tell his story as opposed to me," he said.

"Councillors always need to be aware of what's going on and establish those guardrails for the city and that was an opportunity to do that prior to today's announcement."

Mayor Tom Tate, who is overseas, said in a statement that Mr Baker had helped the city prepare for the 2032 Olympic Games.

"The City strengthened its long-term financial sustainability, modernised its operating model, delivered major infrastructure and service improvements, enhanced organisational capability and positioned itself to meet the opportunities and challenges associated with the Gold Coast's continued growth," he said.

World.title: Inquest hears from woman who took it into her 'own hands' to solve 1989 murder
World.content:
A long-running inquest into the death of a Queensland teenager almost 40 years ago has heard a woman she did not know took it into her "own hands" to solve her murder.

Annette Mason, 15, was found dead in her Toowoomba home in 1989.

An inquest probing her death was held in the subsequent years, but there was insufficient evidence for a coroner at the time to rule if anyone was likely responsible.

The coronial inquiry was reopened in 2018, and further hearings were held between then and 2022.

After a lengthy adjournment it resumed on Wednesday, where a new witness was called to give evidence, in relation to two men who have previously been accused of being involved in Annette's death.

The woman, whose identity has been suppressed, testified about conversations she said she had with them, including Robert Speedy.

In 2018, the court heard the woman spoke to Mr Speedy about another man who he implied was responsible for the alleged murder.

The woman told the court Mr Speedy said that man, whose identity had also been suppressed, had used a stool and "got through a window" of Annette's home on the night of her death.

"[Mr Speedy] didn't say how he knew those things," she said.

The inquest into Annette Mason's (right) death has resumed after a long pause. (Supplied: Mason family)

The woman told the court Mr Speedy also claimed the man "just asked me if you can get fingerprints off a piece of wood".

She testified Mr Speedy had never discussed the cold case with her before.

When asked why she did not go to police with this information at the time, she told the court it was because she did not know if he was making it up, or if they would believe her.

Several years later, the court heard the woman reached out to the same man Mr Speedy had been talking about.

The woman told the court the man divulged details to her about Annette's death.

She testified he admitted to being at Annette's house the night she died, but she accepted he never said he was involved in her death.

Instead, the woman told the court the man named two other men as having some involvement.

She said the man also said Annette was "bashed before she got to the house" and the person who killed her was a police officer.

"[He said] that's why all the evidence went missing," she said.

Under cross-examination, the woman admitted she had a keen interest in the case despite not knowing the teenager.

She accepted she had listened to podcasts and read multiple articles about the case since the inquest was reopened in 2018.

The woman, who Annette Mason did not know, acknowledged it was "very reckless" but said she was "proud" of what she'd done. (Qld Police Service)

When asked if she had taken it upon herself to try to solve Annette's murder, she agreed, acknowledging it was "very reckless".

"I just took it into my own hands," she said.

She told the court although it was a "big risk", she was "proud" of what she had done.

The two men the woman said she had spoken to were recalled as witnesses and questioned about her evidence.

They rejected her statements and maintained they had nothing to do with Annette's death.

The public hearings have now concluded with the legal parties expected to make written submissions to the state coroner over the next six months.

His findings will be handed down at a later date.

World.title: Rural suburb flagged as home for proposed $40b 'hyperscale' data centre
World.content:
A suburb on the outskirts of Darwin has been earmarked as the future site for a $40 billion data centre, powered by gas fracked and piped directly from the Northern Territory's Beetaloo Basin, south of Katherine.

Weddell, in Darwin's rural area, was previously flagged as the location of the Top End's next satellite city, but has now been selected as the site of a possible hyperscale data centre and gas-fired power station.

Lands, Planning and Environment Minister Joshua Burgoyne today announced the NT government had signed a "do-not-deal" agreement over a 185-hectare parcel of land, to allow gas company Beetaloo Energy to explore plans for an energy and data centre precinct.

Loading...

The agreement gives Beetaloo Energy exclusive rights over the land, granting them time to secure investors and work out whether the project is viable.

"It gives a clear signal to investors out there that this government is open for business," Mr Burgoyne said.

'The next wave of the Industrial Revolution'

Beetaloo Energy managing director Alex Underwood said the company's vision for the project was "bold but simple" — "to create a fully-integrated energy and digital infrastructure precinct".

"The demand for power into data centres, both here in Australia and globally, is truly insatiable," he said.

"This, in my opinion, is the next wave of the Industrial Revolution."

Alex Underwood (centre), pictured with government ministers Joshua Burgoyne and Gerard Maley, says the company plans to "deliberately oversize" the facility's proposed power plant to feed back into the grid. (ABC News: Olivana Lathouris)

Mr Underwood said the project had the potential to generate tens of billions of dollars of investment and hundreds of jobs, but acknowledged there was still a long way to go before the project could become a reality.

The data centre would require two gigawatts of power to operate — more than six times the maximum demand for all of Darwin and Katherine in 2024-25.

Mr Underwood said if completed, the project would rival the scale of Western Australia's Ichthys LNG facility, one of gas giant Inpex's biggest oil projects in the world.

He said the company planned to "deliberately oversize" the proposed Weddell power plant to feed energy into Darwin's energy grid, instead of drawing from it.

Beetaloo Energy says it will consult widely before the proposed data centre project goes ahead. (Supplied: Beetaloo Energy)

"If you add to supply, that should put downward pressure on prices," he said.

Mr Underwood emphasised the project was "at day one" and would require "significant government approvals and financing" to come to fruition.

"To the people of the Northern Territory, I say this — I know you will have questions and potentially concerns about what we are planning to do here," he said.

" We intend to hold town halls, open up consultation lines for people to share their questions and concerns with us. "

The area, about a 40-minute drive away from the Darwin CBD, is still a far cry from the company's vision. (ABC News: Olivana Lathouris)

He would not confirm who the commercial partners for the cconstruction or development of the data centre might be or how water allocations would be managed.

Calls for data centre moratorium

Mr Underwood said the centre would present an opportunity to partner with renewable energy projects such as SunCable's proposed outback solar farm, but could not say to what extent renewable energy sources would be used.

The proposed data centre has drawn criticism from environmental groups, which want to see such projects paused. (Supplied: Beetaloo Energy)

"We do see an opportunity for both gas as base load and then, as renewables are available, then they can be integrated into the project," he said.

Mr Underwood said the project would be done in "an environmentally responsible manner" and "with the full backing of the Northern Territory community".

Loading...

"We believe in the next three to four years we could see this project move into production," he said.

The announcement has sparked renewed calls from environmental groups, including the Environment Centre NT, for a moratorium on data centre projects in the Territory.

Greenpeace Australia Pacific head of climate and energy Joe Rafalowicz described the announcement as a "shocking example of the unchecked expansion of hyperscale data centres in Australia".

World.title: Miners and energy stocks push ASX higher; Origin, Lynas decline
World.content:
Updated BusinessMarketsWorld markets Miners and energy stocks push ASX higher; Origin, Lynas decline Staff writers Updated July 22, 2026 — 6:10pm ,first published July 22, 2026 — 5:13am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The Australian sharemarket advanced on Wednesday after Wall Street was pushed higher by gains in makers of computer chips and other winners of the AI boom, shrugging off inflation concerns amid the intensifying hostilities in the Middle East. The S&P/ASX 200 finished up 29.7 points, or 0.3 per cent, at 8823, boosted by energy companies benefiting from the latest jump in oil prices and the mining giants. The local bourse closed flat on Tuesday. The Australian dollar was trading at 69.96 US cents. Wall Street’s gains set the tone for the local market. AP Energy and materials stocks pushed the ASX higher, thanks to higher prices for oil, copper and gold overnight. Oil extended gains after US President Donald Trump played down the prospect of near-term talks with Iran while threatening broader strikes, as risks to global supply spread beyond the Middle East to the Black Sea.



Brent crude rose to trade around $US92 a barrel, climbing for a fourth day. That’s up from less than $US72 in early July, which was roughly where it was before the war with Iran. Trump vowed to respond if Tehran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen disrupted shipping in the Red Sea and reiterated threats to strike soon at Pickaxe Mountain, a suspected Iranian nuclear site. Related Article Opinion

Middle East at war The real oil shock from the Iran war might be just beginning Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist Local oil giants Woodside and Santos rose 1.3 per cent and 1 per cent, respectively, and refiners Ampol (up 2.1 per cent) and Viva Energy (up 1.6 per cent) also advanced. Coal producers Yancoal and Whitehaven gained 5 per cent and 1.5 per cent, respectively, as higher oil prices boost demand for coal as a fossil fuel alternative. Beetaloo Energy Australia surged 5.9 per cent, having jumped as much as 20 per cent during the session, on news that the Northern Territory has given it 85 hectares of land to develop two hyper-scale AI data centre campuses. The company plans to build up to 2 gigawatts of power generation for the sites, using fuel from a massive shale gas deposit that is set to start commercial production this year. Mining heavyweights BHP and Rio Tinto both climbed 2.5 per cent after copper futures jumped 3.3 per cent overnight. After demand for iron ore peaked, the mining giants have pivoted to the red metal to become their main earnings driver.



Copper futures on the London Metal Exchange surged close to $US14,000 a tonne overnight on signs that supply is struggling to keep up with demand, including in the key Chinese market. However, they pulled back during the day as traders watched for any announcement from the White House on its plans for import tariffs on the metal. Meanwhile, gold prices held their gains as traders monitored the war-induced threats to energy supply routes that risk stoking inflation and putting pressure on the Federal Reserve to increase interest rates. Bullion was trading at about $US4080 an ounce, after gaining almost 2 per cent the previous session. Northern Star Resources rose 3.5 per cent, while Evolution Mining jumped 4.3 per cent and Newmont added 3.5 per cent. Silver miner South32 climbed a further 4.6 per cent, adding to its 6.6 per cent rally on Tuesday. Related Video Video icon 0:24 Origin Energy investigating suspected cybersecurity breach The mining outlier on Wednesday morning was Lynas Rare Earths, which fell 3.6 per cent after the company revealed in a trading update a more than 10 per cent slump in the June quarter compared with a year ago in its output of NdPR, an important alloy blend of rare earths elements crucial for making the strong magnets that power traction motors used in electric cars and wind turbines. The slump was blamed on issues at the company’s new Mount Weld water recycling plants and ore concentrate quality issues.



While rising oil prices boosted energy stocks, the flip side is threatening a re-acceleration of inflation, which in turn could push the US Federal Reserve and other central banks to raise interest rates, slowing economies and undercutting stock prices. Real estate investment trusts, which tend to suffer when rising rates boost the returns of bonds, were trading lower, with warehouse and AI data centre owner Goodman Group down 2 per cent, Westfield shopping centres landlord Scentre down 1.5 per cent and Stockland down 1.9 per cent. Origin fell 1.9 per cent after the nation’s biggest energy retailer said it was investigating a potential security breach that may have resulted in unauthorised access to the personal details of some of its 4.7 million Australian customers. If confirmed, the attack would be one of the worst cyberattacks in recent Australian business history. Tech stocks gave back their gains from Tuesday, with software makers bearing the brunt of the losses. Xero, the nation’s biggest tech stock, lost 2.6 per cent. WiseTech fell 0.5 per cent after saying it bought a developer of AI-powered supply chain risk and compliance intelligence technology for $10 million and shares, and Technology One dropped 2.3 per cent. Wesfarmers lost 2.1 per cent after the conglomerate said it would spend between $645 million and $715 million to expand the Mount Holland lithium mine and concentrator with its partner Sociedad Quimica y Minera de Chile. It will pay for the investment using existing cash and debt facilities.



The big four banks were mixed. CBA was up 0.7 per cent, Westpac and ANZ Bank both edged up 0.1 per cent, but National Australia Bank slipped 0.1 per cent. Related Article Opinion

Media & marketing It’s News Corp v the ‘byte burglars’: Murdochs fire up in AI content battle Elizabeth Knight Business columnist On Wall Street overnight, the S&P 500 climbed 0.9 per cent. The Dow Jones added 385 points, or 0.7 per cent, and the Nasdaq composite rose 1.3 per cent. AI stocks once again were at the centre of the action, rising for a second straight day after tumbling the week before. After rocketing higher because of the boom in investment in AI chips and data centres, they’ve come under pressure in recent weeks on worries that they shot too high. Concerns are also weighing that investment in AI may fall off if it doesn’t produce as much profit as hoped.



Micron Technology jumped 12.2 per cent and added to its 1.9 per cent gain from the day before, coming off its 13.3 per cent drop from last week. Nvidia added 2 per cent. They were the two strongest forces lifting the S&P 500. On Wall Street, several stronger-than-expected profit reports from big companies also helped the market higher. 3M climbed 7.3 per cent after topping analysts’ expectations for both profit and revenue in the latest quarter. It also raised its forecast for profit over the full year of 2026. General Motors cruised 4.9 per cent higher after the vehicle maker’s profit for the latest quarter beat analysts’ expectations and CEO Mary Barra said demand in North America remains strong. Alphabet slid 1.5 per cent after Google released a trio of cheaper versions of its Gemini AI model, but shared no timing updates for the flagship Pro model that has already delayed its launch by several weeks. With AP, Reuters, Bloomberg The Market Recap newsletter is a wrap of the day’s trading. Get it each weekday afternoon.

World.title: Labor is feeding on the misery of gambling addiction
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

As a life-long Labor voter, I was sickened to read that not only is the party receiving substantial donations from gambling companies, but members will also be drinking champagne and eating canapes at a party fundraiser paid for by a hospitality and pokies giant (“Labor’s millions in gambling donations revealed amid last-ditch push for reform”, July 22). These luxuries are being funded by the misery of the very voters who rely on these MPs and officials to look after their interests. I would like to see a list of those attending such functions to ensure I never vote for them again. Shame on any Labor Party member who feeds on the sour fruits of gambling addiction. It’s time the party had the intestinal fortitude to take on these companies, not benefit from their questionable largesse. Jim Richardson, Croydon Anthony Albanese at the NSW Labor conference this month. AAPIMAGE Well, at least we now know why despite promising to bring gambling under control at the 2022 election, the government hasn’t done anything meaningful: it’s in the pocket of the gambling industry, having accepted $4 million in the past five years. If we thought the Coalition was in a better position we’d be wrong there, too – they accepted $2.6 million over the same period. It just goes to show how insidious and determined the gambling industry is. It seems that for all his promises, the prime minister is under the thumb of the party machine. It will be interesting to see how this revelation is handled at the Labor national conference. Ian Adair, Hunters Hill Labor appears to be lining its electoral war chest with blood money. A great deal of the gambling industry’s most lavish political donation has come from the pockets of addicted gamblers, which in turn is leading to misery, broken families and suicide. John Millard, Mullumbimby Last night on Annabel Crabb’s ABC Kitchen Cabinet, Prime Minister Albanese said he was driven primarily to develop policies that would benefit people and the country, not the Labor Party. I was impressed. Now I read your headline about gambling donations and wonder. People and the country first? Not the party? Hardly.
