Albanese’s actions speak louder than his words, which now sound simply hypocritical. Jennifer Fergus, Croydon It seems that when it comes to gambling, the main difference between Australian citizens and the Labor Party is that Labor’s addiction leaves them financially better off. Colin Stokes, Camperdown



Outside intervention Mathew Knott’s report shows yet again that the Israeli government thinks it should have a say in what Australia does (“Israel accused of “extraordinary” intervention in Labor politics”, July 22). There have now been a number of totally inappropriate attempts to tell the Australian government, our prime minister and now the Labor Party, what to do in relation to events in the Middle East. I can’t recall any other country trying so persistently to make such interventions. Our Jewish citizens have every right to the same protection under our laws as anyone else, and clearly we should have done better with that, but that doesn’t mean we need Israel to tell us what to do. Here in Australia, we have a democracy that allows opposing points of view to be expressed. May it always be so. Garry Feeney, Ashfield Fix medical mayhem Your editorial is a harrowing read (“Our medical devices are not fit for purpose”, July 22). It details the difficulty in getting meaningful data out of the Therapeutic Goods Administration regarding the number and nature of incidents involving people wearing failed medical devices. The TGA defends its position and claims to treat its stakeholders (patients) as a priority. Another group of stakeholders that fail to get a mention is the public. This was recently evident in a tragic accident in country Victoria in which five people were killed by a driver wearing a failed blood glucose monitor. It’s simply not good enough. An urgent intervention is required to fix this mess. Mike Keene, Mollymook Beach Wrong priority I can’t help but wonder about the urgency to build data centres in NSW to prop up our economy when we are facing “one of the toughest construction markets in decades” (“Signature Labor housing policy at risk of falling thousands of homes short of target”, July 22). It’s baffling that housing for computers takes precedence over housing for people. I wonder if Labor ministers actually talk to each other. Elizabeth Darton, Lane Cove West



Sardines? Can do I’m dismayed but not surprised by all the announcements about additional high-rise towers being planned and the number of apartments that will be squeezed into them (“Car yards, churches and bowlos: sites earmarked for new towers”, July 22). Soon they’ll become so small you won’t be able to swing the proverbial cat in one. Sydney is often called Emerald City or the Harbour City. I’d say a name change is in order. How about Sardine City? Peter Skrzynecki, Eastwood A proposed 186-apartment development at St Francis Xavier Church in Lavender Bay has attracted fierce opposition from residents. Stop dress dross Just as we need to break the social media algorithms that feed hate, we must break the business model behind ultra-fast fashion that is drowning Australia in poorly made plastic clothes (“Australia’s hooked on fast cheap gear”, July 21). France is legislating against this, but all we have is a voluntary stewardship scheme with a pitiful 4¢ levy. Environment Minister Murray Watt needs to get serious and pass legislation to tackle this problem. Jill Robinson, Randwick It seems to me that the effects of fast fashion are wider than just waste. I recently tried to donate clothing to a well-known, church-based op shop and was told that they weren’t taking clothing because they had too much stock. What am I supposed to do with perfectly decent but unwanted clothing? Randi Svensen, Wyong



Costs of clearing In the context of threats to biodiversity and the impact on climate change, it is disturbing to read that the rate of land clearing in NSW is increasing (“Land clearing spikes despite government reform pledges”, July 22). Nearly half targets native woody weed, a type of plant that was not as prevalent under traditional Aboriginal land management by fire. However, some western graziers appreciate its benefits through reducing localised dust storms, providing shelter for lambing ewes and providing some nutritional relief during droughts. The need for frequent cleaning of critical water-troughs is substantially reduced and the wool achieves higher returns as contamination from sand and dust is minimised. Roger Epps, Armidale Better than bullets With the brumby cull now over, it seems a more humane method of controlling feral animals in Australia would be to put them on “the pill”. There must be a way of delivering long-lasting contraceptive medicine via food drop, injections or darts. Yes, it may take longer to make achieve results, but it’s far less cruel. Helen Howes, Collaroy Refusal didn’t float The proposal to scrap another retired Manly ferry deserves greater public scrutiny (“Retired Manly ferry to be scrapped”, July 22). More than 14,200 people signed a parliamentary petition supporting the creation of a new artificial dive reef, yet the NSW government has never fully explained why this option was rejected. If cost was the determining factor, the government should release the figures. Preparing a vessel for scuttling as a dive attraction is widely understood to cost a similar amount to scrapping it, but with the potential to create environmental, tourism and recreational benefits for generations rather than producing only scrap metal. No one suggests that every retired ferry should become a dive wreck. However, when a publicly owned asset is disposed of despite a substantial expression of public support for an alternative use, the community deserves a clear explanation.

Good government is not simply about making decisions. It is about openly explaining them. John Rowe, Exeter The Collaroy, right, tied up beside the Freshwater ferry at Cockatoo Island on Tuesday. Sam Mooy



It’s the end of the line for the Collaroy, the iconic ferry that carried the Olympic torch across Sydney Harbour in 2000. Another large Manly ferry, the Freshwater, will be towed to Yamba for refurbishment and then back again at a cost of $200,000. May I suggest that Transport for NSW allow the Freshwater to make her own way to and from the Yamba shipyard. She has often crossed the heads in huge seas, so the voyage should be a breeze and taxpayers will be spared the hefty towing fees. Kay Abrahams, Freshwater Midterm madness I wouldn’t get too excited that the US midterm elections in November will rein in Donald Trump’s madcap lawlessness and maverick behaviour (“Midterms to steer Trump’s agenda”, July 22).

He’s clearly already laying the groundwork for declaring any adverse results as rigged against him, just like the tiresome nonsense he still spouts about his loss in 2020. He and his slavish minions have a manic determination to trample on anything that diminishes their stranglehold on power. And if gerrymandering congressional districts in friendly states and dirt files on their opponents aren’t enough, they will simply ignore any outcome they don’t like or use legal contortions to invalidate unwelcome results and get yet another spinelessly compliant Congress. The US, at least at a federal level, no longer has a government of, by or for its people – if it ever did. The outlaws have squatted in city hall, tied up the sheriff, installed their own judges and pointed loaded weapons at anyone who even looks like they’re wearing a white hat. Adrian Connelly, Springwood If the midterm elections are fair and square, there seems little doubt that the Democrats would secure control of the House, at least. However, it seems Trump plans to rig these elections in favour of the Republicans. The question is whether he can get away with it. Historians argue that he is one of the most corrupt presidents in US history and can’t be trusted to respect the will of the people. For the sake of America and indeed the rest of the world, the Democrats need to secure both houses. Voters have the power to make this possible, provided Trump is prevented from interfering in the midterms. Graham Lum, North Rocks Down boy The fuss about Barnaby Joyce yelling at his dog is overblown (Letters, July 22). Farm dogs operate at distances up to 500 metres away from the farmer and it is normal that instructions are yelled. Although distances are shorter around the house, loud commands help to convey that instructions are serious. Farm dogs understand that. It is all about communication with a trusted offsider. Anthony Healy, Centennial Park It seems that those who are protesting the way Joyce shouted at his dog have not owned a barking dog, or worse, had neighbours whose dog barked all day after they left for work. As a former street “dog marshal”, I thought his language to be temperate. Indeed, he was the perfect gentleman by making it clear at whom he was shouting. A real drover might not have been as polite. Les Sisley, Kelso

World.title: Justin Hemmes’ $19m new Sydney precinct in doubt after RSL veterans block sale
World.content:
NationalNSWCommercial real estate Justin Hemmes’ $19m new Sydney precinct in doubt after RSL veterans block sale Harriet Alexander July 22, 2026 — 6:07pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Justin Hemmes’ $19 million purchase of a former Tattersalls Club building is in doubt after RSL members used a bureaucratic process to block the sale from proceeding, throwing into disarray his plans for a hospitality precinct at the base of Martin Place. Members of the Combined Services RSL sub-branch, whose trustees hold the title to the Barrack Street property, voted on Tuesday against the RSL custodian being appointed among the trustees to handle the proceeds of the sale, which was a precondition to the transaction proceeding. Justin Hemmes and the Barrack Street property in Sydney’s CBD. Artwork: Matt Willis Sub-branch member Nikhita Sahay said the building was the last RSL property in Sydney’s CBD and veterans did not want to see it disappear in a “flash sale”. “Once it’s lost, it’s gone forever,” Sahay said.



“It’s valuable to veterans of all generations because of its historical significance, and its location close to the Martin Place cenotaph and defence establishment precincts gives it strategic relevance.” But RSL NSW has insisted that the sale will proceed, and declared that the sub-branch was now in breach of its governance obligations. This “governance issue” would be considered at the next board meeting. Merivale’s Hemmes want the property to form part of a nightclub, restaurant, bar and hotel precinct in the western CBD. Dominic Lorrimer “A group of members voted against the custodian arrangement in the mistaken belief that a ‘no’ vote would stop the sale,” the spokesman said. “It cannot. The sub-branch and the purchaser contracted for the sale, and the sub-branch members and the RSL NSW Board approved it.”



Hemmes declined to comment on how the turbulence might affect his plans for a nightclub, restaurant, bar and hotel precinct in the western CBD, where he already owns the adjacent properties to the RSL’s building. He turned up in person to bid for the 341.5-square-metre property in May, and bought it for $19,000,001, a single dollar higher than the reserve. The dispute comes as the administrator for the City Tattersalls Club, which occupied the building until last year, announced that two of its other venues – the Castlereagh Club, World Gym and squash courts – were closed effectively immediately due to the “dire financial position” of the 130-year-old gentleman’s club. Administrator PKF told City Tattersalls members on Wednesday it would also apply to the NSW Supreme Court for instructions on how to wind up the club as it was an unincorporated association. A general meeting of the Combined Services RSL sub-branch was told in June that Tattersalls owed them nearly $300,000. Treasurer Alexander Ekert told the meeting that the sub-branch’s trustees terminated the lease with Tattersalls after discovering “significant issues” with the agreement. “The lease was not being [administered] in accordance with the terms, rent was not being charged at the appropriate rate, outstanding debts were accumulating and financial obligations were not being met,” Ekert told sub-branch members.



The trustees also learnt that the building and all the RSL memorabilia contained in it were not insured. After reviewing the overall situation, the trustees decided that the best option was to sell the club, Ekert said. Related Article Commercial real estate Justin Hemmes turns up, bids big, and buys himself a $19m club Sub-branch members voted 12-9 in favour of selling the building at a general meeting in March. However, some members claimed that they were not in favour of the sale but had not been able to vote as the meeting was scheduled on a workday and proxy or online voting were not available. They also claimed that a staff member who voted in favour of the sale was not eligible. They learnt later that the sale was conditional on RSL Custodian being appointed as trustee and raised that matter with RSL NSW lawyers, after which a motion to appoint the custodian was added to the July 21 meeting agenda. Members voted 18-16 against the motion, and two other motions that presupposed the sale going ahead were then dropped from the agenda. The meeting was told that the board would have to consider its next steps.



Combined Services RSL sub-branch president Bill Forsbey said the executive wanted to sell the Barrack Street property and move to another location in central Sydney. “We are a charity for veterans. That means our money goes to veterans, not into a rundown building,” Forsbey said. “For too long our sub-branch has been an office on the second floor of a tired old building. We want somewhere veterans can drop in, somewhere modern, warm, and welcoming, somewhere that feels like ours. If you served, we are here.”

World.title: Ex-Eels prodigy backs Luai signing as Bears table offer to Paulo
World.content:
Key points Ex-Eel Talagi says Luai will help Parramatta’s young halves

Panthers facing contract juggle with stars

Latrell Mitchell is battling to play again in 2026

Cameron Murray headlines mounting Rabbitohs injury toll

Panthers five-eighth and former Eels prodigy Blaize Talagi believes Jarome Luai could prove to be a $700,000 circuit breaker for his old club as the Perth Bears target Parramatta captain Junior Paulo to lead their forward pack. Talagi will line up against his old side on Thursday night in the No.6 jersey Luai wore in four premierships with Penrith. Luai’s 2027 shift to Parramatta has divided opinion since his one-year deal was confirmed last week. Loading Eels coach Jason Ryles defended the Luai signing – Wests Tigers will pay $500,000 of his salary – once again on Wednesday, as Perth stepped up their pursuit of 32-year-old Paulo. The Bears are prepared to offer Paulo a two-year deal after coach Mal Meninga met with the ex-NSW Origin prop. Parramatta have been in talks with Paulo about a one-year extension for some time, and he will now weigh up the added security of the Bears offer against moving his family to WA.



Meanwhile, Ryles insisted Luai’s 12-month pit stop before joining PNG in 2028 won’t undermine Parramatta’s development of playmakers such Lorenzo Talataina, Lincoln Fletcher (both 19) and Joash Papalii (22), and denied it points to a lack of long-term roster planning. Talagi has emerged as an unlikely ally in the debate around Parramatta’s roster, having knocked back a lucrative three-year Eels extension to join Penrith in 2024. Eels veteran Junior Paulo is weighing up an offer from the Bears. NRL Imagery Talagi played fullback, centre and off the bench in his debut season when Dylan Brown and Mitchell Moses were entrenched as Parramatta’s halves, albeit with contract options that allowed Newcastle to poach Brown with a record-breaking 10-year deal. Talagi stressed that playing alongside Nathan Cleary in the Panthers’ title-winning system was the driving factor behind leaving his junior club.



But having been mentored by Luai when playing in the halves for Samoa and touring the UK together, he said Luai’s short-term stint could work out perfectly for Parramatta’s next generation of playmakers. “I don’t see anything but good things coming from signing Romey for Parramatta to be honest, especially the younger guys coming up,” Talagai said. “He’s definitely someone who knows how to lead and lead with his actions, and his record speaks for itself. Blaize Talagi has backed Parramatta’s signing of Jarome Luai. Wolter Peeters “For me when I was at Parra, it was the biggest call of my life to leave, and the club was struggling at the time. “So moving to a club where I could tell there wouldn’t be all the focus on me, knowing there would be older guys, obviously someone like Nath to play alongside, that was a big attraction.



“I’ve matured a lot since I’ve been here. I think that’s just natural, but I also think it could have been very different if I’d stayed, too. Being a half in the NRL, there’s pressure that comes with that and I think timing of when you play first grade and how you develop is really important. “You’ve got to be properly prepared, and everyone develops at different times. Even when I first got here, there were no promises and I started in reserve grade. “It ended up being the best thing for me, it gave me extra time to adapt to how Penrith do things, so I don’t think anyone should get too disheartened as a young half.” Parramatta have high hopes for Talataina and Fletcher as long-term playmakers. But given they are both still teenagers, the pair are considered another 12 to 18 months away from being ready for the NRL. Ryles bristled at comparisons between the short-term deals of Luai and Broncos-bound half Jonah Pezet, who has been stuck in NSW Cup behind Ronald Volkman recentlt.



“Jonah’s an up-and-coming player who’s done a great apprenticeship and is on his path to being a seasoned first-grader, and Jarome is a four-time premiership winner,” Ryles said. Related Article Updated

NRL 2026 Joey Manu’s $1.6m contract call signals latest shift in cross-code talent stoush “So there’s a little bit of a difference there. I don’t apologise for anything that we’ve done … Is there a fear of [upsetting other players]? No, there isn’t, because we’re sitting in a spot on the ladder that we don’t want to be. “It’s no one’s fault directly, but we need more experienced players. Jarome fits that bill at the moment. “We have got younger players that are coming through our pathways and our system that may be ready in 12 months.



“But this gives them an extra bit of time to give them their reps in [NSW] Cup and learn off a true pro that’s won a lot of premierships.” Penrith typically pause contract talk to win titles. Will this year be any different? Dan Walsh Ivan Cleary remains unfazed by Penrith’s multimillion-dollar roster juggle revolving around the future of his son and superstar halfback Nathan ahead of a critical few weeks before the club traditionally pauses contract talks to win premierships. Penrith’s 2027 off-contract list has dominated rugby league’s rumour mill all year, with Nathan Cleary’s next contract move key to the Panthers salary cap and 10 NRL squad members who will become free agents if they are still unsigned come November 1.



Cleary was front-page news of The Daily Telegraph on Monday, which declared the game’s best player would test the market. Nathan Cleary’s future has been a talking point all season. Tertius Pickard Sources speaking on the condition of anonymity due to the confidential nature of discussions have told this masthead he is yet to decide whether he goes to November 1, and that he will begin giving his future genuine consideration after Thursday’s clash with Parramatta. Father Ivan said he didn’t know when asked on Tuesday if Cleary planned to test the market, and said he couldn’t “remember the last time” he spoke to his son about his contractual future. Ivan announced mid-year that 2027 will be his last season as head coach, with assistant Peter Wallace anointed as his successor.



The Panthers remain confident a long-term extension can be sorted for their prize-winning No.7 to keep Cleary from entertaining rival offers. The club first discussed a new deal with his management at the start of the season and have continued to negotiate with the rest of their roster in the background. Further talks are scheduled with star front-rower Moses Leota after he was recently granted a brief window to negotiate with rival clubs for 2028 and beyond. Underrated hooker Mitch Kenny was the first off-contract Panther to recommit to the club on a lucrative four-year deal last week. Throughout Penrith’s run to four straight premierships, the club typically paused contract talks leading into the end of the regular season and finals to avoid off-field distractions. No hard and fast rule enforced the policy, but a similar stance looms once another few weeks of negotiations take place, and there is further clarity on Cleary’s future.



The Panthers have suffered three of their four losses this season in the past five weeks, but have most importantly come through the Origin period unscathed. Kenny is their only top-line player sidelined through injury, though a return date from his badly broken leg is still unknown. Focus on the club’s retention’s fight has intensified since Cleary, Isaah Yeo, Liam Martin and Brian To’o’s NSW Origin commitments wrapped up, but Ivan Cleary said contract talk hadn’t proved any more a distraction than previous years. “It is in the background,” Cleary said. “Obviously our GM Shane Elford’s done a lot of work in the background all year, because ideally we don’t want [players] to go to market, but we respect if they do.



“I don’t think it’s a distraction any more than any other time…I’m confident it’ll work out the way it’s meant to work out for all of them. I feel pretty confident that we’ll get our share of wins there, and if we don’t, then it won’t be through lack of trying.” Luckless Latrell to see specialist for ‘complex nerve damage’ Adrian Proszenko Latrell Mitchell may have played his last game in 2026, with the South Sydney superstar consulting a neurologist for treatment on “complex nerve damage” in a desperate bid to return to the field this year. Mitchell’s prognosis is one half of a double blow for the Rabbitohs, with captain Cameron Murray also sidelined for up to a month with a calf injury he suffered in the loss to Canberra. The pair are the highest-paid members of the playing squad and represent about $2 million of talent unavailable to coach Wayne Bennett in the run to the finals.



Latrell Mitchell is struggling to get back on the field in 2026. Getty Mitchell’s scheduled return from a back injury last month was aborted after he tore his calf in training. It was hoped Mitchell could be fit for the round-23 clash against Parramatta on August 8, but it’s increasingly likely he has played his last game for the season. This masthead broke the news of Mitchell’s diagnosis on Tuesday, with the club providing a further update later in the day. “Centre Latrell Mitchell has undergone further investigations and consultation with a specialist neurologist last week,” the club statement said. “Mitchell is trying to overcome complex nerve damage that initially created complications with a lower back injury, and now a calf issue in his left leg. Mitchell will remain a week-to-week proposition as to a return to the field of play.”



Cameron Murray and Latrell Mitchell, Souths’ highest-paid players, are due for more time on the sidelines. In further bad injury news, centre Tallis Duncan has sustained a hamstring strain that will sideline him for two to three weeks. Latrell Siegwalt will replace Duncan for Friday’s clash against the Storm at Accor Stadium, while Lachlan Hubner comes in at lock for Murray. “Trelly is doing good, he obviously wants to be out there with the boys,” Souths centre Jack Wighton said of Mitchell. “He’s a presence we’re missing, he’s an awesome player to have on the field with you. He just gives you that confidence and belief. The quicker we can have him back, the better. We can’t wait to have him back, we love big Trell.” Murray and Mitchell are part of an already bulging casualty ward that includes Sean Keppie (thumb, expected return round 23), Dayne Jennings, (knee, TBC) Adam Elliott (ankle, season) and Talanoa Penitani (hamstring, round 26).



Murray’s teammates acknowledged the significance of his absence, but believed the team would be able to cover for him. “Huge [loss]. Any team that Cam Murray is playing in, he has a massive positive impact on how they play,” Campbell Graham said. “We are obviously no different. He’s our captain, he’s our leader and he’s one of those blokes who gives you confidence when you’re running out there with him. “He’s a loss for us over the next few weeks or so, whatever it is. As I said before, it takes an NRL squad to do something in this competition and we believe we’ve got the depth. Latrell Mitchell injured his calf in training last month as he attempted to return from a back injury. Steven Siewert



“The boys have filled that position before and done the job for us. We’re still confident we can steer the ship while he’s out and hopefully we’re in a good position when he’s back ready to play.”

Junior Tatola added: “It’s obviously a big loss for us, he does a lot of work. “He’s great to be next to and play with. It’s a big loss, but we have got boys in there that can step up to the plate and do the same job as what came does as well.” Related Article NRL 2026 ‘It’s people’s jobs’: Dragons take aim at costly refereeing calls In other team news, Canterbury have named Stephen Crichton to make his return at five-eighth, pushing fill-in Sean O’Sullivan onto an extended bench. Manly have named Lehi Hopoate as the fullback replacement for Tom Trbojevic, while the Storm welcome back Jarome Hughes after the halfback missed one game with a hamstring injury.

World.title: First look: Design of Brisbane Olympics aquatic centre revealed
World.content:
NationalQueenslandRoad to Brisbane 2032 First look: Design of Brisbane Olympics aquatic centre revealed Jessica Millward and and Dominique Tassell July 22, 2026 — 6:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The first official render of the National Aquatic Centre for the Brisbane Olympics has been unveiled. ARM Architecture and NH Architecture, in partnership with Queensland’s Arkhefield, will help deliver the Spring Hill centre on the edge of Victoria Park. As this masthead revealed two weeks ago, the Centenary Pool Complex will be handed over to the Games Independent Infrastructure and Coordination Authority by Brisbane City Council on September 1. A render of the new National Aquatic Centre, to be built at the Centenary Pool site in Spring Hill for the Brisbane 2032 Olympic Games. The construction timeline for the National Aquatic Centre has not been confirmed, but August 30 will be the existing pool’s last day of operation.



Related Article Brisbane 2032 Olympics Centenary Pool to be closed and handed over to Games authority within weeks Deputy Premier Jarrod Bleijie would not confirm on Wednesday whether the venue’s capacity would be downgraded from the planned 25,000 to save money, after Australian Financial Review reporting this week that ARM had been asked to scale back the centre to manage costs. “GIICA [is] required to go through all that at the moment and the budget [for all Games venues] is $7.1 billion, and they’re required to deliver those projects within budget,” Bleijie said. “Capacity has been detailed in the delivery plan, but ... we are going through a process with GIICA at the moment for all the venues, and we did ask them to look at the costings. “When you appoint architects and designers, they have to do it within budget, and we’ve been abundantly clear on that.”



The render does not include how the heritage-listed elements of the site will be handled, and Premier David Crisafulli has previously refused to address whether the current complex will be demolished. It is unclear if, or how, the heritage-listed elements of the site will be incorporated into the site plan. Dominique Tassell Bleijie confirmed on Wednesday that affected tenants would be compensated, but said when and how much was a matter for Brisbane City Council. Tenants at the site have still not received official confirmation of their eviction date, and have not been informed about compensation. World.title: Brown-and-gold bonanza: Gun Hawks forward recommits to form star tandem with Ben King
World.content:
Exclusive SportAFLAFL 2026 Brown-and-gold bonanza: Gun Hawks forward recommits to form star tandem with Ben King Sam McClure Updated July 22, 2026 — 5:56pm ,first published July 21, 2026 — 8:25pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Mitch Lewis is set to line up alongside Ben King in brown and gold next year, knocking back interest from other clubs to recommit to Hawthorn despite the recruitment of another key forward. Clubs such as Collingwood had hoped that Hawthorn’s pursuit of King could’ve persuaded Lewis to have his head turned by rival offers. But two competition sources with knowledge of the situation, speaking anonymously, have confirmed the 27-year-old has told the club he will stay with the two parties putting the final touches on a long-term deal. Not going anywhere: Mitch Lewis is set to stay put at Hawthorn. Getty Images Hawthorn’s list management believes Lewis – an athletic marking forward – can play further up the ground, which would allow King to lead out of the goal square. Sam Mitchell and his team will now work on luring at least one star midfielder from an opposition team to kick to King and Lewis, with Essendon’s Zach Merrett and Gold Coast’s Bailey Humphrey firmly in their sights.



Merrett will almost certainly get his wish a second time around – barring the Bombers playing hardball again – while the contracted Humphrey is also being aggressively hunted by Steven King and the Demons. Lewis’ recommitment comes as Ben King is poised to complete one of the most dramatic contract backflips in recent AFL history, with the Suns spearhead set to reject their lucrative long-term offer and instead nominate Hawthorn as his preferred destination for 2027. The stunning change of heart comes barely two months after King told The Age he intended to remain on the Gold Coast, insisting he loved the club and saw his future in Queensland. Ben King wants to play for Hawthorn next season. AFL Photos But three industry sources, speaking on the condition of anonymity because discussions remain confidential, have confirmed King’s position has shifted significantly in recent weeks, with Hawthorn now firmly in the box seat to secure one of the competition’s premier key forwards.



Related Article AFL 2026 ‘If you’re out there, Bobby’: McRae’s public plea to premiership star King’s contract at Hawthorn is expected to be a six-year deal, taking him until the end of 2032. Gold Coast have not yet officially been told of his intention to leave. King will be in Melbourne this week ahead of the Suns’ game against Carlton at Marvel Stadium on Saturday. The decision is a bitter blow for the Suns, who had been confident they would retain the 26-year-old despite intense Victorian interest. Several factors have contributed to King’s dramatic reversal.



His partner is keen to return home to Victoria, while Gold Coast’s alarming on-field slide has also weighed heavily. The Suns have now lost eight consecutive matches after appearing well-placed to challenge for a second-consecutive finals campaign earlier this season. King’s own form has only enhanced his value. The powerful key forward sits second in the Coleman Medal race and has established himself as one of the AFL’s most reliable goalkickers, kicking at least 40 goals in every completed season since 2021. Last year he produced a career-best campaign with 71 goals, underlining why Hawthorn have been prepared to aggressively pursue his signature. How the trade period plays out is yet to be determined.



As King is a restricted free agent, Gold Coast have the power to match the bid and force a trade. But given the Suns’ disastrous form slump has now landed them 14th on the ladder, the Queensland club could opt to accept first-round compensation, which, if the season finished now, would be pick No.6. Editor's pick AFL 2026 Hawthorn want Ben King and Zach Merrett. This is how Gold Coast losses help their cause The Hawks would much prefer to land King without a trade, given they are also in the box seat to land Merrett, who will once again request a move to Hawthorn despite a failed attempt last year. For the Hawks, landing King would represent another significant statement of intent as the club continues to build a list capable of challenging for premierships over the coming years. The Hawks have invested heavily in assembling one of the AFL’s youngest and most exciting lists under Mitchell, and adding a proven goal-kicking machine entering the prime of his career would significantly strengthen their premiership credentials.



Related Article Analysis

AFL 2026 How the Pies can avoid wildcard round, as we rate every team’s run home The Suns have long viewed King as a cornerstone of their future, but after months of confidence they would secure his signature, they are now confronting the prospect of watching one of the competition’s elite key forwards walk out the door. If it results in a move, King’s decision would rank among the most extraordinary contract reversals in recent AFL memory – a player who only weeks ago expected to stay, now preparing to head home to Victoria and reshape the landscape of the upcoming trade period. King’s management has been contacted for comment. Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.

World.title: NSW has Australia’s worst child psychiatrist shortage
World.content:
July 22, 2026 — 5:47pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Fifty per cent of all mental health disorders emerge before the age of 14, yet access to early specialist care remains appallingly limited, with services increasingly focused on adolescents in acute distress. Ethan Annetts is emblematic of the crisis facing many. He was 11 when he started self-harming and spent years on assessment waitlists, trapped in a cycle of hospital presentations and discharges with no ongoing care until, as a desperate and suicidal adult, he finally saw a psychiatrist. Many children with mental health problems don’t get the professional attention they need. Fairfax Media Ethan’s story, as told to the Herald’s health reporter Rachel Rasker, is the victory of the human spirit at a time when the well-being of Australia’s young people is declining, with depression and anxiety diagnoses skyrocketing and suicide now the leading cause of death for young people. More than 300 die annually. A new report from the Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists finds too many children are missing out on specialist mental health care until they are older, sicker and in crisis.



About one in seven children is living with a mental health disorder, and the college predicts a shortfall of at least 230 child and adolescent psychiatrists by 2028. NSW has the worst child and adolescent psychiatrist shortage in the country. The college said 64.3 full-time child and adolescent psychiatrists are needed just to meet the current demand of families across NSW. By 2048, that shortfall is projected to grow to 119. The state’s psychiatrist shortage is almost triple that of Victoria. Nationwide, there is just one specialist for every 571 children with moderate to severe mental illness. NSW community mental health teams receive the lowest state government funding per capita of any Australian state. The dire situation has also been exacerbated by the flight of some child psychiatrists into private medicine since 2024, when more than half of the state’s staff specialist psychiatrists resigned in protest over pay rates in an attempt to save the state’s failing mental health system. Not all have returned to the public system. Potentially adding to the crisis, the federal government’s Thriving Kids policy will move children with mild to moderate developmental delays or autism off the National Disability Insurance Scheme and into state-based mental health systems.



Details about the transition have yet to be finalised despite its rollout date of October 2026. But Professor Valsamma Eapen, who led the RANZCP report, said resourcing constraints meant children could access help only after their condition became severe, and Thriving Kids could “add more pressures onto the already stressed system”. NSW Mental Health Minister Rose Jackson said in a statement she recognised the growing demand and acknowledged there was “always more work”, adding her government had invested in recruitment, training and new models of care to strengthen the mental health workforce and improve access. Clearly there is a disconnect between the state and the profession. But child psychiatrists are not optional extras. They are professionals essential to the mental health system. The government needs to make sure there are enough of them to do it. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Miners and energy stocks push ASX higher; Origin, Lynas decline
World.content:
Updated BusinessMarketsWorld markets Miners and energy stocks push ASX higher; Origin, Lynas decline Staff writers Updated July 22, 2026 — 6:10pm ,first published July 22, 2026 — 5:13am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The Australian sharemarket advanced on Wednesday after Wall Street was pushed higher by gains in makers of computer chips and other winners of the AI boom, shrugging off inflation concerns amid the intensifying hostilities in the Middle East. The S&P/ASX 200 finished up 29.7 points, or 0.3 per cent, at 8823, boosted by energy companies benefiting from the latest jump in oil prices and the mining giants. The local bourse closed flat on Tuesday. The Australian dollar was trading at 69.96 US cents. Wall Street’s gains set the tone for the local market. AP Energy and materials stocks pushed the ASX higher, thanks to higher prices for oil, copper and gold overnight. Oil extended gains after US President Donald Trump played down the prospect of near-term talks with Iran while threatening broader strikes, as risks to global supply spread beyond the Middle East to the Black Sea.



Brent crude rose to trade around $US92 a barrel, climbing for a fourth day. That’s up from less than $US72 in early July, which was roughly where it was before the war with Iran. Trump vowed to respond if Tehran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen disrupted shipping in the Red Sea and reiterated threats to strike soon at Pickaxe Mountain, a suspected Iranian nuclear site. Related Article Opinion

Middle East at war The real oil shock from the Iran war might be just beginning Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist Local oil giants Woodside and Santos rose 1.3 per cent and 1 per cent, respectively, and refiners Ampol (up 2.1 per cent) and Viva Energy (up 1.6 per cent) also advanced. Coal producers Yancoal and Whitehaven gained 5 per cent and 1.5 per cent, respectively, as higher oil prices boost demand for coal as a fossil fuel alternative. Beetaloo Energy Australia surged 5.9 per cent, having jumped as much as 20 per cent during the session, on news that the Northern Territory has given it 85 hectares of land to develop two hyper-scale AI data centre campuses. The company plans to build up to 2 gigawatts of power generation for the sites, using fuel from a massive shale gas deposit that is set to start commercial production this year. Mining heavyweights BHP and Rio Tinto both climbed 2.5 per cent after copper futures jumped 3.3 per cent overnight. After demand for iron ore peaked, the mining giants have pivoted to the red metal to become their main earnings driver.



Copper futures on the London Metal Exchange surged close to $US14,000 a tonne overnight on signs that supply is struggling to keep up with demand, including in the key Chinese market. However, they pulled back during the day as traders watched for any announcement from the White House on its plans for import tariffs on the metal. Meanwhile, gold prices held their gains as traders monitored the war-induced threats to energy supply routes that risk stoking inflation and putting pressure on the Federal Reserve to increase interest rates. Bullion was trading at about $US4080 an ounce, after gaining almost 2 per cent the previous session. Northern Star Resources rose 3.5 per cent, while Evolution Mining jumped 4.3 per cent and Newmont added 3.5 per cent. Silver miner South32 climbed a further 4.6 per cent, adding to its 6.6 per cent rally on Tuesday. Related Video Video icon 0:24 Origin Energy investigating suspected cybersecurity breach The mining outlier on Wednesday morning was Lynas Rare Earths, which fell 3.6 per cent after the company revealed in a trading update a more than 10 per cent slump in the June quarter compared with a year ago in its output of NdPR, an important alloy blend of rare earths elements crucial for making the strong magnets that power traction motors used in electric cars and wind turbines. The slump was blamed on issues at the company’s new Mount Weld water recycling plants and ore concentrate quality issues.



While rising oil prices boosted energy stocks, the flip side is threatening a re-acceleration of inflation, which in turn could push the US Federal Reserve and other central banks to raise interest rates, slowing economies and undercutting stock prices. Real estate investment trusts, which tend to suffer when rising rates boost the returns of bonds, were trading lower, with warehouse and AI data centre owner Goodman Group down 2 per cent, Westfield shopping centres landlord Scentre down 1.5 per cent and Stockland down 1.9 per cent. Origin fell 1.9 per cent after the nation’s biggest energy retailer said it was investigating a potential security breach that may have resulted in unauthorised access to the personal details of some of its 4.7 million Australian customers. If confirmed, the attack would be one of the worst cyberattacks in recent Australian business history. Tech stocks gave back their gains from Tuesday, with software makers bearing the brunt of the losses. Xero, the nation’s biggest tech stock, lost 2.6 per cent. WiseTech fell 0.5 per cent after saying it bought a developer of AI-powered supply chain risk and compliance intelligence technology for $10 million and shares, and Technology One dropped 2.3 per cent. Wesfarmers lost 2.1 per cent after the conglomerate said it would spend between $645 million and $715 million to expand the Mount Holland lithium mine and concentrator with its partner Sociedad Quimica y Minera de Chile. It will pay for the investment using existing cash and debt facilities.



The big four banks were mixed. CBA was up 0.7 per cent, Westpac and ANZ Bank both edged up 0.1 per cent, but National Australia Bank slipped 0.1 per cent. Related Article Opinion

Media & marketing It’s News Corp v the ‘byte burglars’: Murdochs fire up in AI content battle Elizabeth Knight Business columnist On Wall Street overnight, the S&P 500 climbed 0.9 per cent. The Dow Jones added 385 points, or 0.7 per cent, and the Nasdaq composite rose 1.3 per cent. AI stocks once again were at the centre of the action, rising for a second straight day after tumbling the week before. After rocketing higher because of the boom in investment in AI chips and data centres, they’ve come under pressure in recent weeks on worries that they shot too high. Concerns are also weighing that investment in AI may fall off if it doesn’t produce as much profit as hoped.



Micron Technology jumped 12.2 per cent and added to its 1.9 per cent gain from the day before, coming off its 13.3 per cent drop from last week. Nvidia added 2 per cent. They were the two strongest forces lifting the S&P 500. On Wall Street, several stronger-than-expected profit reports from big companies also helped the market higher. 3M climbed 7.3 per cent after topping analysts’ expectations for both profit and revenue in the latest quarter. It also raised its forecast for profit over the full year of 2026. General Motors cruised 4.9 per cent higher after the vehicle maker’s profit for the latest quarter beat analysts’ expectations and CEO Mary Barra said demand in North America remains strong. Alphabet slid 1.5 per cent after Google released a trio of cheaper versions of its Gemini AI model, but shared no timing updates for the flagship Pro model that has already delayed its launch by several weeks. With AP, Reuters, Bloomberg The Market Recap newsletter is a wrap of the day’s trading. Get it each weekday afternoon.

World.title: Justin Hemmes’ $19m new Sydney precinct in doubt after RSL veterans block sale
World.content:
NationalNSWCommercial real estate Justin Hemmes’ $19m new Sydney precinct in doubt after RSL veterans block sale Harriet Alexander July 22, 2026 — 6:07pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Justin Hemmes’ $19 million purchase of a former Tattersalls Club building is in doubt after RSL members used a bureaucratic process to block the sale from proceeding, throwing into disarray his plans for a hospitality precinct at the base of Martin Place. Members of the Combined Services RSL sub-branch, whose trustees hold the title to the Barrack Street property, voted on Tuesday against the RSL custodian being appointed among the trustees to handle the proceeds of the sale, which was a precondition to the transaction proceeding. Justin Hemmes and the Barrack Street property in Sydney’s CBD. Artwork: Matt Willis Sub-branch member Nikhita Sahay said the building was the last RSL property in Sydney’s CBD and veterans did not want to see it disappear in a “flash sale”. “Once it’s lost, it’s gone forever,” Sahay said.



“It’s valuable to veterans of all generations because of its historical significance, and its location close to the Martin Place cenotaph and defence establishment precincts gives it strategic relevance.” But RSL NSW has insisted that the sale will proceed, and declared that the sub-branch was now in breach of its governance obligations. This “governance issue” would be considered at the next board meeting. Merivale’s Hemmes want the property to form part of a nightclub, restaurant, bar and hotel precinct in the western CBD. Dominic Lorrimer “A group of members voted against the custodian arrangement in the mistaken belief that a ‘no’ vote would stop the sale,” the spokesman said. “It cannot. The sub-branch and the purchaser contracted for the sale, and the sub-branch members and the RSL NSW Board approved it.”



Hemmes declined to comment on how the turbulence might affect his plans for a nightclub, restaurant, bar and hotel precinct in the western CBD, where he already owns the adjacent properties to the RSL’s building. He turned up in person to bid for the 341.5-square-metre property in May, and bought it for $19,000,001, a single dollar higher than the reserve. The dispute comes as the administrator for the City Tattersalls Club, which occupied the building until last year, announced that two of its other venues – the Castlereagh Club, World Gym and squash courts – were closed effectively immediately due to the “dire financial position” of the 130-year-old gentleman’s club. Administrator PKF told City Tattersalls members on Wednesday it would also apply to the NSW Supreme Court for instructions on how to wind up the club as it was an unincorporated association. A general meeting of the Combined Services RSL sub-branch was told in June that Tattersalls owed them nearly $300,000. Treasurer Alexander Ekert told the meeting that the sub-branch’s trustees terminated the lease with Tattersalls after discovering “significant issues” with the agreement. “The lease was not being [administered] in accordance with the terms, rent was not being charged at the appropriate rate, outstanding debts were accumulating and financial obligations were not being met,” Ekert told sub-branch members.



The trustees also learnt that the building and all the RSL memorabilia contained in it were not insured. After reviewing the overall situation, the trustees decided that the best option was to sell the club, Ekert said. Related Article Commercial real estate Justin Hemmes turns up, bids big, and buys himself a $19m club Sub-branch members voted 12-9 in favour of selling the building at a general meeting in March. However, some members claimed that they were not in favour of the sale but had not been able to vote as the meeting was scheduled on a workday and proxy or online voting were not available. They also claimed that a staff member who voted in favour of the sale was not eligible. They learnt later that the sale was conditional on RSL Custodian being appointed as trustee and raised that matter with RSL NSW lawyers, after which a motion to appoint the custodian was added to the July 21 meeting agenda. Members voted 18-16 against the motion, and two other motions that presupposed the sale going ahead were then dropped from the agenda. The meeting was told that the board would have to consider its next steps.



Combined Services RSL sub-branch president Bill Forsbey said the executive wanted to sell the Barrack Street property and move to another location in central Sydney. “We are a charity for veterans. That means our money goes to veterans, not into a rundown building,” Forsbey said. “For too long our sub-branch has been an office on the second floor of a tired old building. We want somewhere veterans can drop in, somewhere modern, warm, and welcoming, somewhere that feels like ours. If you served, we are here.”

World.title: Ex-Eels prodigy backs Luai signing as Bears table offer to Paulo
World.content:
Key points Ex-Eel Talagi says Luai will help Parramatta’s young halves

Panthers facing contract juggle with stars

Latrell Mitchell is battling to play again in 2026

Cameron Murray headlines mounting Rabbitohs injury toll

Panthers five-eighth and former Eels prodigy Blaize Talagi believes Jarome Luai could prove to be a $700,000 circuit breaker for his old club as the Perth Bears target Parramatta captain Junior Paulo to lead their forward pack. Talagi will line up against his old side on Thursday night in the No.6 jersey Luai wore in four premierships with Penrith. Luai’s 2027 shift to Parramatta has divided opinion since his one-year deal was confirmed last week. Loading Eels coach Jason Ryles defended the Luai signing – Wests Tigers will pay $500,000 of his salary – once again on Wednesday, as Perth stepped up their pursuit of 32-year-old Paulo. The Bears are prepared to offer Paulo a two-year deal after coach Mal Meninga met with the ex-NSW Origin prop. Parramatta have been in talks with Paulo about a one-year extension for some time, and he will now weigh up the added security of the Bears offer against moving his family to WA.



Meanwhile, Ryles insisted Luai’s 12-month pit stop before joining PNG in 2028 won’t undermine Parramatta’s development of playmakers such Lorenzo Talataina, Lincoln Fletcher (both 19) and Joash Papalii (22), and denied it points to a lack of long-term roster planning. Talagi has emerged as an unlikely ally in the debate around Parramatta’s roster, having knocked back a lucrative three-year Eels extension to join Penrith in 2024. Eels veteran Junior Paulo is weighing up an offer from the Bears. NRL Imagery Talagi played fullback, centre and off the bench in his debut season when Dylan Brown and Mitchell Moses were entrenched as Parramatta’s halves, albeit with contract options that allowed Newcastle to poach Brown with a record-breaking 10-year deal. Talagi stressed that playing alongside Nathan Cleary in the Panthers’ title-winning system was the driving factor behind leaving his junior club.



But having been mentored by Luai when playing in the halves for Samoa and touring the UK together, he said Luai’s short-term stint could work out perfectly for Parramatta’s next generation of playmakers. “I don’t see anything but good things coming from signing Romey for Parramatta to be honest, especially the younger guys coming up,” Talagai said. “He’s definitely someone who knows how to lead and lead with his actions, and his record speaks for itself. Blaize Talagi has backed Parramatta’s signing of Jarome Luai. Wolter Peeters “For me when I was at Parra, it was the biggest call of my life to leave, and the club was struggling at the time. “So moving to a club where I could tell there wouldn’t be all the focus on me, knowing there would be older guys, obviously someone like Nath to play alongside, that was a big attraction.



“I’ve matured a lot since I’ve been here. I think that’s just natural, but I also think it could have been very different if I’d stayed, too. Being a half in the NRL, there’s pressure that comes with that and I think timing of when you play first grade and how you develop is really important. “You’ve got to be properly prepared, and everyone develops at different times. Even when I first got here, there were no promises and I started in reserve grade. “It ended up being the best thing for me, it gave me extra time to adapt to how Penrith do things, so I don’t think anyone should get too disheartened as a young half.” Parramatta have high hopes for Talataina and Fletcher as long-term playmakers. But given they are both still teenagers, the pair are considered another 12 to 18 months away from being ready for the NRL. Ryles bristled at comparisons between the short-term deals of Luai and Broncos-bound half Jonah Pezet, who has been stuck in NSW Cup behind Ronald Volkman recentlt.



“Jonah’s an up-and-coming player who’s done a great apprenticeship and is on his path to being a seasoned first-grader, and Jarome is a four-time premiership winner,” Ryles said. Related Article Updated

NRL 2026 Joey Manu’s $1.6m contract call signals latest shift in cross-code talent stoush “So there’s a little bit of a difference there. I don’t apologise for anything that we’ve done … Is there a fear of [upsetting other players]? No, there isn’t, because we’re sitting in a spot on the ladder that we don’t want to be. “It’s no one’s fault directly, but we need more experienced players. Jarome fits that bill at the moment. “We have got younger players that are coming through our pathways and our system that may be ready in 12 months.



“But this gives them an extra bit of time to give them their reps in [NSW] Cup and learn off a true pro that’s won a lot of premierships.” Penrith typically pause contract talk to win titles. Will this year be any different? Dan Walsh Ivan Cleary remains unfazed by Penrith’s multimillion-dollar roster juggle revolving around the future of his son and superstar halfback Nathan ahead of a critical few weeks before the club traditionally pauses contract talks to win premierships. Penrith’s 2027 off-contract list has dominated rugby league’s rumour mill all year, with Nathan Cleary’s next contract move key to the Panthers salary cap and 10 NRL squad members who will become free agents if they are still unsigned come November 1.



Cleary was front-page news of The Daily Telegraph on Monday, which declared the game’s best player would test the market. Nathan Cleary’s future has been a talking point all season. Tertius Pickard Sources speaking on the condition of anonymity due to the confidential nature of discussions have told this masthead he is yet to decide whether he goes to November 1, and that he will begin giving his future genuine consideration after Thursday’s clash with Parramatta. Father Ivan said he didn’t know when asked on Tuesday if Cleary planned to test the market, and said he couldn’t “remember the last time” he spoke to his son about his contractual future. Ivan announced mid-year that 2027 will be his last season as head coach, with assistant Peter Wallace anointed as his successor.



The Panthers remain confident a long-term extension can be sorted for their prize-winning No.7 to keep Cleary from entertaining rival offers. The club first discussed a new deal with his management at the start of the season and have continued to negotiate with the rest of their roster in the background. Further talks are scheduled with star front-rower Moses Leota after he was recently granted a brief window to negotiate with rival clubs for 2028 and beyond. Underrated hooker Mitch Kenny was the first off-contract Panther to recommit to the club on a lucrative four-year deal last week. Throughout Penrith’s run to four straight premierships, the club typically paused contract talks leading into the end of the regular season and finals to avoid off-field distractions. No hard and fast rule enforced the policy, but a similar stance looms once another few weeks of negotiations take place, and there is further clarity on Cleary’s future.



The Panthers have suffered three of their four losses this season in the past five weeks, but have most importantly come through the Origin period unscathed. Kenny is their only top-line player sidelined through injury, though a return date from his badly broken leg is still unknown. Focus on the club’s retention’s fight has intensified since Cleary, Isaah Yeo, Liam Martin and Brian To’o’s NSW Origin commitments wrapped up, but Ivan Cleary said contract talk hadn’t proved any more a distraction than previous years. “It is in the background,” Cleary said. “Obviously our GM Shane Elford’s done a lot of work in the background all year, because ideally we don’t want [players] to go to market, but we respect if they do.



“I don’t think it’s a distraction any more than any other time…I’m confident it’ll work out the way it’s meant to work out for all of them. I feel pretty confident that we’ll get our share of wins there, and if we don’t, then it won’t be through lack of trying.” Luckless Latrell to see specialist for ‘complex nerve damage’ Adrian Proszenko Latrell Mitchell may have played his last game in 2026, with the South Sydney superstar consulting a neurologist for treatment on “complex nerve damage” in a desperate bid to return to the field this year. Mitchell’s prognosis is one half of a double blow for the Rabbitohs, with captain Cameron Murray also sidelined for up to a month with a calf injury he suffered in the loss to Canberra. The pair are the highest-paid members of the playing squad and represent about $2 million of talent unavailable to coach Wayne Bennett in the run to the finals.



Latrell Mitchell is struggling to get back on the field in 2026. Getty Mitchell’s scheduled return from a back injury last month was aborted after he tore his calf in training. It was hoped Mitchell could be fit for the round-23 clash against Parramatta on August 8, but it’s increasingly likely he has played his last game for the season. This masthead broke the news of Mitchell’s diagnosis on Tuesday, with the club providing a further update later in the day. “Centre Latrell Mitchell has undergone further investigations and consultation with a specialist neurologist last week,” the club statement said. “Mitchell is trying to overcome complex nerve damage that initially created complications with a lower back injury, and now a calf issue in his left leg. Mitchell will remain a week-to-week proposition as to a return to the field of play.”



Cameron Murray and Latrell Mitchell, Souths’ highest-paid players, are due for more time on the sidelines. In further bad injury news, centre Tallis Duncan has sustained a hamstring strain that will sideline him for two to three weeks. Latrell Siegwalt will replace Duncan for Friday’s clash against the Storm at Accor Stadium, while Lachlan Hubner comes in at lock for Murray. “Trelly is doing good, he obviously wants to be out there with the boys,” Souths centre Jack Wighton said of Mitchell. “He’s a presence we’re missing, he’s an awesome player to have on the field with you. He just gives you that confidence and belief. The quicker we can have him back, the better. We can’t wait to have him back, we love big Trell.” Murray and Mitchell are part of an already bulging casualty ward that includes Sean Keppie (thumb, expected return round 23), Dayne Jennings, (knee, TBC) Adam Elliott (ankle, season) and Talanoa Penitani (hamstring, round 26).



Murray’s teammates acknowledged the significance of his absence, but believed the team would be able to cover for him. “Huge [loss]. Any team that Cam Murray is playing in, he has a massive positive impact on how they play,” Campbell Graham said. “We are obviously no different. He’s our captain, he’s our leader and he’s one of those blokes who gives you confidence when you’re running out there with him. “He’s a loss for us over the next few weeks or so, whatever it is. As I said before, it takes an NRL squad to do something in this competition and we believe we’ve got the depth. Latrell Mitchell injured his calf in training last month as he attempted to return from a back injury. Steven Siewert



“The boys have filled that position before and done the job for us. We’re still confident we can steer the ship while he’s out and hopefully we’re in a good position when he’s back ready to play.”

Junior Tatola added: “It’s obviously a big loss for us, he does a lot of work. “He’s great to be next to and play with. It’s a big loss, but we have got boys in there that can step up to the plate and do the same job as what came does as well.” Related Article NRL 2026 ‘It’s people’s jobs’: Dragons take aim at costly refereeing calls In other team news, Canterbury have named Stephen Crichton to make his return at five-eighth, pushing fill-in Sean O’Sullivan onto an extended bench. Manly have named Lehi Hopoate as the fullback replacement for Tom Trbojevic, while the Storm welcome back Jarome Hughes after the halfback missed one game with a hamstring injury.

World.content:
NationalQueenslandRoad to Brisbane 2032 First look: Design of Brisbane Olympics aquatic centre revealed Jessica Millward and and Dominique Tassell July 22, 2026 — 6:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The first official render of the National Aquatic Centre for the Brisbane Olympics has been unveiled. ARM Architecture and NH Architecture, in partnership with Queensland’s Arkhefield, will help deliver the Spring Hill centre on the edge of Victoria Park. As this masthead revealed two weeks ago, the Centenary Pool Complex will be handed over to the Games Independent Infrastructure and Coordination Authority by Brisbane City Council on September 1. A render of the new National Aquatic Centre, to be built at the Centenary Pool site in Spring Hill for the Brisbane 2032 Olympic Games. The construction timeline for the National Aquatic Centre has not been confirmed, but August 30 will be the existing pool’s last day of operation.



Related Article Brisbane 2032 Olympics Centenary Pool to be closed and handed over to Games authority within weeks Deputy Premier Jarrod Bleijie would not confirm on Wednesday whether the venue’s capacity would be downgraded from the planned 25,000 to save money, after Australian Financial Review reporting this week that ARM had been asked to scale back the centre to manage costs. “GIICA [is] required to go through all that at the moment and the budget [for all Games venues] is $7.1 billion, and they’re required to deliver those projects within budget,” Bleijie said. “Capacity has been detailed in the delivery plan, but ... we are going through a process with GIICA at the moment for all the venues, and we did ask them to look at the costings. “When you appoint architects and designers, they have to do it within budget, and we’ve been abundantly clear on that.”



The render does not include how the heritage-listed elements of the site will be handled, and Premier David Crisafulli has previously refused to address whether the current complex will be demolished. It is unclear if, or how, the heritage-listed elements of the site will be incorporated into the site plan. Dominique Tassell Bleijie confirmed on Wednesday that affected tenants would be compensated, but said when and how much was a matter for Brisbane City Council. Tenants at the site have still not received official confirmation of their eviction date, and have not been informed about compensation. World.title: Brown-and-gold bonanza: Gun Hawks forward recommits to form star tandem with Ben King
World.content:
Exclusive SportAFLAFL 2026 Brown-and-gold bonanza: Gun Hawks forward recommits to form star tandem with Ben King Sam McClure Updated July 22, 2026 — 5:56pm ,first published July 21, 2026 — 8:25pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Mitch Lewis is set to line up alongside Ben King in brown and gold next year, knocking back interest from other clubs to recommit to Hawthorn despite the recruitment of another key forward. Clubs such as Collingwood had hoped that Hawthorn’s pursuit of King could’ve persuaded Lewis to have his head turned by rival offers. But two competition sources with knowledge of the situation, speaking anonymously, have confirmed the 27-year-old has told the club he will stay with the two parties putting the final touches on a long-term deal. Not going anywhere: Mitch Lewis is set to stay put at Hawthorn. Getty Images Hawthorn’s list management believes Lewis – an athletic marking forward – can play further up the ground, which would allow King to lead out of the goal square. Sam Mitchell and his team will now work on luring at least one star midfielder from an opposition team to kick to King and Lewis, with Essendon’s Zach Merrett and Gold Coast’s Bailey Humphrey firmly in their sights.



Merrett will almost certainly get his wish a second time around – barring the Bombers playing hardball again – while the contracted Humphrey is also being aggressively hunted by Steven King and the Demons. Lewis’ recommitment comes as Ben King is poised to complete one of the most dramatic contract backflips in recent AFL history, with the Suns spearhead set to reject their lucrative long-term offer and instead nominate Hawthorn as his preferred destination for 2027. The stunning change of heart comes barely two months after King told The Age he intended to remain on the Gold Coast, insisting he loved the club and saw his future in Queensland. Ben King wants to play for Hawthorn next season. AFL Photos But three industry sources, speaking on the condition of anonymity because discussions remain confidential, have confirmed King’s position has shifted significantly in recent weeks, with Hawthorn now firmly in the box seat to secure one of the competition’s premier key forwards.



Related Article AFL 2026 ‘If you’re out there, Bobby’: McRae’s public plea to premiership star King’s contract at Hawthorn is expected to be a six-year deal, taking him until the end of 2032. Gold Coast have not yet officially been told of his intention to leave. King will be in Melbourne this week ahead of the Suns’ game against Carlton at Marvel Stadium on Saturday. The decision is a bitter blow for the Suns, who had been confident they would retain the 26-year-old despite intense Victorian interest. Several factors have contributed to King’s dramatic reversal.



His partner is keen to return home to Victoria, while Gold Coast’s alarming on-field slide has also weighed heavily. The Suns have now lost eight consecutive matches after appearing well-placed to challenge for a second-consecutive finals campaign earlier this season. King’s own form has only enhanced his value. The powerful key forward sits second in the Coleman Medal race and has established himself as one of the AFL’s most reliable goalkickers, kicking at least 40 goals in every completed season since 2021. Last year he produced a career-best campaign with 71 goals, underlining why Hawthorn have been prepared to aggressively pursue his signature. How the trade period plays out is yet to be determined.



As King is a restricted free agent, Gold Coast have the power to match the bid and force a trade. But given the Suns’ disastrous form slump has now landed them 14th on the ladder, the Queensland club could opt to accept first-round compensation, which, if the season finished now, would be pick No.6. Editor's pick AFL 2026 Hawthorn want Ben King and Zach Merrett. This is how Gold Coast losses help their cause The Hawks would much prefer to land King without a trade, given they are also in the box seat to land Merrett, who will once again request a move to Hawthorn despite a failed attempt last year. For the Hawks, landing King would represent another significant statement of intent as the club continues to build a list capable of challenging for premierships over the coming years. The Hawks have invested heavily in assembling one of the AFL’s youngest and most exciting lists under Mitchell, and adding a proven goal-kicking machine entering the prime of his career would significantly strengthen their premiership credentials.



Related Article Analysis

AFL 2026 How the Pies can avoid wildcard round, as we rate every team’s run home The Suns have long viewed King as a cornerstone of their future, but after months of confidence they would secure his signature, they are now confronting the prospect of watching one of the competition’s elite key forwards walk out the door. If it results in a move, King’s decision would rank among the most extraordinary contract reversals in recent AFL memory – a player who only weeks ago expected to stay, now preparing to head home to Victoria and reshape the landscape of the upcoming trade period. King’s management has been contacted for comment. Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.

World.title: True-crime sleuth struck up friendship with suspect in ‘reckless’ bid to solve cold case
World.content:
NationalQueenslandCourts True-crime sleuth struck up friendship with suspect in ‘reckless’ bid to solve cold case Rex Martinich July 22, 2026 — 5:27pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A woman obsessed with true-crime podcasts and a teenage girl’s murder started a relationship with a suspect in a bid to solve the cold case, a coroner has heard. The woman spoke of her “reckless” plan on Wednesday, when the long-running inquest into 15-year-old Annette Mason’s murder resumed for a one-day hearing in Brisbane. Annette was bludgeoned to death in a house she shared with friends in Toowoomba, west of Brisbane, in November 1989. Annette Mason’s older sister, Linda, in 2015, amid a push by the family for a coronial inquest into the teen’s murder. Fairfax Media No one has been charged over her death.



The inquest heard the woman, who cannot be named for legal reasons, contacted police claiming to have new evidence in 2025. She claimed a suspect told her previously undisclosed details about the brutal murder while they were living together. The woman consumed podcast episodes and news stories about the cold case before seeking out a suspect, Queensland coroner Terry Ryan heard. “It was a friendship that sort of just went into a relationship,” the woman said. Under questioning by Mason family barrister Clem van der Weegen, the woman agreed she was “trying to solve this murder” herself when she sought out the suspect.



Annette Mason was bludgeoned to death in a house she shared with friends in Toowoomba, west of Brisbane, in November 1989. “Yeah, I was just so reckless,” she said. “Today, sitting here, I’m proud of what I have done. “I know that it is a big risk, and I know my life could have been ended any time, but I just took it in my own hands.” Annette’s body was discovered in her bed, with the cause of death found to be blunt-force trauma to her head, inflicted by a piece of timber found in the laundry.



The woman testified she talked about Annette with the male suspect, who cannot be identified for legal reasons. Related Article Inquest Suspect in 15-year-old girl’s murder denies previous ‘confessions’ “He kept calling her ‘she’. He said she was bashed before she got to the house,” the woman said. “Then she was hit around the head.” The man had previously claimed to be innocent, Ryan heard.



“He said it was a copper that had killed her. He said, ‘That’s why all the evidence went missing and they’re just trying to put the blame on me’,” the woman said. When asked what impact the suspect’s alleged words had on her, she said: “Clearly, he had killed Annette Mason. He had done that.” The woman denied her claims were based on details previously available in podcasts and news stories. The suspect also gave evidence at Wednesday’s hearing, which was attended by Annette’s mother and siblings, who were wearing T-shirts printed with her image. He described the true-crime-obsessed woman as a “nutcase”, and testified they had only been friends.



The suspect said the woman’s claims were “absolutely not” true, and he “would not have a clue” why she made them. “She was good to hang around with – a good friend,” he said. The inquest into Annette’s death was initially closed in 1991 only to be reopened in 2018 after pressure from her family. Hearings were last held in 2022. The inquest will spend the next several months receiving written submissions. AAP

World.title: ‘Russian Amazon’ hit by more massive Ukrainian strikes
World.content:
WorldEuropeRussia-Ukraine war ‘Russian Amazon’ hit by more massive Ukrainian strikes Reuters July 22, 2026 — 5:20pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Moscow: Another attack on the warehouses of Russia’s largest online retailer, Wildberries, has injured several people, the head and co-founder of the company has said. The attacks on a company so central to the consumer economy appear to mark a widening of Kyiv’s strategy of using long-range drones to disrupt Russia’s war effort and pressure the Kremlin to make peace. Wildberries head Tatyana Kim said on Wednesday that the warehouses in Krasnodar and Nevinnomyssk had been attacked. Social media footage, verified by Reuters, showed a huge plume of smoke rising into the air in Krasnodar. Local authorities said one worker had been killed in another southern city, Armavir, when drone debris fell on one of the enterprises.



Krasnodar ​regional governor Veniamin Kondratiev said 10 people had been wounded in an attack on a storage complex. Drone debris has damaged two high-rise apartments in Krasnodar, where no one was injured. Authorities said a helicopter would be deployed to tackle the fire at the warehouse in Krasnodar. More than a hundred people have been engaged in efforts to combat the fire. Residents walk among debris following Russia’s missile attack in Kyiv on Sunday. AP Photo/Efrem Lukatsky A strike by Ukrainian drones on Saturday killed eight workers, sparked fires and disrupted operations at Wildberries. “There are no words to describe all the feelings and emotions caused by the attacks on ordinary people, on our employees, on all of us who are simply doing our jobs,” Kim said in a post on the Telegram messaging app.



Ukraine has not commented on recent attacks. Wildberries started as an online shop reselling apparel from European catalogues. It has since expanded its product range and evolved into a marketplace that includes third-party vendors. Wildberries has not commented on the scale of the damage. Ukraine has stepped up strikes on Russia’s infrastructure, including oil refineries, described by Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky as “long-range sanctions”. X Online sales across Russia rose 28 per cent in 2025 to 11.5 trillion roubles ($210 billion), according to the Association of Internet Trade Companies. Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak said sales of goods and services on digital platforms equated to about 8.5 per cent of GDP.



In a separate development, Russia is no longer willing to return some occupied territories to Ukraine as part of any deal to end the war and plans to retain them as buffer zones, according to people close to the Kremlin. Russian President Vladimir Putin remains committed to taking full control of Ukraine’s eastern Donetsk region by force and would now retain areas of Sumy and Kharkiv regions near the border with Russia as buffer zones, three people said, asking not to be identified discussing sensitive issues. Putin had abandoned territorial concessions because Russia viewed increasingly confrontational statements from the US as evidence that informal understandings reached at his Alaska summit with US President Donald Trump had collapsed, the people said. Related Article Russia-Ukraine war How dodging drones and death became daily life in eastern Ukraine While the US insists no deal to end Russia’s war in Ukraine was reached at the summit last August, Kremlin officials have repeatedly asserted that a package of undertakings existed under a so-called “spirit of Anchorage” agreement between Putin and Trump.



They included pressing Ukraine to surrender territory in its eastern Donetsk region in return for Russia handing back occupied areas of the northern Sumy and north-eastern Kharkiv regions. The Kremlin has hardened its position amid escalating Ukrainian strikes deep inside Russia, including on Moscow, that have damaged oil refineries and sparked a nationwide fuel shortage. Trump also backed a new sanctions bill championed by the late senator Lindsey Graham that would target the top five purchasers of Russian oil and gas with tariff rates of as much as 100 per cent. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov didn’t respond to a request for comment. Reuters, Bloomberg
